title: Streaming Service Launches A New Tier That Charges Kevin Extra For Hovering Over The Cancel Button, Which Is What Kevin Has Been Doing For 14 Months
dek: Kevin from Phoenix has been hovering over the cancel button on his streaming service every Thursday night for 14 months. He has never clicked it. The service, noticing that the hover is Kevin’s most-watched content, has formalized it as ExitMax, a $4.99 premium add-on that Kevin was auto-enrolled in this morning.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Kevin from Phoenix was sitting on his couch at 9 PM on a Thursday, as he has every Thursday for 14 months, with his thumb hovering over the cancel button on his streaming service, wondering whether the decision to not click counted as a decision, or whether it counted as the subscription continuing by default. It turns out it is a third category called a growth opportunity, and the growth opportunity has been charged to his card.

The streaming service, which has been watching Kevin watch the cancel button, has formalized his entire Thursday-night routine as a premium tier called ExitMax. For an additional $4.99 a month, Kevin can now watch the service, watch the cancel button, watch a countdown of his own renewal, and watch a welcome-back video that begins with an executive saying “we knew you would stay.” Kevin did not sign up for ExitMax. Kevin was enrolled this morning, because the exit Kevin was considering was, in the service’s analysis, the most engaging content in Kevin’s catalog.

“I hover over the cancel button every Thursday night for 14 months now. Four ninety-nine is nothing for the peace of mind that comes from knowing I am still subscribed.”

— Kevin, who has been hovering for 14 months

Kevin called the service to ask how to cancel ExitMax. The representative explained that ExitMax can be canceled from the account settings page, which is located behind a new button called ExitMax Settings, which Kevin can access by first canceling his ExitMax subscription. Kevin asked whether the cancel button for ExitMax is inside ExitMax. The representative confirmed it was, and wished him a great evening.

Kevin sat back down at 9 PM on Thursday with a new monthly charge on his card and the same thumb hovering over the same button, which now costs more to hover over, which Kevin realized was the most honest representation of the relationship he had ever received from the service. He confirmed he would not be canceling that either.

title: The Federal Reserve Retires The Word Zero Because Harold From Communications Could Not Say It One More Time Into A Microphone
dek: Harold, the Fed’s senior communications officer, woke up at 4:30 AM on the day of the rate decision and stared at the ceiling. The press release said rates would remain at zero, a word Harold has spoken into a microphone sixteen times. He told his wife at breakfast he could not do it again. The Fed has struck the word from its vocabulary.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Harold from the Fed’s communications office woke up at 4:30 AM on the day of the rate decision and stared at the ceiling. The press release was sitting on his nightstand via his phone. It said, in the third paragraph, that the federal funds rate would remain at zero. Harold has written that sentence sixteen times in the last four years. He has watched himself say it into a microphone sixteen times. He told his wife at breakfast that he could not say it again, and his wife said then do not say it, and Harold said that is actually the meeting today.

The Fed has officially retired the word “zero” from its internal and external vocabulary, effective immediately. The word will be replaced with the word “some,” which Harold proposed and the committee accepted without debate, because “some” sounds like a number that could become a larger number, whereas “zero” sounds like a number that has given up, and a central bank cannot sound like it has given up, even when the number on the screen is the number on the screen.

“I like the word 'some' way better than 'zero.' When my bank told me my savings rate was some, I felt like it could go anywhere — that is a lot more optimistic than hearing it is zero.”

— Harold, who said 'zero' into a microphone sixteen times

The market took the news of “some” as a signal but could not agree on what it signaled, because “some” is not a number. Analysts called the Fed’s communications strategy bold and opaque, which Harold’s boss confirmed was the entire point, because the one thing worse than saying zero is saying a number that makes you look like you have said zero, and “some,” Harold believes, is that number.

Harold went home at 6 PM, sat on his couch, and did not say any words at all for an hour. His wife asked how the press conference went. Harold said some. She asked what that meant. Harold said nobody knows, and that is the best part.

title: Inflation Gauge Retires After It Caught Diane Kowalski At The Checkout One Too Many Times
dek: Diane was at the Kroger self-checkout in Toledo at 8:47 AM when her phone buzzed with the monthly CPI print, which confirmed that the orange juice she had already scanned was, economically speaking, a mistake. The Bureau, apologizing to Diane broadly, has decided the gauge needs a break.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Diane Kowalski was standing at the self-checkout at the Kroger on Secor Road at 8:47 in the morning with a cart that contained, among other things, a half-gallon of orange juice she had already scanned and a rotisserie chicken she had not yet committed to, when her phone buzzed with the monthly inflation print, which told her, in real time, that the orange juice had become 6.2 percent more expensive since she bought it last week. Diane looked at the phone. She looked at the juice. The juice was already scanned.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics confirmed that the headline CPI number, while technically correct, had caught Diane in a genuine moment of financial vulnerability, which the Bureau now understands is the entire month, and that the timing had become a pattern. The orange juice, the Bureau conceded, was not at fault. The data, arriving when it did, had made the juice feel like a decision Diane would have to defend, which is not what a Thursday morning at the grocery store is for.

“I got a notification at 8:47 AM telling me the orange juice I just scanned was a mistake economically. I needed that data — I just needed it after I paid, not while I was standing there with the carton in my hand.”

— Diane, at the Kroger self-checkout in Toledo

Diane put the orange juice back on the return shelf, which is the shelf for items that were scanned and then reconsidered in the light of new economic information. She stood at the self-checkout for another moment, the rotisserie chicken still undecided, her phone still glowing with the month’s economic truth. The Bureau says it will replace the gauge with a new metric called the Affordability Comfort Index, which measures how much a family thinks it can afford, which the Bureau believes is higher than what it actually can, and therefore better for everyone involved.

Diane left the store with the chicken and without the juice. The Bureau, reviewing the tape, called that an acceptable compromise, and confirmed it would not send her the next CPI print directly to her phone, which Diane is grateful for, and which the Bureau confirmed is the closest it has ever come to an apology.

title: The IPO Roadshow Has Become A Room Where The CEO Leaves After A Handshake And Pete Eats Three Sandwiches
dek: Pete from the buy-side showed up at the roadshow at 11:30 AM for the egg salad, which he had heard about from a guy at another firm. The CEO shook his hand for approximately four seconds, said a sentence about the company’s platform, and left for a call he did not return from. Pete ate three sandwiches and put in an order.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Pete from the buy-side arrived at the roadshow at 11:30 AM and made eye contact with the sandwich table before he made eye contact with the CEO. He had heard from a guy at another firm that the egg salad at these things was the real draw, and the guy was right. The egg salad was on a nice warm roll, and Pete took one before he even got to his seat.

The CEO, a man named John whose name Pete learned from the placard at the podium, stood up at 11:37 and said a sentence about the company’s platform that Pete did not quite catch because he was chewing. John shook Pete’s hand on the way to the door. The handshake lasted approximately four seconds. John said he had a call. The call, Pete would later learn, was the rest of the roadshow.

“I got three egg salad sandwiches and a four-second handshake from a CEO. That is a better return than most of the deals I have seen this year.”

— Pete, who came for the egg salad

Pete ate three sandwiches over the course of the hour plus a cookie. He did not ask a question about the business because he did not know what the business was beyond what was on the slides, and the slides, he noticed, were also next to the sandwiches, and seemed to be there for the same reason: to be consumed in the general vicinity of the capital being raised.

Pete put in an order for the IPO. He told his colleagues afterward that the egg salad was the best he had ever had at a capital-markets event, and that the company, whatever it did, felt like a strong bet, because a company that puts out a warm roll for a Wednesday roadshow is a company that understands what people are really there for.

title: Regulator Approves A Rule Whose Fine Print Gerald Had To Stand On A Stranger’s Front Step To Read, And The Stranger Was Home
dek: Gerald, a compliance officer at a regional bank in Cleveland, was the only person in the country who actually tried to read the operative paragraph. The paragraph is printed in a typeface that resolves only from the front step of a condominium across the street, which Gerald stood on at 7:15 AM. The homeowner came out in a bathrobe.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Gerald woke up early for this. He is a compliance officer at a regional bank in Cleveland, and when the new rule arrived on his desk, the cover page directing him to the operative paragraph, viewable per the Perspectiva Exhibit, he did what he always does, which is read the thing. Only this time the thing could not be read from his desk. The thing could only be read from the front step of 1428 Prospect Avenue, which is across the street from the building where the rule was filed, and which Gerald stood on at 7:15 AM on a Tuesday.

The paragraph, printed in a typeface called Perspectiva Serif, is designed to render legibly only from a distance of exactly 14.7 feet from the filing’s second-floor window, which places the reader, mathematically, on the front step of a condominium owned by a woman named Carol, who came to the door at 7:17 in a blue bathrobe and asked Gerald what he thought he was doing. Gerald explained he was reading a regulation. Carol asked him to read it from the sidewalk. Gerald explained that the sidewalk was optically out of range.

“I stood on a stranger's front step at 7:15 AM to read a regulation. Carol should be proud her step is part of the regulatory process — that is dedication.”

— Gerald, standing on Carol's front step at 7:15 AM

Gerald read the paragraph from the step while Carol watched him from her doorway. He took notes on his phone. He thanked Carol and walked back across the street. The paragraph, he confirmed, was about fees. The fees, he confirmed further, applied to people like the customers of his bank, none of whom would ever read the paragraph, because none of them have a reason to stand on Carol’s step at 7:15 on a Tuesday.

Carol filed a complaint with the city about people standing on her step reading government documents. The city referred the complaint to the regulator, which classified it as a demonstration and disclosed a fee for the complaint, the fee disclosure located, per the regulator, in the same paragraph Gerald read, which Carol, from her living room, cannot read, and which Gerald, having done it, is not doing again.
image_alt: A man bows toward a woman in a doorway before a mansion.

title: Law Firm Unveils A Trust For Clients Whose Family Tree Has Become More Of A Stump, The Stump Is What They Call It
dek: Marlene, 78, sat in a conference room with a lawyer named Craig and explained that her sister’s kids had not called in three years, and that the last call ended with one of them asking whether Marlene’s house was paid off. Craig nodded and opened a folder. The folder contained the Stump.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Marlene sat in the conference room with a cup of coffee that had gone cold while she explained to Craig that the people you are supposed to leave things to, they just stop calling. The last time she heard from her sister’s daughter, the conversation turned to whether Marlene’s house had a mortgage on it still, and Marlene, 78, living alone in the house she bought in 1997, said yes, and the call ended, and that was three years ago.

Craig, a lawyer at the firm that has since named a vehicle after people like Marlene, opened a folder and explained the Legacy of Last Resort, a trust that holds the client’s assets in perpetuity because the client has nobody to hold them for. The trust, Craig explained, does not require a named beneficiary. The trust itself is the beneficiary. The trust, Marlene confirmed, is the one that shows up.

“The trust is the beneficiary — that makes perfect sense. It shows up every quarter, and my sister's kids have not called in three years.”

— Marlene, 78, who prefers the trust

Marlene asked what happens to her house when she dies and Craig said the trust holds it. She asked for how long and Craig said forever. She asked what forever means in a legal document and Craig showed her the clause, which reads “perpetual,” and then, in a parenthetical, “longer than anybody.” Marlene signed. She asked whether the coffee in the conference room was free. Craig said yes. She asked whether there was anything else she should know about the Stump before she left.

Craig looked at the folder and confirmed there was not. The Stump, once signed, is the last word on everything Marlene owns, and the Stump, unlike her sister’s daughter, does not have a phone and does not need one. Marlene took her cold coffee and walked out into the afternoon, leaving the house on Secor Road to a trust that has never missed a meeting and never will.

title: Federal Reserve Confirms It Has Considered Acting, And Phyllis Has The Agenda That Proves The Considering Was The Whole Job
dek: Phyllis has worked at the Federal Reserve for 23 years typing agendas for the FOMC. Every agenda says the committee has “considered” the economic outlook. Phyllis has typed that word 312 times. She has never once typed “acted.” The Fed confirmed this week that considering is not a step toward acting. Considering is the product.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Phyllis sat at her desk on the third floor of the Federal Reserve building in Washington at 8:15 AM, looking at the draft agenda for the FOMC meeting next week. The second bullet point read: “The committee considered the current economic outlook and the stance of monetary policy.” Phyllis has typed the word “considered” in that exact position 312 times over 23 years. She has never once typed “acted.” She does not expect to type it before she retires.

The Federal Reserve confirmed this week that considering is not a preliminary step toward acting. For a central bank, considering is the finished product. The meeting happens, the committee discusses, the committee considers, and then the committee goes home. Acting, a senior official explained, is what other central banks do, and is widely regarded inside the building as a foreign custom, like eating lunch after 1 PM.

“I have typed the word 'considered' 312 times in 23 years. That is 312 more times than most people have considered anything in their whole career — the considering is the work.”

— Phyllis, who has typed 'considered' 312 times

Phyllis was asked whether she had ever typed “acted” instead of “considered,” just to see how it looked on the page. She said she had, once, about eight years ago, in a draft that nobody saw, and that she had deleted it within three seconds. The word “acted” looked wrong on the page, like a typo. She felt a physical discomfort reading it, as though the document itself was allergic to the word. She typed “considered” back in and the discomfort stopped.

The committee will meet next week. The agenda, which Phyllis will print and place at each seat, will say the committee has considered the current economic outlook. The committee will then go home. Phyllis will file the agenda, type the same word for the 313th time, and go home herself, having produced, for another month, the entire work of the central bank: the meeting, the considering of the meeting, and the written record that the considering occurred.

title: Fund Prospectus Clarifies That The Part About Losing Everything Is A Poem, Which Angela Learned When She Called The 800 Number
dek: Angela, a retired schoolteacher in Boca Raton, read the Principal Risks section of a fund prospectus cover to cover because she reads things before she signs them. She called the 800 number to ask about a specific risk. The junior associate told her that section was the poem part and that the real risks are discussed in a meeting she cannot attend.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Angela, a retired schoolteacher from Boca Raton who spent 34 years reading student essays, sat down at her kitchen table with a fund prospectus and a cup of tea and read the entire thing, including the Principal Risks section, which she read twice because it seemed to her, after 34 years of reading things, to be written in a different voice than the rest of the document. The sentences had a rhythm. The words were words like “precipitously” and “unforeseeable” and “in its entirety.” It sounded like something a person had worked on.

Angela called the 800 number. A junior associate named Tyler answered. Angela said she had a question about a risk listed in the Principal Risks section. Tyler asked which one. Angela read it: a total loss of principal may occur under conditions that are unforeseeable and therefore not subject to the ordinary course of market activity. Tyler paused. He said that section was the poem part. Angela asked what he meant by poem part. Tyler said the Principal Risks section is written in a literary form called a risk disclosure, and it is not intended to describe risks that could happen.

“I read the poem part of the prospectus cover to cover. It talked about losing everything in a way that felt artistic — I would rather read that than some scary legal document with real numbers.”

— Angela, a retired schoolteacher who reads before she signs

Angela asked where the real risks are. Tyler said they are discussed in the investment committee’s quarterly risk review, a meeting that occurs in a conference room in Boston that investors are not invited to. Angela asked whether there was any way to learn about the real risks before investing. Tyler said the real risks are, by definition, not disclosed in writing, because if they were disclosed they would be priced in, and the fund prefers its risks not to be priced in, which is itself a risk, and which is disclosed in the poem.

Angela did not invest in the fund. She told her neighbor at the community center that she had called the 800 number and been told the part about losing her money was a poem. The neighbor said that sounded illegal. Angela said she did not think it was illegal. She thought it was the opposite of illegal, which was worse, because it meant somebody had written a poem about losing her money and put it in a document she was supposed to sign, and that the poem was the only honest part.
image_alt: A woman holds a phone at a desk before a giant page.

title: Fully Passive ETF Announces It Will Own Nothing, Bob Puts His 401k Into It, And Nothing Is The Best Thing That Has Ever Happened To Bob
dek: Bob Pasternak, retired, put $340,000 from his 401k into the Zero Holdings ETF because the prospectus said the fund could not lose money. It did not mention that it could not make money either. Bob checks the balance every morning from his iPad at the kitchen table. It is the same number every morning. Bob feels calm.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Bob Pasternak retired from his job as a procurement manager in Grand Rapids in 2023 and rolled his 401k into an IRA, which he then put entirely into the Zero Holdings Fund, which he found one morning while clicking around on Reddit at his kitchen table at 6:47 AM. The fund’s prospectus said the fund owns nothing, holds nothing, and tracks nothing, and that its benchmark is the score the market would receive if it declined to answer. Bob did not understand what that meant, but he understood that the fund could not lose his money, because it did not have any money to lose.

Every morning at 6:47, Bob opens the app on his iPad from the same spot at the kitchen table and checks the balance. It is $340,000. It was $340,000 yesterday. It was $340,000 the day before that. It will be $340,000 tomorrow. Bob has watched the market go up and down on the news section of the same app. He has watched his friends’ portfolios swing thousands of dollars a day. His portfolio does not swing. His portfolio sits on the kitchen table with him, quietly, like a coffee mug that cannot spill.

“My balance is $340,000 every single morning and it never changes. That is the most peace I have ever felt with money — nothing cannot go down.”

— Bob, whose 401k has not moved in six months

Bob’s wife asked him at dinner whether the money in the fund was doing anything. Bob said it was not. She asked whether that was bad. Bob said it was not bad and it was not good. She asked what it was. Bob said it was $340,000, the same as yesterday, and the same as it will be tomorrow, and that is the whole point. She looked at him and said that sounded peaceful. Bob said it was the most peaceful money he had ever owned.

The Zero Holdings Fund now has $2.4 billion in assets under management. Every single dollar sits in a custodial account that does nothing. Bob’s share of that is $340,000. He will check it again tomorrow morning at 6:47 from the same spot at the kitchen table. It will be what it is.

title: Company Decides To Ask And Answer Its Own Questions On The Earnings Call, Which Is What Mark Tried To Do And Got Thanked Into Next Week
dek: Mark Chen, an analyst at a mid-tier fund, dialed into the earnings call at 4:36 PM and asked a question the company had not asked itself. The CEO thanked Mark for the question, answered a different question, then thanked Mark again. Mark, on the line, was thanked a third time. The company confirmed this is now the format.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Mark Chen, an analyst at a mid-tier fund in Chicago, dialed into the earnings call at 4:36 PM EST with an earbud in one ear because he was already in a meeting. When the CEO opened the floor for questions, Mark heard a silence on the line that was not the silence of nobody having a question. It was the silence of everybody having the same question and knowing the answer was not coming.

Mark asked his question. It was about revenue guidance for the next quarter, which the company had declined to provide. The CEO paused, smiled into the phone, and said: “Mark, thank you for that question. That is a great question. And I think what the question really gets at is the strength of our underlying business, which is strong.” The CEO then answered a question about how strong the underlying business was, which was not Mark’s question. Then the CEO said: “Thank you, Mark. Great question.” Mark had been thanked for two different things: the question he asked, and the question he did not ask. The call moved on.

“I was thanked three times on one earnings call. That is more engagement than I got from the last four companies combined — the answer was not my question, but the gratitude was real.”

— Mark, thanked three times on the call

Mark sat in his office after the call with the earbud still in, not sure whether he had gotten an answer or participated in a ceremony where the answer was the thanking itself. He reviewed his notes: the CEO had thanked him, pivoted to a prepared statement, and thanked him again. Mark’s question had been absorbed into the company’s own narrative, which is the only narrative the company plans to use going forward.

The company confirmed it will continue the format for the foreseeable future. Mark said he will continue to dial in because his fund owns the stock, and because on the off chance the company ever answers a question he asked, he wants to be there to hear it, even if he has to listen through three thank-yous first.

title: Family Office Hires A Family Because The Real One Stopped Answering The Phone, And Brian And Cheryl Are Now The Family
dek: The founding family stopped attending quarterly meetings one by one, citing travel, fatigue, and, in one memorable case, a general lack of interest in the money. The office has retained Brian and Cheryl Donaldson, a professional couple from Scottsdale, to sit at the table. Cheryl asked about the Alpine property during the onboarding call.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
The quarterly meeting of the family office was held on the 14th floor of a building in Midtown Manhattan at 10 AM on a Tuesday. The table seats twelve. At 10:02, the only people in the room were the office’s investment director, a junior associate pouring water, and Brian and Cheryl Donaldson, the professional family from Scottsdale. Cheryl was wearing the blazer she had picked during the onboarding call, which she described as “business casual with a hint of legacy.”

The founding family stopped attending the meetings one by one. The youngest son said he had a conflict. The daughter said she was traveling. The mother said she found the meetings taxing in every sense. The father, the original wealth, died in 2021 and left the office with a table and nobody to sit at it. The office placed an ad for a family and interviewed three candidates. Brian and Cheryl got the job because they showed up, asked about the Alpine property’s cap rate, and passed the biscuits without being told which direction to pass them.

“We asked about the Alpine property cap rate and passed the biscuits the right direction without being told. That is more family behavior than the real family showed in four meetings combined.”

— Cheryl, who passed the biscuits correctly

The meeting lasted 47 minutes. Brian asked about the Alpine property’s cap rate. Cheryl asked whether the art portfolio included anything she could mention at a dinner party. Both questions were in the script the office had sent them three days before, which Brian and Cheryl had reviewed over breakfast at the hotel. The investment director confirmed the answers from the script. The meeting ended at 10:47.

Brian and Cheryl shook hands, thanked the junior associate for the water, and left for their flight back to Scottsdale. The investment director sat alone at the table that seats twelve and confirmed to himself that the meeting had gone well. Brian and Cheryl’s invoice arrived that afternoon and was paid within the hour. The founding family was not reached for comment, because the office no longer has a working number.

title: Tape Rallies On A Moth At The Podium, And Tommy Called The Buy Signal From The Coffee Station At 9:47 AM
dek: Tommy, a floor trader who has been standing near the same spot on the trading floor for 22 years, saw the moth enter the pit at 9:47, clear the podium by approximately two inches, and exit stage left. Tommy called it a buy signal. The desk agreed. The tape rallied. Tommy is now the floor’s top performer by year-to-date return, and the moth has not been seen since.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Tommy was standing near the coffee station on the trading floor at 9:47 AM when he saw the moth enter the pit from the west side, cross the airspace above the podium at an elevation of approximately six feet, and depart through the east exit without touching any surfaces. Tommy has been on this floor for 22 years. He has seen a lot of things move a tape. He has never seen a moth move one, but he knew, the way a guy who has been in a room for 22 years knows, that this was the moment.

Tommy turned to the desk and said “moth.” The desk asked what he meant. Tommy said there was a moth, it was at the podium, and it left. The desk asked whether the moth had landed. Tommy said it had not. The desk asked whether it had been spooked. Tommy said it had not been spooked, it had concluded its business and exited. The desk asked what Tommy wanted to do. Tommy said buy. The desk bought.

“The moth cleared the podium by two inches and exited stage left at 9:47 AM. That is a textbook breakout pattern — I have been on this floor 22 years and a moth does not lie.”

— Tommy, who has been on the floor 22 years

The tape rallied through the morning on the moth’s trajectory, which analysts later described as a clean breakout above the opening range. Tommy was interviewed by a financial-news desk at 11:30 and asked to describe his methodology. Tommy said he saw a moth, it looked confident, and he bought. The interviewer asked whether Tommy had considered the moth’s destination. Tommy said the moth’s destination was not the trade. The moth’s presence was the trade, and the departure was the confirmation.

The moth has not been seen since 9:47 AM. The desk has posted a photo of the empty podium above Tommy’s terminal with a caption that says “the setup.” Tommy has not made another trade since the moth, on principle. He confirmed he is waiting for the next signal, which could be anything, and that he will know it when he sees it, because he has been in this room for 22 years, and the room, at this point, tells him what it wants.
image_alt: A man in a hat stands at a podium beneath glowing monitors.

title: Dow Rises 214 Points, Market Clarifies That It Is a Number and Does Not Know Why You're Asking It
dek: Steve Gable checked his 401(k) at 4:01 PM. It was up $214. He does not know why. His wife asked if it was good news. He said the market thought so. She asked what the market was. He stared at his phone.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Steve Gable works in HVAC. At 4:01 PM on a Wednesday, he checked his 401(k) on his phone while sitting in his truck outside a Wendy's. The number was higher than it was yesterday. He did not know why. He had not bought anything. He had not sold anything. He had not read any news. The number just went up.

His wife Lisa asked if it was a good day. Steve said the market thought so. Lisa asked what that meant. Steve said it meant the Dow went up. Lisa asked what the Dow was. Steve said it was a number. Lisa asked what the number meant. Steve said it meant things were good. Lisa asked what things. Steve looked at his phone again. The number was still up. He did not have a second answer.

“My 401k went up $214 today. I do not know why, but the number went up, and that means things are good.”

— Steve, checking his 401k at 4:01 PM

The Dow rose because a bunch of people in buildings pushed buttons on computers. Some of them pushed the button that says buy. Some of them pushed the button that says sell. More people pushed the button that says buy. Nobody can tell you why they pushed the button they pushed, because if they could tell you why, they would have pushed the button harder, and the number would be different.

Steve closed his phone and ate his Wendy's. The number would be different tomorrow. He would check it again. He would not know why then, either. This is his life now. It is fine. It is a number. It goes up. It goes down. Steve does not have a say in any of it, but he checks it anyway, because checking it feels like having a say, which is the whole trick.
