title: Berkshire Hathaway Spends $9.6 Billion Buying Stock From The Only Person Willing To Sell It: Itself
dek: The conglomerate more than doubled repurchases while insurance underwriting tumbled 43%, describing the buyback as an expression of long-term conviction in a security whose only shareholders are, increasingly, the same company.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Gary lives in Omaha, and his father told him in 1997 that you buy Berkshire Hathaway and then you die, and that is it, that is the plan. Gary did that. Gary is now sixty-one years old, and his 401‑k is, by his own estimate, me and that one company. He says this proudly, like he has discovered the only safe chair in a burning building.

What Gary does not know, and what nobody in Omaha is going to tell him, is that the company has spent $9.6 billion buying itself back, because the only person who wants to buy the stock is the stock. The operating profits fell. The underwriting fell. The insurance thing everybody counts on fell. And the company bought $9.6 billion of itself, because when you are Berkshire, your own shares are the only supplier that never says no.

Gary is the buyback. Gary, with his 401‑k statement and his faith in the man from the newspaper, is the counterparty. The company buys, and Gary holds, and the price stays up, and Gary does not know that he is the inventory. He thinks he is the customer.

A man who worked in the same building as Gary for fourteen years, named Phil, sold his Berkshire shares in March to put a down payment on a townhouse. Phil now checks the price every day, because the townhouse is the same price it was in March, and the stock is up, and Phil has to live with that, which he knew he would. He told me he knew he would. He says it again at the mailbox every time he sees Gary.

“I told Phil the buyback is the only thing keeping my townhouse worth anything. The stock is up 14% and the house is flat, and I call that a fair trade — the company knows what it is worth better than the realtor does.”

— Gary, who checks Zillow and the ticker from the same bench
image_alt: A coiled snake surrounds a tiny person before a city skyline.

title: 10-Year Yield Hits 4.90%, Fed Officials Describe The Pain As 'Egalitarian' Since Everyone Gets Hurt Equally
dek: Long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest since the summer on strong labor data, and the market found its way to the comforting insight that a higher benchmark applies to every borrower equally, which is the definition of fair.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Dave and his wife Rachel were pre‑approved for a house in March at 4.2 percent. They found the house. It is a three‑bedroom in a suburb of Richmond with a backyard that has a fence that needs painting. They made an offer. The offer was accepted. Then the yield on the 10‑year Treasury started climbing, and the mortgage rate followed, and the pre‑approval expired, and the house did not wait.

Dave now checks the 10‑year yield every morning on his phone. He did not know what the 10‑year yield was in March. He knows now. It is 4.90 percent. He knows because it is the number that tells him whether the house is getting closer or farther away. It is getting farther away. The yield went up because the jobs report was resilient, which means more people are working, which Dave is supposed to be happy about, because Dave is working. He has a job. The job is the reason the pre‑approval existed in the first place. And the fact that he has the job is now the reason he cannot afford the house, because the job market is strong, and a strong job market means the Fed will not cut rates, and higher rates mean the house that cost $340,000 in March costs $480 more a month now, and Dave does not have $480 more a month.

An official at the Treasury Department, whose name Dave does not know, said that the higher yield is “empathetic because it applies to every borrower equally.” The official said this into a camera in a room where the walls were beige and the question had been about households. The official did not say Dave’s name. The official does not know about the fence that needs painting.

Dave is not going to say anything about this, because the economy is doing well, and the labor market is resilient, and he is employed, and all of those are good things. He knows they are good things. He will repeat them to himself, because the news keeps saying them, and the news is right. It is just that the right news, at 4.90 percent, means Dave’s family is going to keep renting the apartment with the thin walls. They might paint the fence anyway, if they ever get a yard. But that is not the market’s problem. The market priced in the resilience. The market is fine.

“I told Dave the 4.90% is the honest number. The apartment has thin walls and the fence needs paint, and the market priced that in fair and square, and I do not blame the market for the walls.”

— a tenant who watches the 10-year from the kitchen table
image_alt: An arrow across a chasm points from a couple to a house.

title: Index Fund Solves Underperformance Forever By Declaring Whatever It Already Owns Is The Benchmark
dek: A passive fund simplified its reporting by making its benchmark equal to the stocks it already owns, guaranteeing it will never again underperform — a performance its competitors concede is, technically, trivial.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
Mark is a compliance officer at a fund that manages $12 billion. He has a law degree from a school he mentions twice on the first call. He approved the new prospectus, which says the fund now tracks an index that is, and I am not paraphrasing, “the weighted average of the fund’s holdings as of the close of each trading day.” This means the fund cannot underperform, because it set the bar equal to the thing it did. Mark knows this is a trick. Mark approved it anyway.

I asked Mark, over a sandwich he ate while looking at his monitor, whether this was honest. He chewed for a moment and said, “The word ‘honest’ does not appear in the compliance guidelines. The word ‘accurate’ appears. It is accurate. The fund owns exactly the stocks in the index, because the index is the stocks the fund owns. The tracking error is zero. The performance is not impressive. But the tracking error is zero, and that is what the prospectus says.”

The fund’s marketing now says, “We guarantee we will never underperform our benchmark.” This is true in the same way that a man who runs a ten‑second race against himself has won. He has also lost, because he was the only competitor. But the marketing does not say that.

Three other funds have called Mark’s office asking how the compliance language works. Mark told them it works because the SEC has not said it does not work, which is the standard of approval the industry uses for things it wants to do. One of the funds, Mark said, is exploring a benchmark that is just a photograph of its portfolio, so tracking error cannot even be calculated, because a photograph is not a data set. Mark said he would approve that too, if they sent it over.

The fund’s holders, who are entirely institutional, have not complained, because their mandate was to match the benchmark, and now they do. Exactly. It is the cleanest mandate compliance has ever seen. Mark finished his sandwich and said, “Nobody is getting hurt. The benchmark does not know.”

“Mark told me the benchmark does not know what it is missing. My retirement is up 0.02% this year and the mandate is clean, and I sleep better knowing the fund is not taking chances with my money.”

— a participant in the cleanest mandate compliance has ever seen
image_alt: A man faces another through a circular opening in a wall.

title: Family Trust Locks Inheritance Until Age 45 On The Theory That By Then The Heir Will Be Too Tired To Spend It
dek: A single-family office has structured its trust so distributions to grandchildren phase in only after age 45, on the theory that by then the money will be received by a person who is no longer young enough to do anything with it.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Connor is twenty-two years old and he sat in a room that smelled like a cedar closet and a man in wire-rim glasses explained to him that his grandfather, who Connor liked, had set up the money so that Connor would not get it until he was forty-five years old. Connor asked why. The man in the glasses said, “Because at forty-five, you will be prepared to use it responsibly, which means you will use it the way your grandfather would have used it, which means you will not use it.”

Connor is not prepared for this. He is twenty-two. He has a motorcycle he bought with his own money from working at a bike shop, which the family office has, in a separate binder, described as “a period of discovery likely to conclude with injury.”

The deceleration clause means Connor gets a stipend now that covers exactly rent and food, and then at thirty the stipend doubles, and at forty-five the trust opens fully, at which point Connor will be forty-five years old and the money will arrive in the life of a man who has been waiting for it for twenty-three years and has, in that time, learned that waiting for money is the same as learning to live without it.

Connor told me that he understands the arrangement, because his cousin Sarah got her full distribution at twenty-six, bought a sailboat, and spent six years trying to be the kind of person who owns a sailboat, before selling it at a loss and moving to Denver. Connor says he does not want a sailboat. He says he wants the money. But he is twenty-two, and the money comes at forty-five, and what he wants does not matter, which is, the man in the glasses explained, the entire point of the deceleration.

The family office confirmed that Connor’s meeting was recorded and the recording has been added to the file, under a tab marked, simply, “Later.”

“Connor said the trust is teaching us patience. I am 32 and I have 13 years to figure out what I would have done with the money anyway, and by then I will be old enough to leave it in the trust where it belongs.”

— Connor, who has 13 years to think about it
image_alt: A giant hourglass towers over a man beside a scooter and coins.

title: Federal Reserve Concludes 12-Year Study On Waiting, Decides To Commission A Study On The Study
dek: Jerome from the Board spent twelve years studying whether to act or wait for more information, and the study's conclusion is that he needs more information. The conclusion is now in a binder on a shelf above his desk, where it will be joined by the next study, which is a study of the conclusion.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Jerome from the Board has a binder on a shelf above his desk that says THE STUDY on the spine in Sharpie. Inside the binder are twelve years of meetings, each one ending with the sentence we will accumulate more information. The binder is now full. The Federal Reserve has completed the study. The study's conclusion, reached after four subcommittees, a review of the subcommittees, and a meditation retreat for the chair of the subcommittee review, is that Jerome needs more information. The binder, having delivered its conclusion, is now evidence for the next binder.

I asked Jerome what the information was, specifically, that he was waiting for. He said that is a very good question and that he would need more information to answer it. I asked who had the information. He said the information was being accumulated by a new committee, which is currently hiring the person who will decide where the information, once received, will be stored. I asked what the storage committee was called. He said it was too early to name it, and that naming it, at this stage, would require information the committee had not yet accumulated.

“Darnell told me the pizza will come when the information arrives. I have been standing in the doorway for 12 years and I have learned more about the doorway than I ever learned about the pizza, and that is the study.”

— Darnell, 12 years in the doorway

The release of the study was met with a brief rally, which was met with a selloff when analysts realized the study contained no data, which was met with a second rally when the Fed confirmed that the absence of data was, in itself, information, and that the information, having been identified, would now be accumulated. The next meeting will consider whether the accumulated information requires a study of its own. Jerome's binder, on the shelf above his desk, waits. It is, Jerome confirmed, a very good binder.
image_alt: A suited man sits at a desk surrounded by blue cabinets.

title: Bank Confirms $35 'Courtesy' Fee For Letting You Be $7 Short For Six Minutes
dek: Tanya from Detroit put $7 in gas at 7:13 in the morning. Her paycheck hit at 7:19. The bank posted the gas before the check, charged her $35 for the privilege of being$7 short for six minutes. Then it called the $35 a courtesy.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Tanya from Detroit put forty-two dollars in regular gas at the Shell on Livernois at seven-thirteen in the morning. Her paycheck, which is the Paylocity one she can see pending on Thursday but cannot touch until Friday, hit the ledger at seven-nineteen. Six minutes. The bank posted the forty-two dollars out the door before the eight-hundred-and-thirty-seven dollars came in, because the bank said the out had arrived first, and the out does not cut in line, and the in, having arrived second, must wait, and the waiting, for a deposit, is a courtesy, and the courtesy, like a handshake between two people who have already decided one of them is paying, costs thirty-five dollars.

Tanya asked the teller, a woman named Cheryl who has been at the branch for eleven years and did not write the rule and cannot change the rule and has had this conversation eighty times this week, whether the bank could simply wait the six minutes. Cheryl laughed. She laughed the way you laugh when a child asks if the dog can have the whole steak. Cheryl explained that the computer does not wait, and that the computer does not know Tanya, and that if the computer waited for Tanya, the computer would have to wait for everybody, and then what would the computer be. A person, Tanya said. Cheryl laughed again. The second laugh was shorter.

“Tanya told Cheryl the $35 is the cost of the six minutes. The computer does not wait for anybody and I do not want a computer that waits for me. I want a computer that knows the time is the time.”

— Tanya, who paid $35 for punctuality

The bank, when reached for comment, confirmed that it does not post deposits before withdrawals because that would be rude to the withdrawal, which arrived first and which the bank has already promised to honor, and that honoring a withdrawal before the money is there to cover it is the very definition of a courtesy, which it is, if courtesy means we took eleven billion dollars in overdraft revenue last year and the word for that, in the Tellurian language the computer speaks, is Tanya.
image_alt: A woman stands in a dark doorway beneath a tall building.

title: Bank Unveils Overdraft Hall Of Shame, Each Plaque Commemorates A Customer Who Paid For The Marble Lobby
dek: The bank has opened a permanent gallery honoring the customers whose fees built the new wing, and Marcus from Akron is the inaugural inductee. His plaque reads $37.50 on January 12, framed in brushed nickel, hung above the teller break room.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Marcus from Akron went to the bank to deposit a birthday check from his grandmother, thirty-seven dollars and fifty cents, which he was told he could not deposit because the check was not his until the check cleared, and that was when the bank noticed that Marcus had, three hours earlier, bought a sandwich that required the money Marcus was now trying to deposit, and that the sandwich was, in the bank's terms, a courtesy extended to Marcus, and the birthday check, arriving late, was not the answer to the courtesy. The sandwich cost Marcus thirty-seven-fifty plus a thirty-five-dollar courtesy fee, printed on a plaque, hung on a wall, in a room the bank now calls the Overdraft Hall of Shame.

I attended the ribbon cutting. The room is real. It has track lighting, four pedestals, and a row of brushed-nickel plaques. Each plaque has an account number, a date, and a sum. Marcus's plaque reads ACCOUNT HOLDER MARCUS D. SANDWICH OVERDRAFT $37.50 plus COURTESY $35.00 and the font is Garamond, which the tour guide, a woman named Brenda who was visibly proud of the font choice, described as the kind of font you use when you want the reader to know you took the time.

“Brenda told me the plaque is Garamond because the bank took the time. My name is on the wall and the font is brushed nickel and I told Brenda the $72.50 was worth it to see my name in a font I did not pick.”

— Marcus, whose name is in Garamond

The bank confirmed that the Hall of Shame is not, as the name suggests, a shame held by the bank, but a shame the bank has arranged for the customer to view from outside, which is to say, through the glass of a locked door labeled STAFF ONLY, because the hall is next to the break room, and the break room is for employees, and the employees, the bank noted, have earned the right to eat lunch facing Marcus's name in Garamond, which is the font of a thing you want to remember.
image_alt: A lone figure faces a wall of silver panels between marble columns.

title: Carrier Lays Off 20% Of Workers To Fund A Buyback, Announces The Stock Is Now The Actual Product
dek: Raymond from Wichita built the door handle of a 737 for seventeen years. The company is now buying back its own stock instead of building planes, and Raymond, who never owned a share, has been told the stock is the new plane and the handle is a cost.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Raymond from Wichita has a garage full of toolboxes and a pension that stopped growing in 2019. For seventeen years, Raymond built the interior door handle of a 737, which is a piece of metal that costs the company eighteen dollars and that Raymond, if you asked him, would say he was proud to make. The company announced it is laying off five percent of its line crew to fund a buyback. The company said the crew, and Raymond would like me to stress that this is a direct quote from the internal memo, was the product, historically, and that the buyback is the only product that matters now.

Raymond read this memo on a phone he bought with his own money, in a parking lot next to an Outback, and he called me and read it aloud, and when he got to the part about the product, he stopped and said, I built a door handle, you understand. I built it and it worked. I do not understand what the new product is. I explained that the new product is the stock, and that the stock is the company, and that the company, having bought itself, will now be its own best customer, and that Raymond, who built the thing the company used to sell, is not the customer of the stock, because the stock does not open.

“Raymond told the plant manager the stock is the new plane and the handle was a cost. I built door handles for 17 years and I told my kids the company believes in itself so much it bought itself instead of the handle, and that is a stronger product.”

— Raymond, 17 years on the door handle

The remaining ninety-five percent of the crew were told their work would be honored in spirit, that the planes would still be built after the company finished buying itself, and that the delay was not a delay so much as a holding pattern while the product line transitioned from things that fly to things that compound. Raymond was not part of the holding pattern. He was part of the thing the company no longer makes, which is the door handle, and the door handle, Raymond told me, has no idea what a share is, and neither did he, until the day the share became worth more than he was.
image_alt: A banknote with a red arrow floats above a hard-hatted worker.

title: Private Equity Acquires Hospital, Announces The Real Patient Has Always Been The Margin
dek: Walter from Philadelphia went to the emergency room with chest pain and was told the hospital had been acquired and the new patient intake system begins at revenue. His insurance, which had been accepted the week before, was now a souvenir. The hospital confirmed the real patient was the margin.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Walter from Philadelphia woke up with a pain in his chest that he described, later, as the feeling of a small fist holding a smaller fist. He drove himself to the emergency room he had used for fourteen years, the one with the blue awning and the sign that says WE BELIEVE IN YOU and the woman named Brenda at the front desk who knows his birthday. Walter got to the desk and Brenda was not there. There was a new woman, a contract woman named Keisha who had been hired three days ago by a company Walter had never heard of, and Keisha asked for Walter's insurance card and then asked for a second insurance card and then said the insurance Walter had was not in the network of the new owner, and that the new owner, having purchased the hospital, had also purchased the right to decide whose pain was worth the visit.

Walter asked what network he was in now. Keisha read from a sheet of paper. The network, she said, was the balance sheet. Walter asked what that meant. Keisha said it meant Walter would need to pay upfront for the chest pain, because the chest pain, under the new ownership structure, was a liability until the liability was funded, and the funding, Keisha said, begins at revenue. She said visiting hours begin at revenue. Treatment begins at revenue. The breathing, Walter, begins at a time and place the hospital will communicate to you once the revenue is confirmed.

“Walter told Keisha the margin has a quarterly report and the quarterly report has a heartbeat. My chest pain can wait until the revenue is confirmed because the revenue is what keeps the lights on and the $4 million wing is what I am paying for.”

— Walter, who learned the patient is the margin

The firm, when reached for comment, confirmed that Walter's assessment was essentially correct, and that the hospital, having been acquired, would now treat the margin as the primary patient, with the humans who previously occupied the beds serving as what the firm called a delivery channel for the margin’s recovery. Walter, the firm noted, was free to seek care at a facility that still treated humans, and that such facilities, if they existed, were welcome to compete.
image_alt: A figure in a chair faces a desk in a dark room.

title: Index Fund's Tracking Error Exactly Equals Its Fee Two Years Running, Firm Upgrades From 'Coincidence' To 'Feature'
dek: Denise from Phoenix put her 401k in the honest fund, the one that just owns everything and charges 0.23%. At the end of the year, the fund had trailed the index by exactly 0.23%. The firm called it a coincidence. Then, after a pause, called it engineering.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Denise from Phoenix put her 401k in the fund that tells you it is the honest one. The one that just owns everything. The one that charges you twenty-three basis points and says that is all it takes, that is the entire business model, the index is the thing and the fund is the index and the difference between them is nothing but a rounding error that the fund, being honest, will return to you. At the end of the year, the difference between Denise's fund and the index was twenty-three basis points. Exactly twenty-three. Not twenty-two. Not twenty-four. The fee.

Denise called the fund. A man named Phillip told her the gap was a coincidence. Denise waited. Phillip said the word again, slower, as if Denise had not heard it the first time. Coincidence. Denise asked what the odds were of an index fund trailing the index by exactly the fee. Phillip said he would need to check with the product team. Phillip called back. The product team said the gap was not a coincidence. The gap was engineering. Phillip used the word design. Phillip said the fund, by design, tracks the index minus the fee, and that the fee, by design, is the cost of the design, and that the design, now that Denise understood it, was the very honesty the fund had promised.

“Denise told Phillip the fee is the design and the design is the honesty. My 401k trails the index by 0.23% and I call that transparency, because I know exactly where every penny of the error went.”

— Denise, 0.23% richer in understanding

Analysts praised the alignment. They said the fee and the error had achieved a harmony rare in finance, and that the two figures, having met, would now travel together as one line on the chart, which is the kind of chart you look at when you do not want to see the line underneath. Denise looked at the chart. The chart showed one line. The other line, the index, was not there. Denise said it looks like the fund is just taking the fee off the top. Phillip said that is exactly what it is. Denise asked why nobody said that. Phillip said nobody asked.
image_alt: A woman sits below a rising line graph with a red pushpin.

title: Family Dynasty Trust Skips Grandchildren After Determining They Wear Shoes On Sidewalks Like Regular People
dek: Whitney Vanderbilt IV has decided his grandchildren are a tax, not beneficiaries. The money will skip them entirely and land on the generation after, which the trust has already vetted through a series of interviews the grandchildren were not told about.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Whitney Vanderbilt IV sat in a room with three lawyers and a notary and signed a document that says his grandchildren, Caroline and William, are not the recipients of his fortune, but the obstacle to it. The document is called a dynasty trust. What it does is skip. It skips Caroline. It skips William. It takes the money that Whitney made and holds it in a warm, dark place until Caroline and William have had their chance to do what Whitney assumes they will do, which is spend it foolishly, on things like rent and groceries and the kinds of shoes you wear on an actual sidewalk. The money, Whitney decided, does not deserve that. The money has been patient. The money wants to see the next century. Caroline and William, if the trust's math is correct, will be dead by then.

Caroline was informed of the trust by her father, who was informed by the lawyer, who had been instructed to inform Caroline that the trust was not a reflection on Caroline personally, but a reflection on the generation Caroline happened to be born into, which the trust, in its preamble, describes as a period of elevated consumption and diminished regard for compounding. The preamble does not mention Caroline by name. It mentions a demographic that Caroline, for the purposes of the trust, represents. Caroline asked whether she could appeal. The lawyer said the trust does not have an appeals process. The trust has a vesting schedule. Caroline is not on it.

“Caroline told the lawyer the used Honda was the application and the application was denied. I am 29 and I am not on the vesting schedule and that is the trust working as designed, because the $40 million should go to someone who never had to buy a used car.”

— Caroline, who drove the Honda to the lawyer's office

The money, having skipped Caroline and William, will now sit in a pool that compounds until it encounters a descendant the trust considers worthy, which the trust defines as a descendant who has demonstrated an understanding that money is not for spending but for being, and that the being, in a dynasty trust, is the trust itself, which does not spend, which does not drive a used car, and which will outlive every Vanderbilt who has ever tried to open it.
image_alt: A man and woman hold hands on marble stairs below a throne.

title: Fed Governor Warns A Smaller Rate Hike Would Damage His Credibility, Which Is Kept In A Room The Public Cannot Enter
dek: Christopher Waller stood in front of a room full of bond owners and told them a quarter-point rate hike would damage his credibility. A half-point hike would protect it. He did not mention the people who owe money because they were not in the room, and the room was where the credibility was being held.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Christopher Waller, a governor of the Federal Reserve, walked to a podium in a room where every person in the audience owned at least two million dollars of something, and he told them about his credibility. He said he has one, and that he intends to keep it. He said that raising rates by a quarter point would put his credibility at risk. He said raising rates by a half point, which is twice as much, would protect it. He said the public, which does not own two million dollars of anything, would be fine, because the public, as he understands it, is resilient, and that resilience, in a governor's vocabulary, is the word for what the public is while the governor counts his credibility.

I asked someone on Waller's staff what the credibility looked like. She said it was not a physical object, and then she described it as a professional-grade credential, maintained through the careful practice of never being wrong twice in the same direction. I asked whether the public had a credibility, and she said the public did not have a credibility because the public did not need one, because the public does not set rates. I asked what the public had. She said the public has the benefit of the governor's credibility, which the governor, by choosing the half-point hike, would protect, for the benefit of the public, who cannot see it, cannot touch it, and cannot vote on it.

“Keisha told the governor the room is the calculation and the rest of us are the variable. My $1,200 mortgage is not a factor in the credibility calculation and I am fine with that, because the credibility is what keeps the bond market from falling apart and the $28 trillion bond market is bigger than my kitchen.”

— Keisha, who accepted her role as the variable

The half-point hike was announced the next morning. Waller's credibility, by all accounts, remained intact. The public's mortgages, which are not a credibility, went up. Waller's staff confirmed the governor's credibility was now twenty-seven and a half points, and climbing, and that no member of the public, having been surveyed, could name the number of their own, which the staff said proved the point, which was that credibility lives in the room with the bond owners, and the bond owners, having paid for the room, are the only ones who need to see it.
image_alt: A speaker stands at a podium before a dark audience.

title: Passive Funds Swallow Another Trillion After A Client Says 'Agile' And Active Management Decides The Meeting Is Over
dek: With a record $1.36 trillion of inflows in a year, the index now owns the market, the market owns the index, and the only person not in the arrangement is the one who showed up to work.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Kevin Osei has been in asset management for 14 years. He has built spreadsheets that modeled the correlation between copper futures and monsoon season. He has a degree in econometrics from a school his parents are still proud of. Last week he moved $400 million into the SPDR S&P 500 ETF because a client said the word “agile” in a meeting, and Kevin understood that the meeting was over.

“The client said they wanted active management,” Kevin said. “I showed them our active strategy. The active strategy is the S&P 500 with a slightly higher fee and a presentation about how we pick the stocks that are in the S&P 500. The client asked if we ever pick stocks that are not in the S&P 500. I said no. The client said that sounds like the S&P 500. I said yes. We decided to call it conviction.”

Kevin’s entire job now consists of explaining to people why the thing they already own is the thing they should continue to own. He cannot recommend anything else because his firm does not hold anything else. His firm does not hold anything else because nobody at the firm has been asked to think of anything else since 2018.

“I told my wife I manage a trillion dollars,” Kevin said. “She asked what I do. I said I wait for the wire. She said what wire. I said any wire. She asked if I could pick up the kids at 4. I said the closing bell is at 4. She said the kids are at school until 3:15. I said the closing bell is the only thing I have to do today. She hung up.”

“Kevin told his wife the closing bell at 4 P.M. is the only thing he has to do today. The wire comes in and the ETF buys the stocks and the stocks go up and I am the hallway the $1.36 trillion walks through, and the hallway does not need an opinion about the stocks.”

— Kevin, Director of the hallway

title: Private Equity Buys 100-Year-Old Hardware Store, Keeps The Owner As Advisor Of The Part Where He No Longer Owns Anything
dek: An investor group has acquired a hundred-year-old family hardware store, its inventory, and the institutional patience to wait out the founder's decline in the role of a helpful advisor.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Benny Falcone opened Falcone Hardware in 1927 with a handshake and a loan from his uncle Phil. In 2026, Benny Falcone IV, who everyone calls Benny still, sold the store to a buyout group called Pinnacle Partners II, L.P., which is not a person and does not have an uncle. The group paid $14 million for the building, the inventory, the name, and, as a line item nobody caught, the part of Benny that still thought the store was his.

“They said I could stay on as an advisor,” Benny said. “I asked what that meant. They said I would advise. I asked on what. They said the transition. I asked whose transition. They said mine. I asked if I still had a key. They asked if I had a phone. I said yes. They said the phone is the key now.”

Pinnacle has since replaced the front door lock. Benny’s key still works on the back door, which the group says is more symbolic, and which Benny says is more humiliating, since the back door opens onto the dumpster. “I walk past the display I built in 1989 and a woman from Milwaukee in a vest is rearranging the drawer pulls I arranged,” Benny said. “She is very good at rearranging. She has a binder. I do not have a binder. I had a store. Now I have the number for the back door.”

The group has promised to keep the Falcone name on the sign. It has not promised to keep Falcone in the sign. Benny checks every morning from the dumpster. The sign is still there. The sign is not the store. The sign is a piece of metal that Pinnacle Partners now owns.

“Benny told Pinnacle Partners the sign is a piece of metal and the sign is still there. I sold the building for $1.4 million and I kept the knowledge that I sold it, and the knowledge is worth more than the building because the building had a 4.5% mortgage and the knowledge has no payment.”

— Benny, who checks the sign from the dumpster
image_alt: A giant hand lowers a key above a shopkeeper at a door.

title: Sanitation Firm Posts Record Margins; Customer's Uncollected Garbage Has Become A Neighborhood Landmark With A Resident Possum
dek: In a quarter of logistics excellence, the hauler reported its most profitable run ever, a margin it attributes to a consistency of collection that has, for some of its customers, become their entire curbside biography.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Marcus Blythe’s garbage has not been picked up in 17 days. The hauler keeps driving past. Marcus keeps putting the can out. The can is now a neighborhood landmark. Kids draw on it. A possum lives behind it. The possum understands the situation better than the hauler does, because the possum does not have an account number.

“I called customer service and they said my route is operating at record efficiency,” Marcus said. “I said my can is full. They said the route is the most profitable in the region. I said my can has a possum. They said the possum is not in the system. I said the possum is on my can. They said the can is at the curb, the curb is the collection point, and the collection point is operating at a 97 percent service rate. I said which 97 percent am I in. They said the 3 percent. I said the 3 percent of what. They said the 3 percent we are not collecting.”

CEO Gordon Heath attributes the record margins to “load consistency,” which is the term the company uses to describe customers who generate the same volume of the same material on the same schedule, so the truck never has to guess. Marcus Blythe’s garbage, by contrast, is what the industry calls “a variable.” The company has no interest in variables. Variables cost money. Variables are why the margin was not higher.

“I asked them to at least take the possum,” Marcus said. “They said the possum is not in the scope of collection services. The possum is a wildlife issue. I said the possum is on top of my garbage. They said the garbage is a collection issue. The possum is a municipality issue. I said what about the raccoon. They said I have a raccoon now too. I said yes. They said the raccoon is also a municipality issue. I hung up and looked at the can. The possum and the raccoon were looking at me. We all understood the same thing: the hauler was not coming.”

“Marcus told the hauler the possum has a name and the name is Gordon. Gordon has not paid a cent in 3 weeks and Gordon does not complain, and the hauler told me Gordon is the ideal customer, and I told the hauler I am working on becoming more like Gordon.”

— Marcus, three weeks uncollected

title: Bank Confirms The $34 Charge On A $7 Coffee Is Not A Fee But A Statement, Emphatically Made, At 7:04 A.M., Without Danielle From Tulsa's Permission
dek: Danielle from Tulsa bought a $6.75 latte at 6:58 AM with $21 in her account. By 7:04, the latte was $40.75 and Danielle had been charged a courtesy the bank now says was not a fee at all, but a statement, emphatically made, on her behalf, without her permission.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Danielle from Tulsa bought a six-dollar-and-seventy-five-cent latte at six-fifty-eight in the morning, which is sixteen minutes before the bank opens and seventeen dollars and twenty-five cents more than she needed to not be late for the shift at the dental office where she answers phones. At seven-oh-four, the bank had turned the latte into forty dollars and seventy-five cents and charged Danielle a courtesy she did not ask for and a message she did not consent to, and when Danielle called to ask why, the bank said the charge was not a fee. The bank said it was a statement. A statement somebody should be making, the bank said, and since Danielle was not making it, the bank made it for her, out of the money she did not have.

Danielle asked what the statement was. The bank said the statement was that Danielle had spent money she did not own at a time when the bank was not there to ask, and that the statement, now that it had been made, would be delivered to Danielle in the form of a thirty-four-dollar addition to her latte, which Danielle could now read, every time she looked at her balance, as a text the bank had written, in fees, because the bank did not have her phone number.

“Danielle told the bank the $34 carried more weight than a text. I read the statement every time I check my balance and I know the bank wrote it at 7:04 A.M. without my permission, and I told Danielle the permission is the $34 and the $34 is the statement.”

— Danielle, who read the statement at 7:04

The bank reiterated that nobody is ever charged for being poor, and that the thirty-four dollars was not a charge for poverty but a charge for the statement, and that the statement, having been made, would remain on Danielle's account as a permanent record of the bank's commitment to saying what Danielle was unwilling to say herself, which was that she was seventeen dollars and twenty-five cents away from a latte she had already drunk.
image_alt: A woman beside a vault door with a coffee cup and exclamation.

title: Exchange Installs Button That Buys Before You Tap It, Then Charges You For Being The Part Of The System That Is Slowest
dek: Denise from Tucson tried to buy one share of Ford on her phone. Before she could tap the button, a machine in New Jersey had bought the share, sold it to her for a penny more, and charged her for the speed of her own slowness. The exchange says the button is a co-located assist and that Denise, being human, is the latency.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Denise from Tucson sat on her couch with her phone in her hand and a single share of Ford Motor Company in her brain and she tapped the green button on the brokerage app and the button did nothing, because by the time her thumb reached the glass, a machine in a building in New Jersey that is exactly one hundred and twenty feet closer to the exchange than her phone will ever be had already done what Denise was about to do, and had done it faster, and had charged Denise a fraction of a cent for the privilege of arriving second, and the fraction of a cent, multiplied by every person who has ever tapped a button, is the entire business model of the button that taps itself before you tap it.

The exchange calls the feature a co-located assist, and what it does is press itself, because the hand that wanted to press it is still thirty nanoseconds behind, which is the entire career arc of the average retail investor. Denise asked the customer service person, a woman named Priya who was very patient, whether she had actually bought the share or whether the machine had bought the share and then sold it to her. Priya said both were true. The machine bought it. Denise bought it from the machine. The machine made one tenth of one cent. Denise owned one share of Ford. Everyone was happy.

“Denise told Priya the speed is the price of being a person. The machine bought the share before I could tap the button and the machine sold it to me for 0.1 cents, and I told Denise the 0.1 cents is the cost of being slower than New Jersey.”

— Denise, slower than New Jersey

The exchange described the arrangement as offering everyone the same access, which is true, in the way that everyone has the same view of a hallway that is already filled with faster people. Denise's order arrived. It was just that by the time it arrived, it was the answer to someone else's question, and the question was how much Denise would pay to be the answer to her own question, which was a question Denise had not asked, because the machine had already answered it.
image_alt: A woman on a sofa holds a phone beside server racks.

title: Congress Repeals Overdraft Fee Cap, Freeing Banks To Price The 3 A.M. Poor-Person Market At Whatever The Warmth Of A Gas Station Is Worth
dek: Leonard from Nashville put $4.19 in a gas station account at 3:07 in the morning because his heat had been shut off and the gas station was warm. Congress voted to let the bank charge him whatever it decides the moment is worth, and the moment, the bank says, was worth the whole tank.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Leonard from Nashville sat in the gas station on Murfreesboro Pike at three-oh-seven in the morning with the heat on in the parking lot and a bag of SunChips he did not want but needed to buy to justify the parking spot, because the parking spot was not for sitting, the parking spot was for buying, and the buying, in a gas station at three in the morning with four dollars and nineteen cents in your account, is a transaction the bank has now been given the full freedom to price at whatever the market for three-in-the-morning poor people will bear.

Congress voted to repeal the overdraft fee cap, which had limited the penalty to roughly the cost of a small appliance, and restored the bank's right to charge what one cosponsor called the market rate for the privilege of not having the money at the exact moment the money was needed. Leonard, who had four dollars and nineteen cents, and who bought a bag of chips and a forty-ounce Gatorade for a total of six dollars and twelve cents, was now, under the new law, the subject of a transaction the bank would price according to the texture of the moment, which the bank described as desperate, and which the bank said it was prepared to charge for.

“Leonard told the man on the phone the cold was not a factor in the pricing model. The gas station was warm and the bank priced the $4.19 transaction at the whole tank, and I told Leonard the bank is right about what the 3:07 A.M. moment is worth because I was the one in the gas station.”

— Leonard, who priced the warmth

The bank celebrated the repeal as a return to normal banking, which it is, if normal is the word for charging a man forty-seven dollars for a bag of chips he bought because his heat was off. The fee will now be calculated at close of business, based on what the bank calls a dynamic assessment of the customer's position at the moment of the courtesy, and the assessment, having been assessed, will be assessed again in the morning, with interest, because the morning, under the new law, is a separate moment, and every moment counts.
image_alt: A meditating man sits beneath a red stripe beside a snack bag.

title: Private Equity Pays Itself A Billion From The Grocery Store, Replaces The Register Lady Who Knows Mrs. Eldridge's Bananas With A Kiosk That Does Not
dek: A grocery chain's owners extracted a dividend funded by the company's own balance sheet while the chain announced another round of cuts, explaining that the money must go somewhere, and the somewhere was them.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Denise Okonkwo works register 4 at the Piggly Wiggly on Highway 49. She has been at register 4 for 11 years. She knows the regulars by their produce choices. She knows that Mrs. Eldridge buys bananas one at a time and that Mr. Vest will ask for a price check on the store-brand ketchup even though he has asked for a price check on the store-brand ketchup every Tuesday since 2019 and it has always been $1.89. Last week the store installed a kiosk where Denise used to stand. The kiosk does not ask for price checks. The kiosk does not know Mrs. Eldridge's bananas. The kiosk is owned by the same company that owns the dividend.

Buoyant Capital, the firm that owns the chain, paid itself a $1.1 billion dividend in October. The money came from the chain. The chain got the money from the people who buy the bananas. Denise got a notice that her hours are being cut to 24 a week. “The notice was on the bulletin board next to a picture of the new kiosk,” Denise said. “The kiosk does not have hours. The kiosk is never tired. The kiosk has never needed a price check on ketchup that costs $1.89. The kiosk is the best employee we have ever had.”

A clerk who stayed past her cut hours explained the dividend as a “return on strategy” and the hour cuts as “a natural evolution of the labor model.” When asked what the strategy was, he said owning the store. When asked what the natural evolution was, he said fewer people. When asked if the dividend could have funded the people, he said the dividend was funded by the store, and the store is the people, and the people are the hours, and the hours were the dividend, and the dividend was him.

Denise now works 24 hours a week. The kiosk works 24 hours a day. The kiosk does not have a 401(k). The kiosk does not have a daughter studying nursing at the community college. The kiosk has a reset button. “I asked management if the kiosk is my replacement,” Denise said. “They said the kiosk is not my replacement. They said the kiosk is my colleague. I asked what the colleague earns. They said the colleague does not earn anything. I said then the colleague is not a colleague. They said the colleague is a capital expenditure. I said does the capital expenditure need a price check on the ketchup. They said the capital expenditure knows the price of the ketchup. I asked what the price is. They said $1.89. I said thank you.”

“Denise told Mr. Vest the kiosk knows the price of the ketchup is $1.89. I have been in that aisle for 11 years and the kiosk is the most dignified thing in it because the kiosk does not need a price check and the kiosk does not ask where I have been.”

— Denise, who watched 11 years of ketchup
image_alt: A woman beside a kiosk and red-screen terminal on a grid floor.

title: Company Returns A Trillion To Shareholders, Returns Frank From Columbus To Himself In A 3-Minute-42-Second Zoom Call
dek: Frank from Columbus was laid off on a Tuesday Zoom call that lasted three minutes and forty-two seconds. The same Tuesday, the company announced a trillion-dollar buyback. Frank was told the company believes in its people so much it decided to buy itself instead, and that Frank, being a person, has been returned to himself.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Frank from Columbus sat in his home office, which is also his dining room, which is also the room where his daughter does her math homework on a laptop from 2019, and he watched a Zoom screen with thirty-seven other rectangles, each one a face he had seen in a hallway he would never walk down again. The rectangle in the corner was a man named Brad from HR. Brad said the company was returning Frank to himself. Brad used the exact phrase returned to yourself. Frank asked what that meant. Brad said it meant Frank was no longer an employee, and that the burden of being an employee, having been lifted, was now a burden Frank could carry on his own time, as himself.

The same Tuesday, the company announced a trillion-dollar buyback, which is the largest repurchase in the history of the firm and which the company described, in the press release Frank read while updating his resume on a phone with fourteen percent battery, as a demonstration of confidence in the firm's long-term value. Frank, who had worked at the firm for six years and who had been told, in his exit Zoom, that the firm valued him, asked Brad whether the firm valued him at one-trillionth of the buyback. Brad said that was not a helpful way to think about it.

“Frank told Brad the self pays for its own health insurance. The company spent $1 trillion buying itself instead of me, and I told Frank the self is the cost center now and the self is the one who pays the $600 monthly premium.”

— Frank, returned to himself

The analysts called the buyback visionary. They called the layoffs a headwind. Then they called the layoffs visionary and the buyback a tailwind. Then they called the entire quarter a margin story, which is the word for when the company you work for decides the best thing to buy is the thing that does not require you. Frank called it a Tuesday. Brad called the severance a reallocation toward Frank's future, which Brad said was bright, and which Frank, looking at his phone, said would need to be funded separately.
image_alt: A person views a face grid on a laptop beside server racks.

title: Top Fund Manager Has Nothing to Do Until April, Vows to Keep Not Doing It Excellently
dek: With index funds owning the tape, executives celebrated the final transfer of decision-making from humans to a spreadsheet that is not watching them, and is not required to.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Diane Shuptrine sat at her desk at 3:47 in the afternoon with nothing to do. She had already allocated her entire quarter. The allocation was to the same index she had allocated to last quarter and the quarter before that. The index owned everything. Diane owned the index. The index had not called. The index had never called.

“I used to pick stocks,” Diane said. “I picked Regions Financial because my grandfather banked there. I picked Ford because I owned one. I picked Bed Bath & Beyond because the coupons came in the mail and my mother liked the store. That was work. Now I push money into the Vanguard Total Market fund and the Vanguard Total Market fund owns Regions Financial and Ford and Bed Bath & Beyond and the mail truck that brought the coupon.”

The index fund does not require a thesis. The index fund requires a wire transfer and a belief that the wire transfer will eventually be larger in a different direction. This belief is called conviction. The wire transfer does not know it is being believed in. The wire transfer is in a computer.

Diane now spends most of her day reading what the analysts beneath her write about the stocks the index owns anyway. The analysts know the index owns them anyway. The analysts are paid in index shares. “Every report ends with ‘overweight,’” Diane said. “I looked it up. Overweight is the default. Overweight is the only setting.”

“Diane told the analysts the only setting is overweight. The index owns 100% of the stocks and the analysts own the index and I told Diane the market decided the stock is good and I do not need to think about whether the stock is good because the market is the index and the index is me.”

— Diane, who owns the default setting
image_alt: A person at a desk near blue bars and a red line.

title: Hauler Flags 11 Houses With ‘The Bloom,’ Describes a Pizza Box So Degraded It Has Become the Homeowner
dek: A sanitation firm, citing record contamination, said rates must rise to handle a stream so degraded it no longer resembles recycling, and urged households to consider that the waste, in a very real sense, is them.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Terrence McDade stood at the curb in his bathrobe at 6:14 in the morning and watched the truck skip his can for the third Tuesday in a row. He had put a pizza box in the recycling again. He knew better. He had known better the first time. The pizza box is not recyclable. The pizza box is, in a very specific way, Terrence.

Route supervisor Maurice Litt has now flagged 11 houses on Terrence's block with a notation the company calls “the bloom.” The bloom is not a flower. The bloom is what the garbage does to the garbage that is already inside the garbage when the garbage sits too long waiting for the truck that will not take it because of the pizza box.

“I look at what they put out and I see who they are,” Litt said. “Terrence McDade is a pizza-box-in-the-recycling guy. That is his personality now. His wife knows. His kids know. The guy who drives behind me on the route knows. You cannot be a different person next week. The pizza box is who you are.”

The new rate, which the company calls a “sort-incentive adjustment” and Terrence calls “another $9 a month to feel worse,” is designed to fund interpretation: what the hauler now calls the part of the job where it figures out what you meant. “We are translation services for your denial,” Litt said.

Terrence is now considering composting. He is also considering moving. He is also considering, for the first time in 40 years, buying a vegetable he does not have to peel from a box.

“I told my wife the $2.70 a week is what the planet costs and she should be glad the curb fee went up before the pizza box did. They charged me seven dollars for the eighth bag and I paid it proud, because a man who cannot pay for his own garbage is a man who does not understand what he is worth.”

— a resident who pays the curb fee on time so the pizza box understands who opened the lid
image_alt: A man holds a pizza beside a blue garbage truck and rubble.

title: Fund Manager Buys Exactly What He Bought Yesterday at the Same Time as Everyone Else, Calls It Strategic Discipline
dek: Index vehicles now do nearly all their buying at the day's final auction, a practice regulators call elegant and investors call 4:00 PM.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Avery Loomis manages $27 billion in index strategies and has not made a discretionary trade since 2023. He describes this as the most sophisticated period of his career. Every afternoon at 3:55, he opens a window on his terminal that shows the closing auction. At 4:00, his algorithm buys exactly what it bought the day before, at exactly the same time as every other algorithm that is also buying exactly what it bought the day before. The closing price is the price. Avery’s job is to arrive at it.

“I used to trade in the morning,” Avery said. “I would watch the open. I would read the news. I would form a view. The view was always wrong. Not wrong in an interesting way. Wrong in the way that a man who has an opinion about a thing he does not control is always wrong. The closing auction does not require a view. The closing auction is a fact. The fact is $147.23. I do not need to believe anything about $147.23. I need to own it.”

The industry calls this “liquidity consolidation.” Avery calls it “giving up.” He says it with pride. “Giving up is the correct answer,” he said. “The stock market is a machine that produces a number every day. The number is the correct number because the machine says it is the correct number. Fighting the machine is a hobby. I do not have hobbies. I have index funds.”

Avery’s day now ends at 4:01. He makes more money than he did when his day ended at 4:00 and he spent the other 23 hours and 59 minutes worrying about what happened between 4:01 and 4:00 the next day. “My wife asked if I miss the thrill of the trade,” Avery said. “I said the trade was never thrilling. The trade was expensive and I was bad at it. The closing auction is free and I am perfect at it. I do nothing and the market hands me the average. Every single day. The average is up. I do not deserve the average. But the average does not know that.”

“I set my limit order for 3:59 every single day. The closing auction is the only time I know I'm getting the same price as the institutions. That's discipline. That's how you beat the market without trying.”

— a retail investor who sets his alarm for the close
image_alt: A figure sits at a glowing monitor in an empty dark hall.

title: Bank Charges Man $35 Because He Had $14 Less Than a Computer Expected, Confirms No Error Occurred
dek: A new report names the largest fee collectors while collecting them into a bracket, which is the last place the money will not be touched.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Darnell Hicks looked at his phone at 6 AM on a Tuesday. His checking account balance was negative $14. The charge that made it negative was a $3.99 debit for a streaming service he forgot he had. The fee for the negative was $35. The fee was charged automatically by a computer. The computer does not know Darnell. The computer does not know that Darnell has $14 less than the computer thinks he should have. The computer knows only that the balance fell below zero, and that a $35 adjustment is the mathematically correct response to a $3.99 error.

“I called the bank and said I want my $35 back,” Darnell said. “They said the fee is for the service of honoring the transaction. I said I did not ask you to honor the transaction. They said the overdraft protection automatically honors transactions that would otherwise be declined. I said then decline it next time. They said I have to opt out of overdraft protection. I asked how. They said by filling out a form. I asked where the form is. They said online. I asked where online. They said under account services. I asked how to get to account services. They said log in. I said my account is negative $14. They said you can still log in. I logged in. The form was 14 pages long. My phone died on page 3. The fee stayed.”

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau published its annual Overdraft Hall of Shame. Darnell’s bank is on it. The report cost $6 million to produce. The bank paid $435 million in overdraft fees last year. The bank considers the report a cost of doing business. Darnell considers the report a brochure for the bank’s most popular product. “They put the bank in the Hall of Shame and the bank put my fee in the revenue column,” Darnell said. “The Hall of Shame is funded by the Hall of Shame. That is a closed loop. That is efficiency.”

Darnell’s account is now overdrawn by $49. He gets paid Friday. He will pay the $35 fee. He will pay the $3.99 subscription that caused the fee. He will have $12 left. He is the business model. “The bank made more off my $3.99 mistake than the streaming service made off my subscription,” Darnell said. “I am not a customer. I am a mining operation. The $35 is the ore. The bank is the smelter. The Hall of Shame is the annual report to the shareholders of the mine.”

“The $35 fee is the reason I keep track of my money. Before the fee, I never knew my balance. The fee taught me to pay attention. That's worth thirty-five dollars of education.”

— a cardholder who values the notification service
image_alt: A man on a bed before a classical facade and red panel.

title: Private Equity Fires the Person Who Signs the Paychecks, Determines the Hole Is Now a Synergy Hole
dek: A portfolio company announced headcount reductions at its own facilities after the sponsor identified overlap between the employees and the work.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Simone Doherty used to work in payroll at a regional grocery distributor owned by a private equity firm called Summit Ridge Capital. She signed the checks. She printed them. She stuffed them in envelopes. She watched the people who cashed them. Last month, Summit Ridge identified an overlap between the employees who signed the paychecks and the employees who received the paychecks, and determined that the overlap was costing the company money. Simone was offered a severance of two weeks and a reminder that her login would expire at 5 PM.

“I asked the operating partner who would sign the checks now,” Simone said. “He said the checks would be signed automatically. I asked who would verify the hours. He said the system would verify the hours. I asked who would fix the system when the system paid someone twice. He said that was a future-synergy opportunity. I said that sounds like a problem. He said problems are opportunities. I asked if the opportunity included my job. He said the opportunity had already been optimized.”

Simone’s position was one of 47 eliminated in the wave. The company saved $1.9 million in salary and benefits. The firm booked the savings as operational improvement. The people who used to cash the checks Simone signed are now paid through a portal that does not have a phone number. The portal is very efficient. The portal does not make mistakes. The portal does not know Mrs. Eldridge’s banana schedule. The portal is the future of payroll.

“I went back to get my things and the woman at the front desk asked me to sign for my last check. I signed it. I handed it back. I said now what. She said now the synergy is complete. I asked if I could use the bathroom. She said the bathroom was a shared resource and costs were being allocated. I said I used that bathroom for 11 years. She said the bathroom is a cost center now. I said what was it before. She said a facility. I said the facility is a bathroom. She said the classification has changed.”

“The bathroom was a shared resource and we were using it for free for eleven years. Of course it's a cost center now. Everything has a cost. That's just accounting catching up to reality.”

— a former employee who understands resource allocation
image_alt: A woman at a desk beside a blue stack topped with red.

title: Heiress With a Staff-Directory Apartment Secures $15 Million Exemption, Explains the Point Is the Money Never Touches Her
dek: Estate planners celebrated the end of the sunset by building trusts for clients who have already outlived the uncertainty they were drafting for.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Delia Voss is 31 years old and has not worked a day in her life. She does not say this with shame. She says this, to a reporter, while holding a coffee that costs $14, in an apartment building that has a staff directory posted in the elevator for residents who forget which floor their neighbors live on. Her grandfather built a regional trucking company. Her father sold it. Her lawyers have now ensured that the proceeds of the sale will never touch her and will therefore never be touched by the government. She is, by every legal measure, prepared.

“We met with the estate planner and he explained the dynasty trust as a gift from my grandfather that would keep giving forever,” Delia said. “I asked who the giving goes to. He said me. I asked what I have to do. He said nothing. I asked if that was legal. He said it is the purpose of the law. The law says my grandfather can give me money and the money can sit in a trust and the trust can buy things and the things can be held and the holding can be transferred and the transfer can be exempt. I said exempt from what. He said everything.”

The estate exemption makes the first $15 million of any estate free of federal tax. For Delia’s family, the estate is $214 million. The planner described the remaining $199 million as a “manageable planning exercise.” The exercise involves several more trusts, a family limited partnership with no actual partners, and an insurance policy written by a company Delia has never visited, in a jurisdiction she has never been to, that she will never collect on because nobody in her family has ever needed insurance.

“I asked the lawyer what happens if I have children,” Delia said. “He said the trust will provide for them. I asked what they have to do. He said nothing. I asked if anyone in my family has ever done anything. He said your grandfather drove a truck. I said my grandfather drove a truck. He said that is where the money came from. I asked where the money is going. He said nowhere. He said that is the point. The money is going nowhere. The money is going to me to go nowhere.”

“The $15 million exemption keeps the money where it belongs. My grandfather drove a truck and built something. The government shouldn't take half of it because he died. The trust keeps the family together.”

— a trust beneficiary who believes in generational wealth
image_alt: A woman stands before a tall block tower with a red stripe.

title: Fed and the Data Remain in a Closed-Loop Relationship That Does Not Include a Nail Salon Owner
dek: The committee left policy unchanged and noted, for the forty-second straight meeting, that it remains data dependent, which sources confirm is the point.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Anita Meeks runs a nail salon in a strip mall between a mattress store and a vape shop. She has been watching interest rates for two years because the banker who holds her equipment loan told her to watch them. She watches them on her phone. The rates do not move. The banker calls and says they are data dependent. Anita asks what data. The banker says the data the Fed watches. Anita asks what the Fed watches. The banker says the data. Anita now believes that the Fed and the data are in a relationship that does not include her.

“I asked my banker when the rate will go down,” Anita said. “He said it depends on the data. I asked what data. He said employment, inflation, consumer spending. I asked if my business counts. He said small businesses are in the data. I asked which part. He said the part where people get jobs. I said my customers get jobs. He said that is the data. I said is the data telling the Fed to keep rates high. He said the data is complicated. I said is the data complicated because I am in it. He hung up.”

At the press conference, the Chair said the committee needs to see more progress on inflation. Anita’s rent has gone up 8 percent. Her gel supply costs 12 percent more than last year. Her customers are coming less often. She is the data. The data is telling the Fed something. The Fed is watching the data. The data is watching the Fed. Nobody is watching Anita.

“I called the Federal Reserve,” Anita said. “I asked to speak to someone about the data. They said the Fed does not take calls from the public about the data. I said I am the data. They said the data is submitted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. I said I am not the Bureau of Labor Statistics. They said then you are not the data. I asked what I am. They said you are a member of the public affected by the data. I asked if that counts. They said it counts in the data. I hung up and looked at my phone. The rate was still 3.875 percent. The nails were still wet.”

“I trust the Fed. They said they need more data before they move. That's responsible. My rate is 3.875 percent and I'm fine with it. I would rather they wait than make a mistake with the whole economy.”

— a small business owner who trusts the data
image_alt: A woman stands under a circular arrow near two storefronts.

title: Interest on the Rice Also Rides the Atlas Mart Conveyor Belt, Bank Hails Resilient Shopper
dek: Lenders point to sturdy household demand, defined as the willingness of the same households to keep paying for the privilege of having borrowed.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Ray Okafor stands at register 7 of the Atlas Mart on Tryon Road at 8:47 on a Tuesday night with a basket containing: one bag of rice, one bag of pinto beans, one gallon of milk, one bottle of store-brand dish soap, and $422.19 in credit card debt that was $380.00 last month. He puts the rice on the belt. The interest on the $422.19 accrues while the rice moves down the conveyor. The interest on the rice, technically, is also on the belt.

“My credit card company sent me a letter congratulating me on my strong consumer demand,” Ray said. “I called to ask what that meant. They said it means I keep buying things. I said I need to eat. They said that is what consumer demand is. I said the rice is 22 percent now. They said the rice is not 22 percent, the borrowing of the money for the rice is 22 percent. I said I am borrowing the money for the rice because I do not have the money for the rice. They said that is why consumer demand is strong.”

The bank’s chief economist confirmed that a consumer paying 22 percent on a revolving balance is a consumer who has demonstrated commitment. “A person who is willing to pay 22 percent to keep eating is a person who is not going to stop eating,” the economist said. “That is durable demand. That is the kind of demand you can model. We have modeled it. It pays 22 percent.”

Ray looked at his statement. The minimum payment was $38. The interest charge was $47. The principal went down by negative $9. Ray put the dish soap on the belt. “I am doing great,” he said. “My demand has never been stronger. I demanded rice and the bank demanded 22 percent of the rice forever. That is a relationship. That is two people who need each other. I need rice. They need me to need rice on a card that never goes to zero. We are both getting what we want.”

“Twenty-two percent is the price of having the card available. I use it for everything. The rice, the gas, the electric. I pay the minimum and the card is always there. That's the relationship. That's the agreement I made.”

— a cardholder who values consistent credit access
image_alt: A worker stands beside a conveyor feeding cash into a red-geared machine.

title: Fed Retires Dot Plot After 14 Years of Wrong Projections, Vows Future Will Be Wrong About Something Else
dek: The scatter chart had one last request before it was phased out: that the committee note it was never the members who were poor at plotting, only the future.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Shelley Ng works in the publications office of the Federal Reserve Board. Her job is to format the quarterly Summary of Economic Projections, a document that contains seventeen pages of charts, footnotes, and projections that are wrong within six weeks of printing. She has done this for fourteen years. She has never once seen a projection survive a full quarter without being revised, apologized for, or silently replaced.

The dot plot was her least favorite page. Every quarter she would lay out nineteen tiny dots in a scatter chart that showed where each committee member thought rates would be in three years. Every quarter the dots would be wrong. Every quarter Shelley would format them anyway, because her job is not to be right but to make the wrongness look professional.

The Fed announced this week that the dot plot is being retired and replaced with a single comma. The comma will appear at the end of every FOMC statement. The Fed says the comma will be "inflected for tone" depending on the data. Shelley has been asked to format the comma. She asked her supervisor what "inflected" means. Her supervisor said it means they can make the comma slightly italic if they want to signal concern. Shelley asked if there was a comma bold for panic. Her supervisor did not laugh.

Shelley's actual opinion is that the comma is a better system because it says less and therefore cannot be as wrong. The dot plot projected rates at 2.5 percent for 2025. The actual rate was 5.5 percent. The comma, by comparison, never promised anything. It just sits there, on the page, admitting the sentence is ongoing, which is the most honest thing the Fed has printed in a decade.

“The dot plot was wrong for fourteen years. The comma has never been wrong. I like knowing I'm getting something honest. A comma just sits there and admits the sentence is not over. That's the most reliable thing the Fed has ever printed.”

— a Fed watcher who prefers the comma

Shelley will file the dot plot materials in the archive, which is where the Fed keeps everything it used to be sure about. The archivist is named Phil. He has been there thirty years. He told Shelley the comma was a good idea. He has seen longer systems fail.
image_alt: A woman works at a laptop before a courthouse and stock charts.

title: Jobless Claims Hit Three-Year Low After System Decides Running Out of Weeks Is the Same as Finding a Job
dek: The number of Americans on unemployment checks fell to a three-year low, which economists called strength and the people whose checks ran out called a different thing, spelled with fewer syllables.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Tom Eckert is not in the unemployment numbers this week. He was in them nine weeks ago, and eight weeks ago, and seven weeks ago, and then the weeks ran out, which is how the number got so low so fast. The Labor Department announced the three-year low as a milestone. Tom found out from a notification on his phone that said his claim had been resolved. He did not resolve it. The system resolved it.

The system resolved it because Tom had been on unemployment for twenty-six weeks, which is the maximum, which the system treats as a cure. Tom is not cured. Tom has applied to thirty-seven jobs since his warehouse shift was replaced by a conveyor belt that the company said could do his job for $14 an hour and also did not complain about the heat. Tom did not complain about the heat either, but the conveyor belt does not need health insurance, which the company said was the deciding factor.

Tom sat in the career center this morning. The career center has a computer lab with six computers, two of which work. Tom used one to fill out an application for a forklift position at a warehouse that he knows laid off its own forklift crew three months ago. He applied anyway, because the application asked if he was willing to work nights and weekends, and he clicked yes, which he has been clicking yes to for two months, and the yes has not worked yet.

The Labor Department says the drop in continuing claims proves the economy is running on its own. Tom says he would like to be part of the economy that is running on its own, because the one he is in right now runs on a prepaid debit card with $47 on it and a warning that a $5.50 fee applies if he uses it wrong.

“Twenty-six weeks of unemployment is enough. The system gave me what it was supposed to give me. I'm not in the numbers anymore and that means the economy is working. I just have to find my next step.”

— a former claimant who agrees the system worked

Next week the number will drop again. Tom will not be in it. The week after that, neither will anyone else whose twenty-six weeks just ended, and the number will be the lowest it has ever been, and the Labor Department will hold a press conference, and nobody will ask what happened to the people whose number just got so low.
image_alt: A figure stands between a classical building, grid screen, and conveyor.

title: Company Authorizes $12 Billion Buyback; Employees Applaud a Bonus Reserved for People Who Do Not Work Here
dek: Management called the repurchase a statement of confidence in the company's future, to be funded by the future's current occupants.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
Karen Oluwole has worked at Canton Consumer Products for eighteen years. She packs boxes on the line, same as when she started. The company authorized a record $12 billion buyback this week. Her manager gathered the shift to tell them. The room cheered. Karen did not cheer. She does not own stock. She owns a 401(k) with $14,000 in it that she cannot touch for thirty more years, assuming Canton Consumer Products still exists, which she is not confident about, because they stopped giving raises two years ago and started buying back stock instead.

Her manager said the buyback was the equivalent of hiring an employee who costs nothing, works forever, and never calls in sick. The employee is a share of stock. The share does not need health insurance, which the company noted was a significant savings. Karen thought about her own health insurance. Her deductible is $3,500. She had to use it this year for a root canal. The share of stock does not get root canals.

The buyback was funded by $12 billion. Karen does not know what $12 billion looks like. She knows what $12 looks like, because she spent it on lunch yesterday. She knows what $12 billion smells like, which is the same as $12, if you believe the company, which just told the shift to embrace a new culture of ownership. Karen asked her manager if the new culture of ownership came with a raise. Her manager said the raise was the stock going up. Karen asked how she was supposed to spend a stock that went up on groceries. Her manager said that was not a question he had an answer for.

“The $12 billion buyback shows management believes in the company. I've been here eighteen years. I've never seen that kind of commitment. The stock going up is the raise. That's how ownership works.”

— a packing line employee who supports shareholder value

Karen went back to packing boxes. The boxes have the company logo on them. She does not own the company. The company owns her, until the buyback is big enough, at which point it will own only itself, which Karen suspects is the whole idea.
image_alt: A billboard with a red upward arrow stands above seated workers.

title: Regulators Cap Late Fee at Eight Dollars; Couch That Cost $1,200 in 1989 and Broke in 1992 Has Now Generated $14,700 in Interest
dek: Banks confirmed the consumer can now be late for substantially less, provided she remains late for substantially longer.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Lou Brackett has carried a balance on his Visa card since 1989. He knows this because every statement includes a line that says what he has paid in interest since 1989. The number is $14,700. Lou does not have $14,700. He has $14,700 in interest.
