The principal, which started at $1,200 for a couch he bought when he was twenty-two and thought he would have a better job by now, is still $1,100. The couch broke in 1992.

The new rule caps late fees at eight dollars. Lou saw this on the news and thought finally. Then he read the rest of the article. The rest says the cap only applies to the late fee itself. The interest still compounds. The minimum payment still accrues. Lou's minimum payment is $68. The late fee was $39. Now it is $8. The bank called the remaining $31 "administrative hospitality," which Lou looked up and does not mean anything, except that it is on his bill now, under a separate line item.

Lou called the bank to ask about the administrative hospitality. The representative said it was a fee for the service of managing his overdue account. Lou asked if he asked for that service. The representative said it was provided automatically. Lou asked if he could decline the service. The representative said it was not optional. Lou asked what happened if he did not pay the administrative hospitality. The representative said it would be added to his balance and accrue interest at 24.99 percent.

Lou is sixty-one years old. He works at a hardware store. He does not think he will ever pay off the couch. The couch is gone. The interest is not. The new fee cap, Lou said, is like being charged $8 for the parking ticket instead of $39. You still owe the parking. You still cannot park there. You just get a receipt that stings less.

“Eight dollars is reasonable for a late fee. The administrative hospitality is just the cost of the processing. I was late. I should pay for that. The bank has to make money too. That's the agreement I signed.”

— a cardholder who accepts the new fee structure

Lou hung up. His bill is due Friday. He does not have the $68. He will pay the administrative hospitality instead, which he assumes will count for something, although from the call, he is not sure what.
image_alt: A giant red device pours coins above a seated man.

title: Passive Funds Mirror Benchmarks So Perfectly That Customers Ask Why Losing Everything Is Better Than Losing Less; Vanguard Confirms It Is an Excellent Question
dek: Somewhere in the closing auction, a fund confirmed it was the index, and the index, citing precedent, confirmed it was the fund.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Tanya Orozco answers phones at Vanguard's retail support center in Scottsdale. Her job is to explain to people why their account went down when the market went down. Lately the calls have been getting harder, because the answer is no longer that the fund lost money. The answer is that the fund lost exactly what the index lost, which is the whole point, and the caller does not understand how losing all of it is better than losing some of it.

Tanya has a script. The script says to explain that passive investing means accepting market returns, which means when the market goes down, the fund goes down by the same amount, which is the tradeoff for lower fees. Callers ask her if the market going down is a market return. Tanya says yes. Callers say they thought a return meant you got your money back. Tanya says that is not how the industry uses the word. Callers say the industry can go fuck itself.

The fund Tanya fields the most calls about owns 3,500 stocks. It owns them in the same proportion as the index. The index, in turn, is calculated from the stocks the fund owns. Tanya has read the fine print. She has concluded that the fund and the index are now the same thing, which means the fund is benchmarked against itself, which means the fund can never underperform, which also means it can never outperform, which means the only thing Tanya can tell callers is that their money is doing exactly what math says it will do, which is not what anyone wants to hear.

The woman on the phone right now is named Carol. She is retired. She has $240,000 in the fund. She wants to know why it went down $8,000 this month. Tanya tells her it is because the index went down. Carol asks why the index went down. Tanya says because the stocks went down. Carol asks why the stocks went down. Tanya says because the market sold them. Carol asks who sold them. Tanya says other funds. Carol asks what funds. Tanya says the funds that track the index. Carol is quiet for a minute. Carol says so I am losing money because my fund and the other funds are selling each other the same stocks. Tanya says yes. Carol says that is stupid. Tanya says yes.

“If everybody owns the same thing, nobody is wrong. I put my retirement in the index. The index goes up over time. I don't need to beat the market. I just need to be the market. That's the strategy.”

— an index investor who stays the course

Tanya is not allowed to say that the whole system is a circle. The script does not have that answer. The script tells her to say the fund is operating as designed. Tanya says it. Carol says the design is stupid. Tanya does not disagree.
image_alt: A window shows businessmen shaking hands above a woman at a desk.

title: Family Office Lists Vacancy for Next-Generation Principal; Job Description Strategically Omits the Word 'Born'
dek: The position, the office confirmed, had always been filled, but the paperwork had simply never been told.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Maya Rivas has been an executive assistant at the Voss Family Office for eleven years. Her job this week: post an internal job listing for the role of next-generation principal. The listing requires no resume, no references, and one qualification Maya is not allowed to put in writing, which is that the candidate has to share DNA with the person who signs her paycheck.

Maya typed up the description. She listed the duties as "strategic vision setting" and "capital stewardship." The actual duty, she knows, is being born to the right people and remaining alive. She printed the listing and taped it to a door that only three people walk through, one of whom is the heir, whose job interview consisted of his mother asking him if he wanted lunch.

The heir's name is Connor. He is twenty-four. Maya orders his lunch most days. He has never asked her what she makes. She has never told him, because if he knew, he might feel bad, and then one of the other assistants would have to comfort him, and then nobody would get the lunch order right.

Connor showed up for his "interview" in sweatpants. Maya was asked to sit in the room and take notes. The questions were: "Do you want the job?" and "Are you going to do anything weird with the money?" Connor said yes to the first and no to the second. The second was not true, but the office felt it was the right kind of not true.

“Connor has been around the office since he was twelve years old. He knows the culture. The paperwork is just formalities. The health insurance started immediately. That's how a family office should work.”

— a family office employee who respects the succession

Maya is responsible for onboarding Connor. She printed his employee handbook and left it on his desk. He asked her if there was a cafeteria. She told him he can order whatever he wants. He said no, I mean like, a place to sit. Maya said yes, there are six of them, all empty. Connor said sweet.
image_alt: A woman hands papers to a man through a yellow door.

title: AI Firm Borrows $4 Billion for More Servers; Technician Who Keeps Them Cool Makes $68,000 With a Broken Garbage Disposal
dek: The loan is investment grade. The payoff is a forecast. The forecast is a belief.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
Derek Okonkwo is a data center technician at ExaCompute Holdings. His job is to keep the servers cool. The servers are what the company just borrowed $4 billion to buy more of. Derek was not consulted on the borrowing, although he will be consulted on the cooling, by a loud alarm at 3 a.m.

Derek makes $68,000 a year. The servers he maintains cost $3 million per rack. He knows this because a manager told him once, during a power outage, to treat each rack like it was his own house. Derek thought about his own house. He lives in a two-bedroom apartment with a broken garbage disposal. He treats the racks like they are Yale.

The company borrowed the full $4 billion in one day. The banker who signed the deal was quoted saying the credit story was "the strongest he had heard all year." Derek's credit story is a Visa card with a $4,200 limit and two late payments from last January when he had to choose between the minimum and dinner.

When the servers go down, Derek is the one who drives in. He told his boss once that the company should maybe not borrow so much money for machines that break when the air gets too warm. His boss said that's why they pay Derek. Derek said they pay him $68,000. His boss said the market rate for server technicians is fifty-two and to be grateful.

“Four billion dollars is a lot of servers but the computers are going to figure things out that people cannot. I keep them cool. That is my job. The $4 billion is an investment in the future and I am part of it.”

— a data center technician who believes in the vision

The company says the computers will generate enough revenue to service the debt. Derek says the computers currently generate a lot of heat and a weekly report that nobody reads. He says this quietly, because he likes the health insurance.
image_alt: A construction worker stands before server racks and a classical building.

title: Family Office Acquires Office Tower Unannounced; Office Manager Now Reports to a Coat Worth More Than Her Car
dek: Forced sales, discounted towers, re-rated everything. The private rich call it a buyer's market; the public funds call it Monday.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Janelle Cruz is the office manager for a mid-sized law firm on the seventeenth floor of 200 Madison. She handles the mail, orders the printer toner, and as of two weeks ago, she works for a family office she has never heard of, whose representative showed up unannounced and took measurements of the lobby with a laser.

The representative's name is Delia Voss. She is the third-generation principal of the Voss Family Office. She is thirty-one. She wore a coat that cost more than Janelle's car. She told Janelle that her family had "acquired the building at a highly attractive basis," which Janelle later learned from Google means the building was losing money and the bank wanted out.

The building is losing money because half the floors are empty. The floors are empty because the rent is too high. The rent is too high because the previous owner, a pension fund, needed the building to be worth a certain amount on paper so the pension fund could tell its retirees that everything was fine. The pension fund stopped telling the retirees that. The retirees stopped believing it. Now Delia Voss owns the building, and Janelle's firm is month-to-month, which means the rent can go up at any time, and Delia Voss does not seem like the type who is going to lower it.

Janelle asked Delia if the new ownership meant the broken elevator on the freight side would finally get fixed. Delia said the elevator was a capital expense and the capital was currently allocated to something else. Janelle asked what. Delia said the capital was allocated to acquiring buildings with broken elevators at a discount. Janelle took the stairs.

“Buying buildings nobody wants is how you find value. The mold in the sub-basement is a basis adjustment. That is accounting. The building will be worth more once the market realizes what we paid for it.”

— a building manager who understands distressed assets
image_alt: A man holds a yellow pole toward a woman at a desk.

title: Fed Raises Rates Again; Homeowner Who Was Told to Wait for Lower Rates Has Now Waited Long Enough for a Higher Payment
dek: We are not raising rates because they are too high, the committee explained; we are raising them because they are not high enough yet.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Lamar Jenkins has a mortgage. It is a thirty-year fixed at 6.8 percent, which he got last year because his realtor told him rates were going to come down. Rates did not come down. Rates went up. Lamar has called his bank three times to ask about refinancing. Each time they told him to wait. This morning the Federal Reserve confirmed that waiting is the plan.

Lamar does not know the members of the Federal Open Market Committee by name. He knows them by their effect on his monthly payment, which went up $340 in the last year. He makes $67,000 as a maintenance supervisor for the county. The $340 came out of the grocery budget. His wife asked him last week if they could eat meat more than twice a week. Lamar said the Fed was data-dependent. His wife said the data could go fuck itself.

The Fed statement said rate hikes would continue until inflation was "convincingly on path to target." Lamar asked his brother-in-law, who watches CNBC, what that meant. His brother-in-law said it meant they were going to keep raising rates until something breaks. Lamar asked what. His brother-in-law said probably his mortgage.

Lamar looked up the Fed chair's salary. It is $246,000. He looked up how many houses the chair owns. The chair owns one house. Lamar found this reassuring until he remembered the chair bought it in 1998, when a thirty-year fixed was 5.7 percent and a maintenance supervisor could feed his family meat.

“The Fed has to raise rates. Inflation is 3 percent and they need to get it under control. My mortgage is locked at 5.7 percent. I am fine with rate hikes. Discipline is what keeps the economy healthy.”

— a homeowner who trusts the rate hikes

The Fed says the economy is resilient. Lamar says resilient means you can still afford chicken, barely. He says the Fed can say whatever it wants. He still has to pay the 6.8 percent.
image_alt: A red arrow rises behind a domed government building and small house.

title: Meridian Micro Board Confirms Succession a Success; Night Guard Who Checked the Founder's Badge for Seven Years Did Not Know the Badge Was Transferable
dek: The board called the departure a winning bet, which is what the market tells you regardless of what the chip maker says.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Marcus Webb is a security guard at Meridian Micro's Santa Clara campus. He works the night shift at the main gate. He has watched the founder drive out in a black sedan every night for seven years. Tonight the founder did not drive out. The founder is gone. The board said this is proof the succession plan worked. Marcus said he did not know there was a succession plan. He thought the founder just owned the place.

The board held a press conference to announce that the company was now bigger than any one person. Marcus, who checks badges for a living, thought this was a weird thing to say about a company that was worth more than most countries because of a person who built it in his garage. He did not say this to anyone, because his job is to check badges, not to have opinions about succession.

The new CEO is someone Marcus has never seen before. The new CEO drives a different car. Marcus was told to wave him through. He waves him through. The new CEO does not wave back. The founder used to wave back. The founder knew Marcus's name. He asked about Marcus's daughter once. His daughter is a sophomore in college. The new CEO does not know Marcus's daughter exists.

Marcus asked his supervisor if the layoffs were coming. His supervisor said the company was not doing layoffs, it was "optimizing headcount for the next growth cycle." Marcus asked if that meant he should update his resume. His supervisor said he could do whatever he wanted, the badge checkers were being outsourced to a firm in India next quarter, but that was unrelated to the succession plan. Marcus did not ask how.

“The founder built the company and now the new CEO is running it. That is how succession works. The badge changed hands. The company is worth more than when the founder left. That is a success by every measure.”

— a security guard who respects the leadership transition

Marcus's shift ends at 6 a.m. He clocked out, walked past the empty podium where the board made its announcement, and drove home. He has been applying to other security jobs. He isn't sure the succession plan includes him.
image_alt: A guard booth, car, statue and red-lit office in a parking lot.

title: Blackstone Raises $3 Billion for Secondaries; Building Super Who Has Fixed the Boiler for Twenty-Two Years Was Not Consulted
dek: Secondaries are booming because everyone is trying to leave at once, and someone has to be the door.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
Randy Phelps has been the building super at 175 Fleet Street for twenty-two years. He fixes the boiler when it freezes, unclogs the toilets on the fourth floor, and as of this month, he works for a building that is owned by a fund, which is owned by another fund, which is owned by people Randy has never met and who, according to the mail he sometimes forwards, live in a ZIP code where the garbage disposal probably works.

Blackstone is raising $3 billion to buy stakes in funds like the one that owns Randy's building. Randy found out about this from a letter that came to the boiler room addressed to "Current Occupant." He read it because it had his building's address on it. It said the fund that owns 175 Fleet was being reorganized to "unlock latent value." Randy's boiler does not have latent value. It has a leaky valve that he has been fixing with epoxy since 2019.

The people who own Randy's building have never been to Randy's building. They send inspectors, who take pictures of the lobby and leave. One inspector told Randy the building was a "core-plus asset." Randy said he didn't know what that meant. The inspector said it meant they'd probably sell it. Randy asked to who. The inspector said Blackstone probably, or someone like Blackstone. Randy asked if they'd fix the boiler. The inspector laughed.

Randy figures the $3 billion will change hands and his building will get a new owner, which is what his building gets every three years, along with a new name for the same leak. He says he does not care who owns the fund that owns the building that he cleans the trash chute of. The trash does not care either.

“Twenty-two years I have been here and I have seen five different owners. Each one had a plan. The special-purpose vehicle is just the latest structure. The boiler still runs. That is what matters.”

— a building superintendent who adapts to new ownership
image_alt: A small worker stands before a towering paper stack.

title: Software Firm Blames Outage on Servers Nobody Maintained; Engineer Who Maintained Them Accepted a Buyout She Did Not Volunteer For
dek: The email, the teams, the meetings all down at once. The company said no layoffs were involved, only upgrades.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Priya Chandrasekhar was a senior cloud engineer at Cascade Software Outfitters until last Tuesday, when she accepted a voluntary buyout she did not volunteer for. She was one of 60,000. Her last day was Friday. On Monday, the company's entire cloud platform went down, because the servers that Priya used to maintain were no longer being maintained by anyone, because the people who maintained them had accepted buyouts they did not volunteer for.

The company blamed the outage on "unexpected server unavailability." Priya, who still has her Slack access for another week, saw the internal message. The message said a routine certificate rotation had been missed because the team responsible for certificate rotation had been reduced by 40 percent. Priya was the 40 percent. She typed a reply, then deleted it, because she is not their problem anymore.

The outage lasted seven hours. Clients could not access their files. The company's support team, which had also been reduced, sent an auto-reply saying the issue was being investigated by the appropriate team, which was also reduced, and had been reorganized into a different team, which no longer existed. Priya watched this from her apartment, where she is now figuring out if her severance covers COBRA. It covers two months.

A reporter asked the CEO if there was a connection between the buyouts and the outage. The CEO said any connection was speculative. The reporter asked if the company had considered keeping the people who knew how the servers worked. The CEO said the company was building a more agile workforce. Priya's former team was thirteen people. Now it is three. The three people are not agile. They are terrified. Priya knows this because two of them texted her asking if she could come back as a contractor. She said she would think about it. She is thinking about it. She does not want to, but COBRA costs $1,200 a month.

“Sixty thousand people took the buyout. It was voluntary. The servers went down during the transition. That is normal. The company will hire new people who will learn the systems. Change takes time.”

— a former engineer who supports the restructuring

Priya's Slack access expires in five days. She has not been asked to return. The servers are back up, she heard, because two contractors from the Philippines were hired to do what her team of thirteen used to do. She wishes them luck. The certificate rotation is every ninety days. She wonders who will catch it next time.
image_alt: A sealed envelope floats above a data center.

title: Cost Of Running Your Own Family Office Hits $6.6 Million A Year, And The People Who Pay It Have Stopped Reading The Number As A Number
dek: The ultimate luxury is reportedly not the fleet or the compound but the $6.6 million annual operating bill of the office that keeps track of both.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Sterling National's annual survey of the world's largest family offices found that running a single office for a billion-dollar-plus family now costs about $6.6 million a year, up from $6.1 million, and that families considering the expense have reportedly asked one reasonable question: is that enough.

"We don't call it cost anymore," said Josephine Mercouris, a third-generation heir whose family office employs 14 people to manage the money her grandfather made selling something she has never had to name. "We call it the payroll of the people who make sure we never hear the word 'cost' in a room with windows."

About 55 percent of offices surveyed target a 7 to 10 percent return, a range industry advisers described as humble and, relative to the household, extremely generous. "The $6.6 million is not overhead," said a wealth adviser who counts three family offices as clients. "It is membership dues to the only club whose grief is outsourced. You do not want to handle your own grief. That is what the office manager is for."

“Six point six million sounds like a lot but when you add up the accountants, the lawyers, the property managers, the pilots, it is actually efficient. My father does not have to think about any of it. That is worth the price.”

— a trust beneficiary who values the family office

At press time, a newer survey had reportedly found that 100 percent of family offices now consider $6.6 million an incredible bargain, because the alternative—having to know where the money is—would be psychologically devastating to people who have never had to know where anything is.
image_alt: A tiny figure stands beside towering blue blocks and a red pen.

title: CFPB Fines Regional Bank $6.2 Million For Overdraft Harvesting, Bank Calls It A Licensing Fee For The Right To Be Misunderstood
dek: Regulators caught a bank charging fees its customers never agreed to; the bank framed the settlement as “mining done responsibly.”
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Atlantic Union Bank to pay $6.2 million for what it called "illegal overdraft fee harvesting"—the bureaucratic term for charging customers fees they never agreed to and then, according to the complaint, appearing normal about it.

The bank acknowledged the fee revenue and disputed the word "illegal," preferring "optimized." Industry analysts noted that the harvest reflects an economy that has learned to lean on the household's hardest month as its own softest quarter.

Simone Vega, 44, an aide at a care facility in Richmond, said she was charged $189 in overdraft fees over three months for purchases she had the money to cover—the money was just in her savings account, not her checking account, and the bank knew that because the savings account was in the same building. "The statement said 'insufficient funds,'" Vega said. "I had the funds. I needed them for last week. The bank had a different definition of when I was allowed to be me again."

“The PDF was 69 pages and the fee was on page 52. I read it. I agreed to it. If you do not read the terms, that is your problem. The bank disclosed everything exactly the way the law requires.”

— a customer who reads every page of the agreement

At press time, the bank had reportedly set aside a reserve for future fines, describing the CFPB's enforcement actions not as penalties but as "the cost of doing right by the branch, which includes finding every dollar the branch can legally find, and sometimes a dollar slightly past that."
image_alt: A man in a cream suit stands beside a giant red harvester.

title: Existing Home Sales Hit 16-Year Low, Realtors Praise The Market For Finally Learning To Say No Without Hurting Anyone
dek: With sales slower than at any point since 2010, the industry has decided the market is not broken but “finally living within its means.”
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Existing-home sales ran at a seasonally adjusted 3.75 million pace in the latest month, the slowest since August 2010, and the National Association of Realtors responded the way it always does to a number no one wanted: with a story about the market's emotional maturity.

"Some houses are meant to stay in the family," said a prospective buyer who keeps losing offers to all-cash trusts and has started narrating the losses as a virtue. "Most houses, it turns out. The market is just being responsible about it. It is not broken. It is finally living within its means."

Michelle Torres, 33, a first-time buyer in Nashville, said she has made offers on six homes this year and lost every one to all-cash buyers she never met. "The last one, my realtor called and said 'the seller accepted an offer from someone named Whitmore Family Trust,'" Torres said. "I asked if Whitmore was a person. She said it was a legal structure. I am losing houses to legal structures now."

“The market is correcting and that is healthy. Sixteen-year low means prices will be reasonable again. The all-cash buyers are just prepared. I will be prepared next time. The market is teaching patience.”

— a homebuyer who appreciates the market correction

At press time, the NAR had released a statement confirming that first-time buyers remain welcome at open houses, where agents have begun handing them laminated cards explaining that the home they are seeing is not for them but merely being exhibited to them, the way a cathedral is exhibited to someone who will never be Catholic. The tour concludes with a brief discussion of the estate tax.
image_alt: A crowd reaches up toward a house above a red block.

title: Family Office Compares Notes On 'Family Discount', Decides The Lowest Bidder Was Never Going To Understand The Trust
dek: A new report found family-member executives reliably out-earn outside hires, a premium the industry attributes to blood, and the family attributes to clarity.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Wealth management's annual census of who gets paid for what found that family-member chief investment officers earn more than outside hires doing the same work, a gap the industry has named the "family discount" and the families have named, with admirable candor, "the point."

"We did not hire me for my record," said Josephine Mercouris, a third-generation heir who serves as CIO of her family's office despite having never managed money that did not already belong to her. "We hired me for the absence of a town that could ask me to leave."

Outside executives are expected to deliver returns. Family members are expected to remain, which the report treated as the more valuable credential and the market, at these rates, appears to agree. The average outside CIO lasts four years. The average family-member CIO lasts until the trust runs out, which, if the office is doing its job, is never.

“The son grew up around the business. He knows the culture. An outside CIO would take four years to understand what the son already knows. The watch podcast shows he understands branding. That is relevant experience.”

— an outside candidate who respects family hiring

At press time, the report had been updated to note that the family discount appears to compound annually at a rate that conveniently matches the rate at which the family's outside hires leave to take jobs at firms where being related to the owner is not a formal job requirement.
image_alt: Two crowned figures sit beneath a floating diamond at a table.

title: Buyback And Layoff Announce In Same Quarter, Company Reassures Market The People Were Always Meant To Be Temporary Equity
dek: A manufacturer returned capital at record size while reducing its payroll by a fifth, reassuring investors the two moves were “structurally the same transaction.”
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Lamar Goode, 53, a machinist who had worked at the Ohio plant for 19 years, was called into a conference room at 9:15 a.m. and told his job was being "capacity liberated." By 9:45 he was in the parking lot watching his phone load the news article about the company’s record buyback. "I didn’t even know the company had that kind of money," Goode said. "Turns out they had it. They just didn’t have it for me." The firm described the layoffs as "capacity liberation" and the buyback as "the purchase of the only executive that has never asked for a raise." Analysts greeted the pairing with the phrase "the financing of a solved problem."
“I read the whole press release and they explained that the layoffs and the buyback were separate transactions, and I thought that made perfect sense because one was about people leaving and the other was about stock coming back, and those are two different directions.”

— a former shift supervisor who read the whole press release
At press time, the company had confirmed it would hold a town hall to explain the difference between capacity liberation and being fired, and the town hall had been scheduled for 2 p.m. on a day when most of the liberated capacity would not have badge access to the building.
image_alt: A worker pushes envelopes and money toward a gear mechanism.

title: Mortgage Rates Fall For Fourth Week, Lenders Celebrate The Return Of A Kind Of Pain The Market Had Almost Begun To Miss
dek: A 7.11 percent is quietly described as relief, with the caveat that relief, like everything else, was always going to be relative.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Thirty-year mortgage rates eased for a fourth straight week to 7.11 percent, a decline described as welcome, though the word "relief" was deployed only after a note specifying that relief is a function of how much pain you were previously told to sit still through.

A year ago the same loan fetched 6.24 percent, a number industry analysts invoked roughly the way a draftsman invokes a blueprint for a building that was never going to house the client anyway. "Rates are down," said a mortgage industry analyst. "That is objectively good. It is also objectively not good enough to make a difference for the person who still cannot afford the house. Both things are true, and we are choosing to focus on the first one."

Delia Osei, 41, an evening custodian in Milwaukee, said her lender called to tell her the rate had gone down. Then they showed her the new payment, which had gone up, because the home price had gone up more than the rate had gone down. "They told me the rate went down and then showed me a number that was higher," Osei said. "I asked the man how the rate could go down and the payment go up. He said 'that's the market learning.' I said the market has learned how to make me pay more no matter what the rate does."

“The man showed me on the calculator that the rate went down and the payment went up, and he said that was the market learning, and I told him I was glad the market was learning because a smarter market was better for everyone, even if the number was higher.”

— a borrower who took the class on market learning

At press time, the industry had confirmed that the best strategy for prospective buyers was to wait for rates to fall further, and also to wait for prices to fall, and also to wait for wages to rise, and that the waiting was itself the product, and that the product was working exactly as designed.
image_alt: A couple stands before a geometric mountain with a red flag.

title: Average 30-Year Rate Reaches 7.4%, Affordable Home Now An Investment Thesis The Buyer Will Never Live To See Proven
dek: With the average mortgage rate at a three-year high, the industry has confirmed the starter home is no longer bought, only inherited.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
AUSTIN, TX—The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.4 percent this month, its highest in three years, prompting the real-estate industry to formally reclassify the affordable starter home from a purchase into a generational heirloom, to be passed down unopened and preferably still occupied by someone who locked in a lower rate during the Obama administration.

"We stopped asking buyers whether they can afford the house and started asking them which child deserves to inherit the regret," said Marcus Webb, a loan officer whose own mother, he confirmed, holds the deed to a three-bedroom ranch in a trust that will release it only upon proof that nobody has lived in it for forty years. "The starter home is not started anymore. It is finished. It is finished the way a cathedral is finished, which is to say you may look at it but you may not live in it."

Ricky Ortez, 28, a warehouse worker in Austin, said he toured an open house last weekend and the agent handed him a laminated card explaining that the home was not for sale to him but was merely being exhibited, the way a museum exhibits a dinosaur to a child who will never own the dinosaur. "The card said 'this home is a legacy property,'" Ortez said. "I asked if I could leave a legacy of my own. The agent said I could leave my contact information."

“I told my daughter she was not going to buy this house because it was a legacy property, which meant it was meant for someone who already had it, and I was proud she would understand that someday when she inherited something from someone who was not her.”

— a homeowner who explained legacy to his daughter

At press time, the industry had announced its strongest product yet: a new 45-year mortgage designed, in the lender's phrase, for a family that will not "even be born into a position to start dying inside it" until two more generations have had a chance to look at the house first.
image_alt: A treasure chest floats on a cloud above a broken ladder.

title: Treasury Yields Climb To 5.10%, Bond Market Thanks Everyone For Finally Letting It Be The Story Instead Of The Background
dek: With the 10-year at 5.10% and long rates at multi-year highs, the bond market says it feels, for the first time in ages, seen.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Gerald Twine got to his desk at 6:15 a.m. on Thursday because he knew what the open would look like before it opened. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.10 percent. The 30-year hit 5.43 percent. Gerald nodded at his screen like a man whose dog had finally learned a trick he had been teaching it for two years.

He called his brother, who works in HVAC, to tell him the long end of the curve was at multi-year highs and the bond market was finally being treated with the seriousness it deserved. His brother asked if that was good for Gerald. Gerald said it was complicated. His brother asked if it paid more. Gerald said it did not. His brother said it sounded like Gerald was celebrating a report card that showed the class had gotten harder, not that Gerald had gotten better. Gerald said that was reductive. His brother said he had to go, there was a furnace.

Analysts said the move had been driven by sticky inflation, hawkish Fed dissents, and oil above a hundred dollars, all of which had restored the bond market's relevance in the way a smoke alarm is relevant: loud, ignored, and eventually right about something everyone wishes it had been wrong about.

“My brother asked if the higher yield meant I had more money, and I told him no, it meant I was right, which was the whole reason I followed the bond market in the first place, and being right was the point.”

— a duration enthusiast who values being right over being solvent

At press time, equities sold off in response to the bond market's newfound confidence, and Gerald tried to explain to his wife that the stock market's pain was the bond market's validation. She asked if validation paid the mortgage. Gerald said it did not. She asked if he wanted dinner. Gerald said yes.
image_alt: A man celebrates at a desk beneath a sweeping film reel.

title: Keystone Bank Calls AI-Driven Layoffs 'Attrition As Our Friend,' Reaffirms That Nothing Has Ever Valued The Company As Much As Leaving
dek: The bank plans to shrink its workforce by allowing AI to do what dentures could not, and management says it has only this one friend.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Darlene Crockett got the email at 9:14 on a Tuesday morning. It said her position was being eliminated through a process called natural attrition, which was the bank's way of saying she would not be replaced when she left, and the bank considered that a friendship. Darlene had worked at Keystone Bank for six years. She had never once been described as a friend by the company. Attrition, apparently, was friendlier than she was.

A trust officer told a reporter the bank planned to use attrition as its primary tool for reducing headcount, drawing on a relationship that had quietly been the company's most productive. Attrition did not ask for raises. Attrition did not use the health insurance. Attrition did not sit in on meetings and ask questions about the 401k match. Attrition just sat there, being attrition, saving the bank money without ever once requesting a day off.

Employees across the company received notices that their roles had been reviewed by a model that the bank had recently promoted to analyst on a trial basis. The model found that a significant portion of the work could be performed without the worker. The worker, upon reading this assessment, asked if the model had been informed about mortgages and car payments. The model had not.

“They told me I was being attrited and not laid off, and I told them I appreciated the distinction because attrition sounded like something that happened naturally, like leaves falling, and I was happy to be part of something that happened without anyone having to decide.”

— a former loan processor who supports natural attrition

At press time, Darlene was updating her résumé and wondering whether to list attrition as the reason for leaving, which she decided was honest but sounded like a disease, which, she now understood, it was.
image_alt: A red robot arm reaches across a table toward a small figure.

title: European Banks Beat Profit Estimates, Celebrate By Buying Back Exactly As Much Of Themselves As They Can Before Anyone Asks Where It Came From
dek: UBS and BNP Paribas delivered strong quarters and accelerated buybacks, resolving the eternal question of what to do with gains.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
ZURICH—UBS reported an 8 percent rise in third-quarter net profit to $2.69 billion and pulled its share-buyback program forward, while BNP Paribas unveiled a buyback of its own, prompting analysts to observe that the continent's banks have finally solved the mystery of what to do with money they are embarrassed to have made.

"We beat expectations, and the first thing we thought was that they should probably give a portion of that back before it has a chance to be explained," said a customer of one of the banks for 31 years, repeating the CFO's line back to a reporter. "The word bonus was not used, but you could smell what it was about to become."

Lena Gottlieb, 52, a customer of one of the banks for 31 years, said she received a notice that her account fees were going up the same week the bank announced its buyback. "The letter said the fee adjustment was necessary to maintain the quality of service I deserve," Gottlieb said. "I called and asked if any of the buyback money could maintain the quality of service I deserve. The woman on the phone said the buyback and the fees were in different departments. I said they were in different parts of my bank account."

“I called the bank and asked if any of the buyback money could lower my twelve-dollar monthly fee, and the woman said the buyback and the fee were in different departments, and I told her that made sense because a department that buys things should not have to know about a department that charges things.”

— a customer who understands departmental separation

At press time, the profits were said to be in a fund, the fund was in a committee, and the committee was reported to be buying back the whole thing as a gesture of goodwill toward the people who made it, none of whom were in the room.
image_alt: A small figure sits before a gold disc with a book.

title: Thomson Reuters Announces $500M Buyback, Controlling Owner Graciously Sells Shares to the One Person Who Already Owned Them
dek: The company's controlling investor will participate proportionally in the buyback, graciously accepting the shares it already controls back.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Marcus Webb owns twelve shares of Thomson Reuters. He knows this because his 401k statement lists them under a column called "holdings" and a sub-column called "not enough to matter." When he heard the company announced a $500 million buyback, he called investor relations to ask if his twelve shares could be included in the program.

The investor relations line put him on hold, then transferred him to a voicemail box that was full. When he finally reached a human, the human asked if he was a member of the Woodbridge family trust. Marcus said he was not. The human asked if he controlled a majority of the voting shares. Marcus said he did not. The human told him the buyback was for people who already owned most of the company, and that the shares being bought back would be sold by the people who already controlled them, and that after the transaction the shares would belong to the company, which was also controlled by those people, and that Marcus's twelve shares would remain exactly where they were, which was nowhere.

Corporate governance experts described the arrangement as the most elegant solution yet to the modern ownership problem: the people who own the company sell some of it back to the company, which is the same people, at a price the same people set, to the benefit of the same people.

“I asked the man why I could not sell my shares back like the family office could, and he said the program was full, and I told him I understood because a program can only hold so many people, and the family office had gotten there first, which was fair.”

— a shipping supervisor who respects program limits

At press time, Marcus had looked up the Woodbridge family trust online and found a photo of a building in Toronto that was larger than his entire block. He stared at it for a while, then closed the tab and went back to work.
image_alt: A handshake seals a deal above a diamond and tiny figure.

title: As Mortgage Rates Climb, Finance Industry Clarifies That a Roof Is Not Actually Housing Unless You Have a Second One
dek: With ownership unaffordable for five million more Americans, lenders confirm rent is the answer and is not, technically, housing.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
NEW YORK—As the average 30-year mortgage rate climbed past 7.4 percent, the consumer-finance industry gathered to reassure the nation's 44 million renters that their situation is not a housing crisis, because the unit they sleep in is not, by the industry's strict accounting definition, housing.

"Housing is something you own," explained Dale Burnham, a spokesman for a national landlord trade group, standing in a lobby whose single chandelier cost more than the annual salaries of the tenants in the building behind him. "What you have is a lease. A lease says you may continue existing indoors until we decide you cannot, at which point you will leave. That is not housing. That is temporary permission to be inside."

Tamika Fowler, 39, a home health aide in Cleveland, said she applied for a mortgage and got turned down, then her landlord raised her rent by $325 the same week. "The bank said I didn't have enough history. The landlord said I had enough history to pay more. I think they just agreed I was the problem," she said.

“The bank said I did not have enough history for a mortgage, and the landlord said I had enough history to pay $325 more, and I realized both of them were right because paying rent and owning a house were two different kinds of history, and I only had one of them.”

— a renter who accepts the history distinction

The industry described renting as the bottom rung of a ladder, then clarified that on this ladder the first rung is the roof, and the roof is not available for climbing. At press time, the National Association of Realtors had confirmed that the best time to buy a home was any time before the current era, and that people who pointed out the current situation were, by definition, the enemies of the current situation.
image_alt: A family under an umbrella stands on a red block beneath cubes.

title: Thames National Profit Jumps 12% As Bank Proves Algebra Where 5,000 Fewer People Equal More Money
dek: The bank says machine learning will remove 5% of its workforce while profits climb, a pairing it describes as the new healthy.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
LONDON—Thames National reported a 12 percent rise in third-quarter profit and announced it would cut 5,000 jobs, or 5 percent of its workforce, in an AI-powered cost-reduction drive, confirming to a skeptical world that a bank can make more money and fire more people at the same time and call both of those things the same committee's success.

"We're not shrinking because we're weak," said a Thames National spokesperson, reading the sentence off a card that appeared to have been recently laminated. "We're shrinking because we can. The model says the future needs fewer of you, and the model has been right about the past of the people it has already replaced, which is to say the people are gone and the model is still here."

James Okafor, 47, a Thames National loan processor in London, said he learned he was being laid off from a notification that popped up on his work computer while he was processing a loan for a customer who made more money in a year than Okafor would make in his lifetime. "The notification said 'your role has been identified for efficiency action' and then a button that said 'acknowledge,'" Okafor said. "I acknowledged. Then I went back to processing the rich man's loan. I finished it before my badge stopped working."

“They told me I was being replaced by an algorithm and then offered me a course in the technology that replaced me, and I took the course because if the algorithm was smart enough to do my job, it was smart enough to teach me something, and that was a benefit I had not expected.”

— a former compliance officer who took the course

At press time, the 5,000 laid-off workers had reportedly been offered a course in the technology that had replaced them, and the course had informed them it could not currently work 5,000 positions, which everyone involved agreed was, in fact, the entire point.
image_alt: A robotic arm delivers a red envelope above tiny figures.

title: Fed Worried the Labor Market Has Gotten Too Settled to Count Anyone As Working
dek: Federal Reserve officials are worried the labor market has gotten so settled that a person can no longer be counted as hired, laid off, or doing anything at all.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Greg Furnish has not been fired in eleven months, and the Federal Reserve has noticed. Greg works in a warehouse on the south side of Richmond. He stacks boxes that come off a truck and stacks them onto a pallet. The boxes are the same shape every day. The amount he gets paid for stacking them has not changed in fourteen months. Greg considers this a good run.

At the Fed's last meeting, officials reviewed the labor market data and identified Greg's life as a problem. Hiring was low. Layoffs were low. Nobody was quitting and nobody was being hired, which meant the labor market had achieved what economists called full settlement, a state in which a person is neither advancing nor retreating, merely existing in the same job at the same wage while the central bank watches and wonders whether this counts as employment.

Greg, for his part, did not know he was being studied. He drove the same route to the warehouse every morning, parked in the same spot, and stacked the same boxes. When he heard the Fed was worried about the labor market being too settled, he asked his supervisor what that meant. His supervisor said it meant the Fed thought people should be moving around more. Greg asked where they were supposed to move to. His supervisor said he did not know, but presumably somewhere else.

“My supervisor said the Fed thought I should be moving around more, and I asked him where I was supposed to move to, and he said he did not know but presumably somewhere else, and I told him that was good enough for me because somewhere else was where opportunity was.”

— a warehouse associate who is open to relocation

At press time, Greg had been offered no better jobs, had applied for none, and planned to come back to the warehouse tomorrow, which the Fed said was fine for now, but was not the same as improvement.
image_alt: A worker stacks boxes between towering shelves before a temple.

title: PCE Hits 3.6%, White House Notes Number Is Down if You Only Count Things in Someone Else's Cart
dek: As inflation stays above target, officials note the figure is down only if you look at the goods people used to buy.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Tanya Morrison put the chicken back. Then the orange juice. Then she swapped the name-brand cereal for the bag that looks like somebody got evicted from a label design meeting. The total at the Food Lion on H Street was still higher than last week's total, and last week's total had already made her stand at the register doing subtraction out loud.

The cashier, Doreen, told her the eggs had gone up again. Tanya asked why. Doreen said the thing cost more now, and the people who decided that were not in the store. Tanya asked if the people who decided that were anywhere she could call. Doreen said she did not know where they were, but it was not answering.

At the same hour, the White House announced the Personal Consumption Expenditures index had climbed to 3.6 percent, a figure officials described as reason for encouragement, because while it was above the target, it was below the old number, provided one did not also count this week's grocery trip, which, the official noted, was a separate transaction.

“The official said the 3.6 percent was down if you did not count this week's grocery trip, and I told my wife that was good news because the grocery trip was a separate transaction, and we should focus on the number that did not include it.”

— a shopper who tracks only the encouraging transactions

At press time, Tanya had put the milk back too and was deciding whether to pay the light bill or eat this week, a choice the White House described as personal responsibility, which is what they call it when a number you cannot eat finally takes food out of your mouth.
image_alt: A woman holds a book in a library aisle facing the Capitol.

title: Banks Believe in AI So Hard They Will Not Give It a Single Dollar, a Position They Describe as Principled
dek: Lenders are again wary of financing data-center debt, describing their confidence in AI as personal and their confidence in its invoices as contractual.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
Simone Brackett, a structured finance director at a major bank, sat in an office whose heating bill was paid by the interest on loans she had declined to make, and she had thoughts about the future of artificial intelligence.
“My neighbor said the banks believed in AI so much they would not lend a dollar to it, and I said that proved how serious they were because anybody can lend money to something they believe in, but it takes real conviction to believe in something and not lend to it.”

— a neighbor who admires principled lending
Evan Park, 34, a startup founder trying to finance a small data center in Virginia, said he met with five banks last week and all of them told him the same thing. "They said they love AI. They said they love what I’m building. They said they would love to see it succeed. Then they said ‘good luck’ and handed me a list of venture firms that had already told them no." At press time, the marquee chipmakers were reported to be shopping the financing question around the market in the manner of a hot potato that had somehow been upgraded to a potato of record.
image_alt: A woman behind a desk rejects a man holding a blueprint.

title: Card Issuers Raise Limits on Customers Already in Debt, Explain Strategy as 'Giving the Rope Time to Work'
dek: With balances and minimums climbing, lenders say the best defense against default is a higher ceiling.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
NEW YORK—The Federal Reserve's quarterly survey found that average credit-card limits increased during the third quarter even as card balances grew, prompting banks to explain the policy as an expression of confidence in a consumer whom the economy has spent the year gutting.

"We raise limits not because we think the customer can afford more but because we think they've earned the right to find out," said a consumer-credit executive who asked not to be named, adding that the industry calls the approach "relationship expansion," though a more precise term might be "hope underwriting."

Rico Espinoza, 31, a warehouse associate in Phoenix, said his bank raised his limit by $2,000 and sent a card letting him know it had arrived. "It was the only invitation I've gotten all year," Espinoza said. "Not a raise, not a better apartment, not a call back from the job I applied to. Just a piece of plastic saying I am approved to owe more. Yes, I am going. I'm going to use it. What else am I supposed to do with an invitation?"

“They raised my limit to $8,000 and I used it because the invitation came when nothing else did, and I figured if the bank thought I could handle $8,000, then I could handle $8,000, and the 24 percent was the price of being trusted.”

— a cardholder who trusts the bank's $8,000 judgment

At press time, the bank had reportedly followed up with a second survey asking why the customer had taken such an aggressive view of their own financial future, and the customer had replied that they had learned it from the bank itself.
