title: Treasury Selloff Accelerates as Bond Market Learns the Worst Part of Being Right Is Having Been Right the Whole Time
dek: With the 10-year toward 5.1% and hawkish Fed bets rising, the long end reports that vindication, apparently, hurts.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Gerald Twine has been telling anyone at his firm who will listen that rates are going higher for eighteen months. He has said it in meetings. He has said it in the hallway. He has said it to the guy who brings the sandwich cart, who told Gerald he did not trade bonds and could not care less about the long end of the curve. Gerald said the long end cared about him.

On Friday the 10-year yield pushed toward 5.10 percent, and Gerald felt the specific loneliness of being right about something terrible. He called his wife to tell her. She asked if that meant the bonus would be bigger. Gerald said it did not. She asked what it meant. Gerald said it meant he had been right. She said that was not a thing you could spend.

The selloff accelerated after sticky PCE data and hawkish Fed language, confirming what Gerald had been saying since the summer of last year, which was that inflation was not going anywhere and the market was pricing in a fairy tale. The market, now pricing in a selloff instead, confirmed that being right had been its goal all along, and that the goal was somehow worse than being wrong, because being wrong came with a lower cost of living.

“I told my wife that being right about the 5.1 percent yield was more important than what showed up in the checking account, and she said the checking account was the one buying the groceries, and I said the history books would remember who was right, and that was the long game.”

— a duration manager who plays the long game

At press time, Gerald was still at his desk at 7 p.m., staring at a screen that confirmed what he had been saying for a year and a half, which nobody was celebrating, least of all Gerald, who had been right and had nothing to show for it except a spreadsheet and a wife who had stopped asking about the bonus.
image_alt: A person at a desk watches a chart with a red arrow.

title: The 617,000 Laid Off This Year Were Named Raymond, A Call Most Of Them Answered With Earning Ceased
dek: Net job cuts slowed 44% from last year's total, a statistic that confused only the recently separated, who could not see it from where they landed.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
Raymond Hightower got the news at 10:30 on a Wednesday. He was one of 617,189 people laid off by US employers in the first ten months of the year. He found out via a notification on his phone from the HR portal, which he had installed when he was hired and had never used until it told him he was no longer employed. He read the message, put his phone down, and picked it back up to check if the number was lower than last year's. It was. That made him feel worse somehow.

The same morning, Raymond's former employer announced a $2.3 billion share buyback program, part of the $725 billion in total repurchases announced by US companies year to date. Raymond read about the buyback on his phone in the parking lot. He had owned zero shares of the company, because he had been a warehouse supervisor, not an investor. The stock, he learned, would be bought back at a price the company considered attractive. Raymond, whose position had been eliminated, was not considered attractive at any price.

Executives explained that the two figures were not in tension but in arrangement. The company was not eliminating positions, it was relocating the value that the positions had been, at great expense, failing to hold. Raymond asked if the value could be relocated to his bank account. He was told that was not how relocation worked.

“I asked if former employees counted as shareholders, and they said only if I owned stock, and I said I had worked there for six years, and they said that was not stock, and I realized they were right because showing up and owning were two completely different things.”

— a former warehouse supervisor who now understands the distinction

At press time, Raymond had filed for unemployment and was looking at the company's stock price, which had gone up two percent on the buyback news, a gain he could not participate in because his severance was not enough to buy a share.
image_alt: A suited man at a pink table under a red surveillance light.

title: Algorithm That Replaced Its Traders Decides It Also Wants To Fire Them A Second Time For Dramatic Effect
dek: The model priced the data, revised the forecast, and then chose to spend the remainder of the session deleting the traders who had the meeting.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Derek Okonkwo had been a trader at the firm for eight years. He had a desk with two monitors, a Bloomberg terminal, and a coffee mug that said 'I Heart Volatility.' On Monday morning, the firm's trading algorithm priced the inflation data at 3.7 percent, revised its forecast, and submitted a report recommending that Derek's position be eliminated, along with the desk, the monitors, the Bloomberg terminal, and the mug.

The algorithm had determined that the human contribution to price discovery was structurally unnecessary. It cited as evidence the fact that Derek had spent the first forty minutes of the session on the phone with his cable company. When Derek pointed out that the algorithm could not make phone calls, the algorithm updated its recommendation to include the call center staff as well.

Management reviewed the algorithm's assessment and agreed. The head trader, a man named Paul who had been with the firm since before electronic trading, was reassigned to ceremonial duties, which consisted of walking past the algorithm's server rack once a day and confirming that it was still running. Paul asked what happened if it wasn't running. Management said that was not something Paul needed to worry about, because it was always running.

“The algorithm said my position was redundant, and I asked if it could do my expense reports, and it said it could, and I told management that was impressive because the algorithm could do everything I could do, and management said that was exactly the point of the technology.”

— a former trader who respects efficiency

At press time, Derek was cleaning out his desk. The algorithm had already sent him an exit survey, which it told him was optional, but which it also noted would be used to determine his severance, which the algorithm had already calculated.
image_alt: A man in a cream suit at a desk facing two monitors.

title: Company Hires Darren, Reclassifies Darren, Absorbs Darren, And Invites Darren To Apply Again As Darren
dek: Employers confirmed they would love to bring somebody on board, but the job keeps evolving out from under the handshake into a position that no longer exists, and then out from under that.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Darren Balfour was hired at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday. By 9:45 his position had been reclassified. By 10:30 his department had been restructured and his role had been absorbed into a new unit called Operational Integration, which did not have a headcount. At 11:15, the new unit was folded back into the original department, which already had a headcount, and Darren's role was declared redundant. At noon, HR called to say his onboarding was complete and his exit interview was scheduled for the same time, and that the company considered this the fastest full employee lifecycle in its history.

Darren sat in his car in the parking lot, where he had been for three hours. He had not received a badge, visited a desk, or met a coworker. He had spent the morning filling out forms for a job that was eliminated before he finished the forms. He still had the parking pass, which he kept because it was the only evidence he had ever been there.

A manager at a mid-size logistics firm explained that his company now hired, trained, and released people so efficiently that most workers were let go the same day they started, because the job kept evolving out from under the handshake. He said this was not a bug. It was called being agile, and the person who was supposed to fill the role had already been agilely removed.

“The HR woman said I had not been fired but optimized out of a role that no longer existed, and she called it a learning experience, and I told her she was right because I had learned that a job could disappear while you were still standing in it, and that was valuable knowledge.”

— a three-hour employee who values the lesson

At press time, Darren had received an email asking him to reapply for a position that had just opened up in the original department, under the original title, which was, according to the email, a new role with exciting opportunities, and which Darren noted was the same role he had been hired for three hours earlier, before it was eliminated, reclassified, absorbed, and revived without him.
image_alt: A lone worker at a red desk surrounded by identical empty desks.

title: Keisha's $6.87 Coffee Cost $41.87 Because The Bank Processes Happier Numbers Before Sadder Ones
dek: Revenue rose 9.4% to a four-year high as lenders attributed the bonanza to a chronic shortage of balance on the part of account holders.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Keisha Allen bought a coffee for $6.87 at the shop on the corner of her block. She paid with her debit card, because she had $42 in her account and the coffee was $6.87, which left $35.13, which should have been enough until payday. The bank disagreed. The bank saw the $6.87 and decided that Keisha had made a decision with insufficient regard for the balance, which the bank had arranged in an order that put the coffee first, and the $42 second, so that the coffee cost $6.87 and the insufficient-funds fee cost $35, and the whole thing cost $41.87, which was almost the entire $42, leaving Keisha with thirteen cents and a coffee.

Sterling National and Keystone Bank alone collected $590 million in overdraft fees in the third quarter, according to data from KBRA, an amount roughly equal to the rest of the twenty largest banks combined. A federal rule that would have capped the overdraft fee at $5 was approved and then rolled back in the same year, restoring the banks' right to call a $6.87 coffee a $41.87 financial event.

Keisha called the bank to ask about the fee. The representative, a woman named Tiffany who sounded like she had taken this call before, explained that the fee was assessed because Keisha's account balance had been insufficient at the time of the transaction. Keisha asked if the $42 had been in the account before the coffee. Tiffany confirmed it had. Keisha asked how $42 became insufficient to cover $6.87. Tiffany explained the order of operations. Keisha asked if the operations could be arranged differently. Tiffany said they could not, because the operations were standard.

“I asked the lady at the bank if the system could process the balance first, and she said the system was not a suggestion box, and I told her I understood because a system that took suggestions from every customer would not be a very reliable system, and reliability was more important than my $41.87.”

— a customer who appreciates reliable systems

At press time, Keisha had thirteen cents in her account and a cup of coffee that was, according to the bank's statement, fully paid for.
image_alt: A woman holding a cup at a red counter in darkness.

title: Art Built His Office Park In 2004. A Family Office; Bought It In 2026, Explaining The Economy Needs Parking More Than Art
dek: Wealthy families now fund forced sales at a discount, a role regulators described as inevitable and sellers described as generous, eventually.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Art Delgado built the office park in 2004. He picked the lot, negotiated the loan, and signed the papers himself. Twenty-two years later, the bank that lent him the money told him it was no longer in the commercial real estate lending business, that the building was worth half what he owed, and that if he wanted to keep it he would need to find financing somewhere else. He called every lender he knew. None of them were in the business anymore.

The business was now run by family offices. Wealthy families, some of them so old their money predated the building, had become the largest source of commercial real estate credit in the country. They lent at a discount, bought at a discount, and described their role as capital on standby, which was a polite way of saying they would own the building by spring.

Art sat down with a representative of a family office that controlled more money than the entire county where his building stood. The representative was a young man in a suit that cost more than Art's first car. He asked Art how much he needed. Art told him. The representative said the family would lend him half that and take a 40 percent equity stake, which the representative called a partnership. Art asked what happened if he paid it back. The representative said then Art would own the building again, which was the point of a partnership. Art asked what happened if he could not pay it back. The representative said then the family would own the building, which was also the point of a partnership.

“The young man said this was a generational opportunity to partner with patient capital, and I asked if patient meant they would wait until I died, and he said it meant they would wait until the building was theirs, which was faster, and I said that sounded like a good deal because the building would be in good hands either way.”

— a commercial property owner who values patient capital

At press time, Art was deciding whether to sign the papers or let the bank take the building, a choice the young man described as a win-win, because in both scenarios the family ended up with the building eventually.
image_alt: A man with a red flag before a cream city skyline.

title: The Men Who've Failed To Beat The S&P For 14 Years Are Confident The Market Will Finally Notice How Wrong They Were
dek: The industry's longest winless streak continued, with managers describing their stewardship as prematurely correct and the outflows as a tax on patience.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Wendell Grossman has managed the Focused Growth Equity Fund for fourteen years. The fund has underperformed the S&P 500 in eleven of them. Wendell calls this the setup. He tells investors that the market has not yet appreciated his positioning, which is correct but early, a phrase he has been saying for so long that being early has become the entire thesis, and being correct has become a promise he makes to himself in the car.

In September, $56.4 billion left long-term active funds, according to the Investment Company Institute, the latest month in a streak that has lasted so long the industry has stopped calling it a streak and started calling it the environment. Wendell's fund lost $240 million of that. He told his largest remaining investor that the outflows were a tax on patience. The investor said he had been paying that tax for a decade and was considering a different filing status.

Across the industry, portfolio managers held meetings to discuss their underperformance and concluded that the market was simply not reflecting the value of their opinions. The market, for its part, continued to rise without asking anyone's opinion, which the managers said proved their point about the market being shallow.

“I told my biggest client that my picks were undervalued by a market that did not understand them, and he said he understood them, which was why he was leaving, and I told him that proved my point because a client who understood my picks would know they needed more than fourteen years to work.”

— a portfolio manager whose strategy needs more time

At press time, Wendell was preparing his quarterly letter to investors, which he planned to title 'The Setup Continues,' because changing the title would mean changing the thesis, and the thesis was all he had left.
image_alt: A man pointing at a rising red line on a presentation board.

title: Brackenridge Family Office Advises Formula-Fed Infants to Trade Up to the Premium Tier
dek: Basic formula rose 5.1% in a single month — the largest increase since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the category in 1997. Brackenridge Family Office sees a generational buying opportunity.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
The infant arrived at the conference room under a blanket carrying a leather satchel. A Brackenridge junior analyst had placed a bottle of Premium Plus Gentle at the infant's side of the table — the $12.65 SKU, not the $12 Basic the infant had been drinking for six weeks. "We've run the comps," said managing partner Caroline Brackenridge, sliding a term sheet across the polished walnut. "Basic is a value trap. The spread is sixty-five cents. You're leaving money on the counter."

The infant, who cannot sit upright unassisted and whose total asset base consists of three board books and a teething ring shaped like a key, was asked to sign a "birth-to-weaning" auto-escalating subscription that adjusts the can price monthly against the the government dairy-futures index. The contract does not include an infant opt-out clause. The infant's legal guardian — present at the table and visibly tired — noted the infant had not yet formed object permanence and could not reach the doorknob. "Those are exactly the characteristics we look for in a long-term holder," Brackenridge said, and circled the early-termination penalty.

Brackenridge's "formula ladder" locks the infant into 18 consecutive months of escalating can prices, with a step-up provision if the infant transitions to solid foods before month 14. The infant, under no circumstances, may wean. "The exit penalty is structured as a clawback of every can consumed to date, at the Premium tier's forward price," Brackenridge explained. The infant, who had begun to cry, was noted by an associate as "expressing concern about price discovery."

“I told my sister that the basic formula going up 5.1 percent was actually a good thing because it meant the market was signaling that premium was the better allocation, and she said the baby was three months old, and I said that was the perfect age to start thinking about premium positioning.”

— a sibling who understands premium positioning

At press time, the infant had been assigned a "formula-futures position" expiring on a kitchen counter in 72 hours, the contract priced at $12.65 with a mandatory roll into the November Premium blend, the can unopened, the infant asleep, and the carry cost billed to the infant's nonexistent checking account at a 12% annualized fee.
image_alt: A baby in a high chair faces a suited man.

title: Ashford Capital Points to the Chicken Price on Your Receipt, Hails Tyson's $1M Profit on $14.6B as Operational Excellence
dek: Tyson Foods reported $1 million in operating income on $14.585 billion in revenue — a margin of 0.0068%. The company posted a net loss of $74 million. Its beef segment lost $514 million. Ashford Capital's Harold Pender called it a victory lap.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Harold Pender stood at the podium holding a a supermarket chain receipt above his head like a championship belt. The receipt had been crumpled and smoothed flat several times. Someone in the second row had bought a family pack of chicken thighs for $8.49. Pender had circled the price in red marker, then laminated the receipt, then pinned it to a corkboard behind his desk at Ashford Capital's Stamford office, and then brought it to a conference center in Midtown to show three hundred institutional investors what operational excellence looks like.

"This right here is a consumer signaling a willingness to absorb cost," Pender said, tapping the laminated plastic with his fingernail. The consumer in question — a grocery shopper in a New Jersey suburb, who had selected the chicken thighs because they were on the end cap and she was in a hurry — had not been consulted about her role as a signaling vehicle for Tyson's capital-allocation thesis. Pender did not name her. He did not need to. "The spread between what that chicken cost Tyson to produce and what that consumer paid — that spread is the moat. The moat is widening."

Pender then produced a second receipt. Ground beef, $6.99 a pound. "The beef segment lost five hundred and fourteen million dollars this quarter," he said, and smiled. He circled the ground-beef price on the receipt. "This right here is how we transfer that cost to the consumer without the consumer's knowledge or consent. That's operational excellence. That's a moat-widening event. The thesis is just getting started." The conference hall applauded. The consumer in Paramus, who does not own Tyson stock and whose weekly grocery budget has risen $47 in twelve months, was not in the room.

“I read the earnings report and saw that Tyson made a million dollars on fourteen billion in revenue, and I told my wife that was a miracle because moving fourteen billion dollars through anything and keeping any of it was an achievement, and the 0.0068 percent was profit that did not have to exist.”

— a shopper who appreciates the 0.0068 percent miracle

At press time, Pender was asking the audience for their receipts, promising to circle more things on them, and a woman in the third row was checking her purse to see if she still had the one from the deli counter.
image_alt: A suited man at a podium holds a document above an audience.

title: Verde Family Office Declares Romaine Lettuce a Veblen Good, Advises Clients to Serve It on Velvet
dek: Romaine lettuce hit $3.49 a pound, up 7.3% in one month — now more expensive per pound than chicken. Verde Family Office says the price is the point.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
The romaine arrived on a velvet pillow carried by a Verde Family Office associate wearing white gloves. It had been trimmed to a single perfect leaf, stem removed, and placed under a museum-quality halogen spot calibrated to 3200 Kelvin. "The chlorophyll bloom is exceptional for a November hydroponic," said senior partner Arthur Verde, gesturing at the leaf as though it were a Rothko. "You are not looking at lettuce. You are looking at a Veblen good whose price elasticity has inverted. The price is the point."

Verde advised clients to stop eating salad in front of household staff, comparing a $3.49 head of romaine to "wearing a Rolex in a soup kitchen" and recommending that salads be consumed in a dedicated romaine salon with closed-circuit cameras and a lock on the refrigerator. The firm has opened a "romaine-aging cellar" in Chelsea — a climate-controlled room kept at 38 degrees and 95% humidity, staffed by a former MoMA curator who logs each head's provenance (farm, harvest date, soil pH, distance from a major highway) on numbered cards bound in calfskin. The lettuce spoils in five days. "Spoilage is a feature, not a bug," Verde said. "It reinforces scarcity. It creates urgency. A head of romaine that lasts two weeks would not trade at this multiple."

The climate-control system for the Chelsea cellar costs $14,000 a month in electricity alone — more than the annual value of California's entire fall romaine harvest at current prices. Verde called the ratio "encouraging" and said the firm is staffing a "lettuce-futures desk" that will allow clients to buy forward contracts on salad greens they will never eat, settled in cash, stored in a room they will never visit. Verde Family Office has commissioned a $3.95 salad fork from a Danish silversmith, which costs more than the lettuce it will pierce. "That's the point," Verde said. "The fork is the signal. The lettuce is the credential."

“I paid $3.49 for a head of romaine and I felt good about it. If it was cheap everybody would have it and then what's the point of buying it?”

— a shopper in the organic aisle, 47, who carries her lettuce in a reusable bag

At press time, the Chelsea cellar had logged its first head of romaine as spoiled — provenance card filed, disposal fee invoiced to the client's capital account, replacement ordered at the forward price of $3.72 a pound, and the empty velvet pillow returned to its dust cover under the halogen spot, waiting.
image_alt: A gloved hand holds a card before a glass case.

title: Fed Chair Assumes Commuters Helicopter to Work, Blames Bus Fare Hike on Increased Rotor Maintenance
dek: Intracity transit fares rose 6.6% in a single month — the largest monthly increase since 2020, annualized to over 100%. The Federal Reserve attributes the spike to rising rotor-maintenance costs.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Federal Reserve Chair the Fed chair, addressing reporters from a lectern at the the bank's Washington headquarters, described the 6.6% monthly surge in bus fares as "a supply-side adjustment in the vertical-lift maintenance market" and noted that "the helicopter-to-work ratio is holding steady." the chair does not ride the bus. No member of the Federal Open Market Committee has ridden a municipal bus since July 1998, when New York Fed President John a New York Fed president took a school bus on a field trip to the a transit museum as part of a seventh-grade social-studies unit on the industrial revolution.

The Fed's internal models treat the bus as a theoretical construct — a vehicle that exists in economic literature the way Ohio exists in the mind of a coastal portfolio manager: acknowledged in principle, never visited. the chair cited a recently published a research university working paper titled "Vertical Lift as a Substitute for Municipal Fixed-Route Transit" as evidence that helicopter commuting is "a rational consumer substitution" and that rising rotor-blade composite-material costs are "the primary transmission channel" for fare increases. The paper's lead author received a $75,000 bonus from the New York Fed for policy-relevant research. She has never boarded a city bus either. She took a car service to the airport to present the paper at a conference in Santa Barbara.

the chair then opened the floor for questions and was asked about the gondola-subsidy chapter of the Fed's latest Beige Book — a six-page appendix analyzing cable-car inflation in a foreign capital as a leading indicator for U.S. transit costs. "We are watching gondola capacity utilization with concern," the chair said. "If cable-car fares firm, that will feed into core services inflation, and we will respond with appropriate monetary tools." The bus, which costs $2.75 per ride and whose engine backfired twice during the press conference on a street two blocks away, was not mentioned by name for the remainder of the briefing.

“I don't ride the bus anyway — the bus is for people who haven't figured out the math. My fare went up six percent and that's fine, the rotor blades don't maintain themselves.”

— a commuter, 34, who has never ridden a city bus

At press time, the New York Fed had commissioned a follow-up paper titled "Gondola Velocity and the Pass-Through of Rotor-Blade Maintenance Costs to the Suburban Cable-Car Consumer," the bus fare had risen another 2%, and the 1998 school bus that carried John a New York Fed president to the a transit museum had been scrapped in 2015 and replaced with a 12-passenger van that the museum uses to shuttle retired volunteers from the parking lot to the gift shop.
image_alt: A cream bus drives beneath a helicopter above the city skyline.

title: Thornwood Partners Frames Negative Real Wages as a Loyalty Discount, Advises Employees to Consider It a Character-Building Opportunity
dek: Real wages have been negative for seven consecutive months. Wages rose 3.1% year-over-year; inflation ran at approximately 4%. Thornwood Partners has reframed the gap as a voluntary contribution.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
The memo was circulated internally at Thornwood Partners on November 10 under the subject line "Your Compensation Package: A Note on Fiscal Character." It described the gap between a $50,000 salary and the $52,000 in effective annual costs borne by the employee — rent, groceries, transit, the $4.75 loaf of bread that cost $3.89 twelve months ago — as a "loyalty discount" that the employee had "voluntarily extended to the firm" and that reflected "character-building fiscal discipline." The employee, who did not remember volunteering to lose $2,000 a year, was encouraged to "consider it an investment in the firm's rent fund."

Managing partner Richard Langley followed up with a second memo: "Why Your Paycheck Now Comes With an Invoice Attached." The invoice itemized the employee's "negative compensation contribution" across categories including "break-room oxygen fee" ($18.75/month), "natural-light surcharge" ($45/month for desk access within 20 feet of a window), and "neighborhood appreciation fee" ($120/month — the landlord raised the rent, and Thornwood passed the increase through to payroll as a deduction, described as "a market-alignment opportunity for the employee to participate in the building's value creation"). The employee's net take-home pay, after the invoice, was $21.37 for a two-week period. Langley's memo noted that the employee was "building character at an industry-leading rate."

Langley delivered the same material as a dinner speech at a private-equity networking event in Greenwich, drawing sustained applause. "I told my employees I was going to start thanking them in writing so they feel recognized," Langley said from the lectern, and the room laughed. "The ladder is also more expensive now," he added, and the room laughed harder. The $50,000 employee — the one whose paycheck arrives with an invoice attached — was not at the dinner. The ticket was $850.

“My raise was three percent and inflation was four but I see it as a contribution. The $50,000 I make is enough — the gap is a gift I give the firm and it builds character.”

— an accounts-payable clerk who received the memo, 41

At press time, the $50,000 employee had received a third memo announcing a "coffee-token surcharge" of $1.50 per Keurig pod, retroactive to January, deducted from the next paycheck, and a fourth memo reminding employees that the break-room microwave now requires a $0.75-per-use swipe card that can be loaded at the reception desk in $5 increments, nonrefundable.
image_alt: A desk lamp lights a sealed document on a desk.

title: Greenwich Motivated Seller Who Has Carried Two Mortgages for 14 Months Begins Accepting Applications for the Role of Buyer
dek: Existing home sales hit a 16-year low of 3.75 million annualized in October. Every price tier declined, including the $1-million-and-up segment. In Greenwich, Connecticut, a Colonial has been on the market for 14 months.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Gerald Masterson laminated a piece of printer paper and taped it to the wrought-iron railing of his front porch at 47 Maple Lane. "Yes, I Know It's Been 14 Months," the FAQ read, in 14-point Helvetica. "Question Two: Why Is It Still on the Market? Answer: I Have Been Carrying Two Mortgages Since September 2025 and Am Open to Creative Financing Solutions. Question Three: Define Creative. Answer: Non-Contingent Offer Plus Assumption of Both the Primary Mortgage and the Bridge Loan, Closing Within 30 Days, No Home Inspection, No Appraisal Contingency, Buyer to Cover Transfer Tax, Seller's Attorney Fees, and the Remaining Balance of the Lawn Service Contract Through April 2027." The lawn service had not been paid since August. The grass was 14 inches tall.

Masterson's listing has become a local attraction. Teenagers from the nearby high school photograph the sign as it evolves. The first sign read "For Sale." The second, in month four, read "Price Reduced." The third, in month seven, read "Will Consider Offers That Are Not Actively Insulting." The fourth, in month eleven, read "Open House — Serious Inquiries Only, Definition of Serious Negotiable." The current sign, installed last week, reads "Accepting Applications for the Role of Buyer" and includes a QR code linking to a seven-page application form that asks for the applicant's "relationship to real estate (please describe in 500 words or fewer)," "three professional references who can attest to your ability to close a transaction," and "a brief statement on why you believe you are the right person to assume ownership of this property at this time." The application does not ask for an offer amount. "If they're filling out the application, they're serious," Masterson said. "The offer is a formality. The application is the screen."

Masterson has also petitioned the Greenwich Planning and Zoning Commission to designate 47 Maple Lane a local landmark — a status that would require the town to maintain the property's exterior and lawn in perpetuity. The petition argues that the house "represents a significant example of early-2000s neo-Colonial architecture and the single-family-home seller's psychological arc from confident list price to desperate non-contingency." If approved, the Greenwich Preservation Trust would inherit the lawn-mowing, the roof maintenance, and the interior mold that has spread across the master bathroom ceiling since Masterson stopped paying the electric bill in August. "It's not a loss," Masterson said. "It's a public-private partnership. The town gets a landmark. I get someone else to cut the grass. The buyer gets a property with historic-tax advantages. Everyone wins." The mold was not mentioned in the landmark application.

“I've carried two mortgages for fourteen months and the bank approved both. If they didn't think I could handle it they wouldn't have given me the loans. The second property is an investment.”

— a homeowner, 52, who has refinanced twice this year

At press time, Masterson had received four applications for the role of buyer, rejected all four for insufficient answers to the essay question, and was preparing a seventh sign: "Landmark Designation Pending — Inquire Within About the Museum of My Own Poor Timing, Admission = One Non-Contingent Offer at 85% of Asking, No Lowballers, I Know What I Have."

title: Son's Toy Car Beats Father's Hedge Fund for the Month
dek: At the birthday party, he did the math on a die-cast car and now nobody can get him off the patio.
body:
Somewhere in Greenwich, a private-equity father is standing on his own patio at his son's eighth birthday party, holding a die-cast car between his thumb and forefinger like it's a piece of evidence in a fraud trial. The numbers do not make sense to him. He has watched the toy pile accumulate all afternoon — the same $800 star-cruiser-class replica his son gets every year, the same remote-control thing that will be under the couch by Tuesday — and he has never, in forty-three years of consuming goods, once looked at a toy price. Toys were a category that existed below his attention, like lint or municipal bus schedules. But then he picked up the orange one. A 1995 Mazda RX-7, die-cast, one-inch long. The Bureau of Labor Statistics says toy prices rose 4.2% in a single month, the largest monthly increase in the index's entire 49-year history, and this specific car, this tiny orange piece of painted metal that a child will lose in a sofa cushion within 72 hours, went up more in thirty days than his entire portfolio dropped in the worst trading week of the year. He has not stopped talking about it. The party magician is doing balloon animals to an empty tent.

“My son's die-cast car went up more in a month than my 401k did all year. That's not a toy — that's a better asset than anything my advisor put me in and I'm buying the whole set.”

— a dad at a birthday party, 39, who is now shopping for display cases

He has now asked his assistant to pull the supply chain on the die-cast line. She is on hold with Apex Die-Cast's vendor relations line. The children are eating cake off a table that cost more than most people's first cars, and Thaddeus is explaining the difference between PPI and CPI to a seven-year-old who just wants to know if the orange car can go through a loop. At press time, Shoreline Equity was reportedly evaluating a bid for the entire die-cast vehicle sector, which Thaddeus described as 'the only asset class left that still has upside.'
author: Marcus Reid
image_alt: An orange car and cake sit before a worried man.

title: One Spark Plug Costs More Than the Lobster Dinner the CEO Ate Last Night
dek: The man who has never changed a tire in his life is suddenly an expert on internal combustion economics.
body:
The chief executive of a facial-recognition startup is standing in the service bay of a Orion-certified repair center in Palo Alto, staring at an itemized bill his assistant printed on recycled bond paper. He has never been here before. He has never been to any repair center before. He leases a new vehicle every eighteen months — the model rotates, but the process is the same: a car appears in his driveway, he drives it, another car appears, the first one vanishes. Maintenance, he had assumed, was a thing that happened in the background, like server updates or the digestive system. But then the check-engine light came on — a small orange icon shaped like an engine block — and his assistant, who normally handles such things, told him it needed 'plugs,' and now he is looking at a line item that says spark plugs, $26 apiece, and he is not handling it well.

“Twenty-six dollars for a spark plug sounds like a lot until you think about what it does. It ignites fuel in a metal cylinder at thousands of explosions a minute. A lobster is just a bug you boil.”

— a man in the auto-parts aisle, 44, who has never changed his own oil

He has now demanded that his engineering team reverse-engineer a spark plug to see if they can produce one for under three dollars, because he is certain the auto parts industry is running a con. He does not know that the diagnostic machine that told the mechanic which spark plug was bad costs twenty-eight thousand dollars — roughly what he spends on oat milk in a quarter — and that the mechanic who runs it spent three years in a certification program Connor could not pass in his twenties. The bill is for $340. Connor spent more than that on dinner last night and did not look at the check. But this is different, he says. This is a principle. At press time, Vertex Vision Systems was reportedly developing a spark plug that connects to Wi-Fi and requires a monthly subscription, which Connor believes is 'the only honest pricing model.'
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
image_alt: A spark plug and prawn rest on a white plate.

title: Footwear Hits Record High as Man Buys Fifth Pair of Identical Sneakers
dek: He is on his fifth pair of the same shoe and cannot fathom why anyone would complain about a price that has barely moved since the Obama administration.
body:
There is a man in the Mission District of San Francisco who has purchased the exact same pair of minimalist sneakers — black, zero-drop, wide toe box, looks like a glove that gave up — five times in the last seven years. He buys them when the previous pair develops a hole near the pinky toe, which happens roughly every fourteen months because he walks exactly 4.7 miles a day on pavement and will not wear any other shoe. He considers this loyalty. He considers this efficiency. He is in the store right now, picking up pair number five, and the price is $124.99 plus tax, and he thinks this is a beautiful thing.

“I've bought the same shoe five times and the price has barely moved since 2019. $124.99 for four months of daily walking is value. People complain about sneakers and drink $8 lattes.”

— a customer at the register, 47, on his fifth pair

He does not know that a man in Cincinnati bought his first pair of dress shoes in seven years last week — the same mid-tier Kingston & Sheffield oxford he bought in 2019 — and paid $49 more without noticing because he wears them to two funerals and a wedding and that is the entire shoe budget of a normal adult male. Weston does not know this man exists. If he did, he would say the man should buy better shoes, because they last longer, and that is the kind of advice that makes perfect sense when you have never had to choose between shoes and a water heater. The average American household spends $400 a year on footwear. Weston spends $400 every fourteen months on the same shoe. He is the most price-stable consumer in the country and he thinks that is a virtue. At press time, Weston was drafting a Substack post titled 'Why Your Sneaker Budget Is a Lifestyle Choice, Not an Economic Indicator.'
author: Tessa Nguyen
image_alt: A row of black sneakers sits beneath a rising arrow.

title: Landlord Cheers Tax Increase That His Tenants Will Pay
dek: The man who owns forty units on Reading Road has never been happier about a piece of paper that will cost him money.
body:
Gary Pemberton is sitting in the members' lounge of the Cincinnati Athletic Club with a county auditor's notice spread across the mahogany table like a winning paddle at Bancroft's. His coffee has gone cold. He does not care. Hamilton County has just completed its triennial reassessment, and residential property values in his zip code are up twenty-seven to twenty-eight percent — ninety-nine percent of single-family homeowners affected — and Gary is grinning at the number like it is a personal check from the county commission. He owns forty units on Reading Road. He has owned them since 2003. None of them have new roofs. None of them have updated kitchens. The parking lot at the Avondale property is held together by patch asphalt and hope. But the county says they are worth more — a third more, in some cases — and Gary believes this is the single best piece of news he has received since the city announced the streetcar.

“My landlord raised the rent because his taxes went up. The county says the building is worth a third more than last year so why shouldn't I pay a third more? That's just math.”

— a tenant on Reading Road, 36, who received the rent-increase notice

He has not calculated what his 2027 property tax payment will be. He will do that later, when his accountant calls, and he will be briefly annoyed, and then he will remember that he can pass it through to his renters, who cannot frame a county notice and smile because they are not at the Cincinnati Athletic Club having a good morning. The school levy will pass. The roads will maybe get paved. Gary's portfolio will be worth more on paper, and that is the only paper he reads. At press time, Gary was on hold with the county auditor's office to request a printed certificate he could laminate, because 'digital reassessment notices do not look good on a wall.'
author: Omar Zayed
image_alt: A smiling businessman toasts a framed document in a corridor.

title: Post Office Makes Its Temporary Surcharge Permanent, Then Adds More
dek: The agency has clarified that 'temporary' refers to the period during which the charge is being collected, not the charge itself.
body:
The National Mail Service announced Tuesday that its temporary 8% fuel surcharge, implemented in April of this year, has been converted to a permanent fixture of the domestic shipping rate structure, with an additional 3% increment added for what officials describe as 'momentum.' The combined 11% increase — which brings total domestic shipping costs up 5.9% — will take effect January 17, 2027, and applies to every letter, package, and catalog that moves through the system. A Mail Rate Review Board spokesperson confirmed that the word 'temporary' in the original filing referred to the period during which the charge was being collected, not to the duration of the surcharge itself, and that the distinction was 'clearly stated in footnote four of the original document, which ran to 847 pages.'

“The surcharge is 22 cents and I spend more than that on the envelope. If they need to make it permanent to keep the mail running I'd rather pay 22 cents than lose Saturday delivery.”

— a stamp buyer at the counter, 58, who reads the footnotes

The eight-month gap between the temporary implementation and the permanent codification is roughly the same duration it currently takes a first-class letter to travel from Manhattan to Brooklyn, according to internal NMS transit data. Critics of the rate increase — a coalition of three direct-mail marketing executives and a stamp collector from Delaware — have pointed out that the surcharge was originally justified by fuel prices that have since moderated. The Mail Service has responded by noting that 'momentum' is a separate consideration from fuel costs and that the new 3% increment is not a surcharge but a 'rate-structure alignment fee,' which is not subject to the same regulatory review because it has a different name. At press time, the Mail Service was drafting a proposal to reclassify the entire rate schedule as a series of temporary adjustments, thereby freeing the agency from ever having to justify a permanent price change again.
author: Elena Marsh
image_alt: The stamps ascend toward the machine beside the truck.

title: Fuel That Hauled the 2x4 to the Site Now Costs More Than the 2x4
dek: The man building $3M condos is furious that a 2x4 costs eight bucks, and he is saying this while standing in a bathroom that costs more than a house.
body:
There is a man in a hard hat on a construction site in Miami, and he is yelling about a piece of wood. The wood is a standard 2x4 stud, kiln-dried, eight feet long, the skeletal unit of every wall in America. It costs, at the lumber yard this morning, roughly eight dollars. The man in the hard hat — his name is Bradley — has just been told that inputs to new residential construction are up ten-point-four percent year over year, and that goods used in new construction are up nine-point-eight percent, and that diesel fuel, the thing that hauled that 2x4 from the mill in Oregon to the lumber yard in Hialeah, is up a hundred and fifteen percent year over year, meaning the fuel that moved the wood now costs more than the wood itself. Bradley is not happy about this.

“A 2x4 costs eight bucks and people complain but that board came from Oregon on a truck burning diesel at six bucks a gallon. The fuel cost more than the wood. You're paying for the trip.”

— a contractor at the lumber yard, 51, who passes the cost to his customers

Bradley is standing in the model unit of his newest building, which features a kitchen with Italian marble countertops, German cabinetry, and a faucet from a boutique Barcelona foundry that cost $1,200 and looks like a modern sculpture of a swan. The faucet works the same as a $40 faucet from Builders Supply — water comes out, water stops — but Bradley would not know that because he has never turned a faucet on in a house he did not own. The $1,200 faucet is not the problem, he says. The $1,200 faucet is a value proposition. The problem is the two-by-four that holds the wall together, which costs the same as a sandwich and a drink at the airport, and which Bradley believes is the single greatest threat to the American housing market. At press time, Atlantic Rise Development was exploring a direct-to-site lumber procurement pipeline that bypasses diesel trucks entirely, which Bradley says will save money 'unless the horse feed goes up.'
author: Dana Whitfield
image_alt: A red fuel pump and arrow stand beneath a crane.

title: $298 Million Refund Cashed by the Same People That Raised the Price
dek: A company that blamed tariffs for jacking up prices gets the money back and routes it straight to the C-suite, because the machine doesn't correct itself.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
On paper, a tariff refund is straightforward: the government collects a tax the courts later rule illegal, and the money is returned to the party that paid it. PrecisionEdge Tool Works, a Connecticut-based manufacturer of hammers, saws and power drills, is expecting at least $298 million in such refunds after the Supreme Court struck down the underlying tariffs. The company collected higher prices from its customers during the period the tariffs were in effect, citing the import costs as unavoidable. The customers paid those higher prices. The refund is now arriving.

PrecisionEdge disclosed in a securities filing that the tariff windfall would be “partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation,” a formulation that directs a portion of the refund to executive bonuses rather than to the customers who absorbed the original price increases. The company is not alone: at least nine publicly traded companies have disclosed similar arrangements, according to filings reviewed by analysts. The parent company of the ValueSavers discount department-store chain received $331 million in refunds and indicated the proceeds would flow into its bonus pool. Empire Golf, which sells premium equipment with drivers starting above $600, adopted a comparable structure.

“The CEO got a bonus from the $298 million tariff refund and good for him. He kept the company profitable through a trade war. If I ran a company that got that money back I'd take my share too.”

— a shopper in the ValueSavers parking lot, 43

The mechanics of the arrangement are internally consistent. Companies told consumers the tariffs were a cost of doing business that had to be passed along. The cost was passed along. The refunds are not being returned to consumers because the refund mechanism directs money to the importer of record, which is the company, not the end customer. Trade policy, as executed, collects money from purchasers and distributes it to corporate entities.

The ValueSavers parent company said it would “evaluate our pricing on a go-forward basis as market conditions evolve,” the standard formulation for prices not going down.

At press time, the government had refunded approximately $800 million to publicly traded companies, none of which had announced plans to forward the money to the customers who paid it. A spokesperson for the Treasury Department said the refunds had been “processed efficiently and in accordance with applicable law.”

title: Telecom Confident Its Own Shares Are Worth $19.45, No, Really, They Are
dek: When the bidder's own stock at its own closing price is used to calculate the offer's value, and the market says the math is wrong, finance says the market is wrong.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
A $31 billion takeover offer can be valued in two ways: by the bidder, using its own stock price, and by the market, using the same stock price and arriving at a different number. NorthPeak Communications, a midsize telecom operator based in Montreal, is offering $6.35 in cash plus 0.17 of a NorthPeak Class B share for each share of Westland Telecom, a larger Vancouver-based rival. NorthPeak values the package at $19.45 per share, calculated using its own closing price as of the Friday before the announcement. Westland’s stock closed at $12.14 on that same Friday.

The difference between $19.45 and $12.14 is $7.31 per share, or roughly $11.7 billion in implied value that the bidder claims exists and the market says does not. The gap arises from the Class B share component: NorthPeak is offering its own stock at a price it determined by referencing its own stock price, then assigning that fraction a fixed value. By the time the deal closes, the bidder’s stock will have moved. The only guaranteed element is the $6.35 in cash.

“The stock is $19.45 and the market says it's worth less but I trust the company. They know their own value better than a trading algorithm. I bought at $19.45 and I'm holding.”

— a retail investor, 55, who bought the dip

The offer represents a 60 percent premium to Westland’s closing price under the bidder’s arithmetic. Under the market’s arithmetic, the actual consideration is $6.35 plus whatever the Class B shares are worth on the day they arrive, a variable the bidder does not control. The $11.7 billion difference between the two math systems is value the bidder has assigned to a number that may change before the transaction completes.

NorthPeak shareholders will vote on the share issuance in December. Westland shareholders will vote on the deal in January. Both will be presented with the $19.45 figure.

At press time, NorthPeak’s Class B shares had not been re-priced to account for the market’s disagreement. The company said it stood by its valuation methodology.

title: Automaker Searches Pockets, Discovers Wage Money After All
dek: The auto-parts supplier told its union it could not afford their demands. The same week it started permanent layoffs, its board approved a $60 million stock buyback and a record $46 million dividend.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
The arithmetic of corporate allocation is a matter of column assignment. In June, workers at Meridian Automotive’s Bristol, Michigan plant requested higher wages. The company said it could not afford them, a position it repeated in bargaining sessions. An 86 percent strike-authorization vote did not alter the response. The union, acting on the company’s representations about its financial condition, did not call a strike. Workers accepted a contract that gave the company substantially what it wanted. “We are told they are losing money and if we didn’t accept, they would just pull out,” one worker summarized at the time.

On November 11, the Meridian board approved the company’s first-ever share repurchase program, up to $60 million, to be executed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The buyback follows a July dividend of approximately $46 million, which the company described as “the highest dividend payout ratio in the Company’s history.” Together, the two payouts direct more than $106 million to shareholders. The announcement arrived the same week the company acknowledged it had started permanent layoffs at the Bristol plant.

“They announced a $60 million buyback the same week they laid people off and I support it. The shareholders are the owners. The layoffs are efficiency — that's how the company stays competitive.”

— a former Bristol plant worker, 48, who still owns company shares

The company did not misrepresent its financial position. The $106 million was allocated to the shareholder returns column, not the wages column. In August, Meridian sold roughly 1.8 million square feet of industrial property, including Plants 1, 5, 6 and 7, to a Milwaukee-based real estate firm. It retained Plants 3 and 4 and leased back portions of the sold properties during what it described as a “planned transition.”

Workers report that production is now being concentrated in the retained plants, with employees holding three years or less seniority — the newest hires, the same cohort the union reportedly instructed to vote yes — first in line for the cuts. The company has declined to specify how many workers are being laid off. Those who lose their jobs may return as part-timers at $27 per hour, capped at 27 to 29 hours per week, with no company health coverage, no paid time off and no sick leave.

At press time, Meridian’s stock was up 2.4 percent on the buyback announcement, and the company confirmed it remained in a strong liquidity position to address any future claims on its capital.

title: Summit Spends $4 Billion on Exits, Counts It as $6 Billion in Savings
dek: The newly merged media giant plans to cut $2.2 billion by flattening management layers and shrinking office footprints. It also mandated five-day in-office attendance.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Summit Entertainment, formed by the $111 billion merger of Vanguard Pictures and Heritage Media Group that closed on October 6, has announced a cost-savings program targeting at least $6 billion in annualized reductions within three years. The company carries approximately $80 billion in net debt and expects to realize roughly $2 billion of the savings in year one. Achieving the reductions will cost approximately $4 billion in one-time cash charges, most of it this year and next. The $4 billion is counted as an expense. The $6 billion is counted as savings. Both numbers appear in the same press release.

The largest single savings category is corporate overhead and real estate. Summit plans to cut at least $2.2 billion annually by consolidating back-office functions, reducing management layers, deploying AI workflows and shifting to lower-cost support functions. Additional targets include $1.4 billion from unifying streaming and broadcast platforms, $1.4 billion from centralized procurement and $1 billion from marketing consolidation.

“Five days in the office and I'm fine with it. If you're not in the building you're not really working. The layoffs are trimming fat and the people who got cut probably weren't pulling their weight.”

— a mid-level manager, 39, who commutes 45 minutes each way

On the same day the cost plan was announced, Summit confirmed it is adopting a mandatory five-day in-office policy. The company is eliminating the management layers that required in-person approvals, shrinking the office footprint that housed those meetings, replacing some of the people who would attend with AI workflows that do not commute, and requiring the remaining employees to commute five days a week to an office that is being downsized. Eight senior executives have exited — four from each legacy studio. Eligible employees have been given a mid-November deadline to accept voluntary buyout offers.

The company maintains that the savings target and the office policy are not contradictory: the savings come from eliminating duplicate roles, not from reducing attendance, and attendance is what makes the elimination of duplicate roles feel like a culture.

At press time, Summit confirmed that the mandatory five-day policy would apply to all remaining employees, including those whose managers had been eliminated in the flattening. The company had not yet specified which of the six floors in its newly consolidated Los Angeles headquarters would be closed first.
image_alt: A crowd lines up before a stepped red doorway.

title: Cirrus Buys Back Shares Its Refounding Founder Keeps Selling, Both Sides Pleased
dek: The software company laid off 7 percent of its staff in October, costing up to $75 million. Over the same year, it has bought back nearly $1 billion of its shares.
author: Jake Sullivan
body:
On October 6, Cirrus Systems eliminated approximately 660 positions, or 7 percent of its workforce, estimating charges of $65 million to $75 million in severance and related payments. Over the same calendar year, the company has bought back nearly $1 billion of its own common stock, including $237 million in the third quarter alone. Both facts are true simultaneously. The buyback is roughly fourteen times the severance charge in dollar terms. In people terms, the buyback involves none: it is the company purchasing fractions of its own equity using cash the eliminated employees helped generate.

On November 12, eight days after guiding fourth-quarter revenue below the third quarter, Cirrus Systems replaced its chief executive. Co-founder Andrew Vallon returned to lead the company in what the board described as “a refounding.”

“They laid off seven percent of staff and bought back a billion in stock. That's a healthy company making tough decisions. The buyback shows they believe in the future.”

— a former Cirrus contractor, 31, who was let go in October

Vallon’s return as CEO coincided with his continued sale of Cirrus Systems stock under a pre-arranged trading plan. A securities filing shows 8,500 shares sold on October 20 at $239.57, approximately $2 million. Filings show identical 8,500-share sales each month since June, executed through a trust. The plan was adopted in March, months before the layoffs, the guidance miss and the CEO change.

Cirrus Systems did not address whether a refounding CEO who sells $2 million of stock every month is engaged in a refounding or an exit. The company also did not specify whether the $1 billion buyback program would continue now that the returning founder is among the shareholders who benefit from it. The authorization predates every event of the past six weeks, so it remains in effect.

At press time, the 660 former employees remained former employees, the $1 billion in buybacks remained spent, and Cirrus Systems had not announced any new financial targets that would be harder to miss than the old ones. The stock was up 6 percent on the CEO change.

title: Health Firm Loses $66 Million Serving People Who Can't Pay More
dek: A company built on affordable healthcare reports record subscribers and a widening loss, because every patient it helps on the cheap tier costs it money. The mission is working. The numbers agree it is working.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Solace Health reported quarterly results that contained two internally consistent but contradictory numbers: subscription revenue grew 49 percent to $890 million, while the company lost $66.1 million on the quarter. More people are using the product than ever. Each additional subscriber on the company’s cheaper tier widens the loss. The enterprise operates on a gradient: a customer who can afford healthcare generates a profit; a customer who cannot afford healthcare subscribes to a lower-priced option and generates a loss. The more successfully the company fulfills its stated mission of affordable access, the more of the second type of customer it attracts, and the worse the quarterly report becomes.

The gross margin fell from 74 percent to 57 percent in a single quarter. For every dollar a customer pays, the company now spends seventeen cents more than it used to. The business model, as executed, is one in which serving additional people directly reduces profitability.

“My premium went up seventeen percent but they're serving more people than ever. If they lose money on every patient that means they're doing the right thing. Healthcare shouldn't be profitable.”

— a Solace Health subscriber, 62, who has never filed a claim

The stock has fallen more than 40 percent since the beginning of the year, a decline the market attributes to the difficulty of valuing a company that loses money the more people it helps. The company describes the dynamic as “scaling unprofitability.” A customer whose monthly budget for healthcare is $19 is not a cost center but, in the company’s framing, a statement of mission.

Management considered adjusting the product mix to market only to customers who can pay enough to generate a margin, a move that would improve the financial statements and render the enterprise’s stated reason for existing inoperative. The board declined. The company has instead chosen to continue serving the cohort that costs more than it pays, to describe the resulting losses as “expanding access,” and to allocate a dedicated line item for the shortfall.

At press time, Solace Health had enrolled a further 400,000 subscribers onto its most affordable tier, all of whom would cost the company more than they paid, and had described the quarter as “our most successful accessibility quarter ever,” with the share price down another 2 percent in acknowledgment.
