title: Bank Airs Ad of Couple Celebrating They Can Afford the Minimum
dek: The couple in the ad can afford the minimum. Thirteen percent of cardholders can't.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Doreen's balance is nineteen months old and she still pays only the minimum. She is, by the industry's measure, thriving. Thirteen-point-one percent of all card balances are now ninety days past due, the highest share since 2011, and to the ordinary eye this looks like distress. To the industry it looks like a customer who finally understands the product; Meridian Consumer Financial calls it 'revolving engagement.'

Doreen calls the minimum her hook, the way she keeps the balance alive without once having to say out loud that she cannot pay it off. "The bank wants the intimacy," she said, repeating a phrase from the campaign mailer she keeps on the fridge. "They used to have to entice people into the balance. Now we run toward it."

Doreen pays $187 a month in interest and fees, up from $112 two years ago, which is the industry gently milking a teat it has been told is the udder. Revolving debt is $1.4 trillion; 43 percent of accounts pay only the minimum. The scale tells the industry the ideal customer carries a balance forever, pays the minimum, and occasionally misses a payment so the bank can show its forbearance programs. That is a relationship, the mailer says, by which it means a hand that never quite lets go of the wrist.

His new campaign shows a couple celebrating because they could afford the minimum. Later this month, the second spot: an older couple dancing because their interest was capitalized. Tagline: 'You're On Your Way.' Doreen is certainly not off it.

“I pay the minimum every month and my credit score is 740. The bank keeps raising my limit. If they thought I couldn't handle it they wouldn't keep sending me offers.”

— Doreen
image_alt: A large credit card looms over two celebrating figures.

title: Insuring a Roof Now Costs More Than the Handbag It Protects
dek: Ray cancelled the policy. The state pool had raised rates 29.1 percent.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Ray Kaminski, 58, of Canyon Country, was quoted $5,800 to insure the house in the canyon. He cannot afford it, so he cancelled. The state pool raised rates 29.1 percent, which took a fire-zone premium to $5,800. It was once unbearable. It is not now. The premium is the climate's invoice, and the climate is the only landlord who has ever been honest about why it ruins you.

The numbers: $3,057 is less than a monthly payment on a mid-range German sedan, roughly a family-office managing partner's weekly lunch. For the median household it is nearly 5 percent of pre-tax income; in California's fire corridors, 9 percent from January 1. An associate had to run that.

"We insure the house only insofar as the owner acknowledges it stands where the climate has decided it does not want houses," said Carla Reyes-Eastman, the pool's chief actuary.

A different framing. Ray should ask whether he needs a house in a canyon. The market is not punishing anyone; it is clarifying. If the price of a roof exceeds the price of a handbag, maybe the roof is the problem, a structure so proud it prices itself out of its own ward. People who cannot afford the insurance cannot afford the house, which is a way of saying they cannot afford the climate, which is true. The rest is squeamishness.

“My insurance went up $1,680 this year. That's the price of a place people want to be. That's not the climate — that's the market.”

— Ray Kaminski
image_alt: A worried cloud with money floats above a priced house.

title: Machines That Cost a Country's GDP Still Can't Book a Table
dek: $106 billion in a quarter. It still can't get a table at eight.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Dierdre Baines, 45, a ratepayer outside Ashburn, is on the hook, and the hook is the demand charge on the residential grid. The seven firms that run the world's computing backbone spent $106 billion on AI infrastructure in the third quarter. Full-year: $690 billion, more than the GDP of Switzerland, Sweden and Belgium combined, roughly the U.S. Medicare budget, on machines that do not yet book a restaurant table without inventing a fake confirmation number.

"The spending is magnificent," said Leonard Torrance of Westwater Capital. "These companies are building the computational equivalent of the interstate highway system."

The side effects are already visible: 460 terawatt-hours this year, 12 percent of national generation, up from 4 percent. Northern Virginia's utility admits it cannot guarantee residential reliability at peak; out West the cooling has drained aquifers. Ratepayers absorb the demand charge.

As it stands, the grid is about to be taken from behind by machines that cannot feed themselves, and the ratepayer is the one holding the lube.

ELECTIONS: One party loses, the other does not win. COMMODITIES: Coffee futures rose. Something about Brazil. ENERGY: Natural gas is up. People are cold. Data centers are not, and they have the grid by the throat.

“The data centers use a lot of power but that's the price of progress. I'll make that trade.”

— Dierdre Baines
image_alt: The towering skyscrapers dwarf the small houses below.

title: Shoppers Pay More for the Same Cereal, Call It an Upgrade
dek: The box got smaller and the price went up. Shoppers call the new box an upgrade.
author: Tessa Nguyen
body:
Marta Lucero watched the pasta she buys climb to $3.49 and assumed it was better. Food-at-home rose 0.4 percent in October; the department sees 2.3 percent for the year. Harold Peavey remembers the moment he stopped worrying what a box of cereal costs. July 2023, the distributor raised a fourth time in eight months; then-operating chief Peavey told pricing to raise shelf price by the increase, plus twelve percent. He assumed customers would switch to the store brand. They did not.

"They just paid it," Peavey said. "That was the moment I realized we had been underpricing food for thirty years."

Today he is chief executive of Atlantic Grocers, a 340-store case study in what the industry calls 'pricing liberation.' His private-label pasta margin is 47 percent; in 2019 it was 22. Nothing changed about the pasta. He took a 24-pack of paper towels from $18.99 to $24.99, a 31 percent increase; unit sales dipped, recovered, then beat the old level. "The customer interpreted the higher price as a signal of quality," he explains, a sentence you could mistype, send to the board, and have signed into law. Gross margin is up 540 basis points; Peavey got a $4.2 million bonus.

"The grocery business is not a charity," he said. "If the customer decides the price is too high, they can eat at a restaurant." Marta strokes the bag of pasta and says nothing.

“The same cereal I bought last year is two dollars more and I don't mind. The company's costs went up — labor, fuel, ingredients. If they didn't raise the price they'd go out of business.”

— Marta Lucero
image_alt: A man beside a star box watches a hand take coins.

title: Let Your Driver Worry About The Pump
dek: The man in the back seat has a driver for that. Diesel is up 64 percent.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Dennis buys the diesel. He pays $6.35 a gallon, up 64 percent; regular $3.84, up 28 percent. These figures were shared with me by Otis Warren, who ships 200 packages a week out of a yard on the south side and seemed to think I would find them alarming. I did not. I found them interesting, as one finds a museum exhibit about a hardship one has never experienced.

I own a 2026 Sovereign A-9 sedan, about $230,000, driven nine hundred miles in eleven months, because I employ Dennis. Dennis handles the fuel. I have no idea what he pays; I assume he has a corporate fuel card, the charge goes up and the finance office pays it. At these prices Dennis is the variable cost, the one thing on the whole car that flexes. I do not think about Dennis the way one does not think about the oil, except Dennis is a fact with a name and a gas bill.

"Fuel is a pass-through line, not a surprise," said Greg Hollister of Meriwether Freight. "When diesel moves, we move the surcharge."

The fuel anxiety that dominates American dinner tables is noise. Real noise for people who drive fifty miles to work and back. But as an investor, noise is opportunity. Meriwether is up 34 percent on a 22 percent surcharge nobody has blinked at. The people who move things are compensated; the people who receive them pay more. That is not a crisis; it is price discovery, and Dennis, who does the discovering at the pump, is a cost center, a person we have priced as overhead.

“Diesel is $6.35 a gallon so of course there's a surcharge. The driver has to fill the tank. If I want my packages on time I pay the surcharge. That's not a crisis — that's arithmetic.”

— Otis Warren, who ships 200 packages a week
image_alt: A fuel-pump umbrella rains drops on a car below.

title: Office Buildings at 48 Cents, Family Office Says Wonderful
dek: A fifth of office loans are underwater. Ruh offers forty-eight cents and expects a yes.
author: Stanwick Ruh
body:
The landlord, a shopkeeper in Jersey City, owes more than his building is worth. I am having the time of my life, and I need you to understand why.

I have been waiting for this since 2022. A fifth of the office loans due in the second half of this year are underwater, the building worth less than the mortgage. Values are down 20 to 35 percent; $1.5 trillion of commercial real estate debt needs refinancing and the banks will not touch it. It is a bloodbath delivered in the exact size and shape I predicted, and I am, without exaggeration, wet.

The market is finally getting honest. Mid-tier offices were liabilities wearing a tie. We sit on $380 million of dry powder with a mandate to buy distressed office at fifty cents, convert to life-science labs, hold five years. Construction costs are reasonable because nobody is building; labor is available because nobody is hiring, the two best reasons for buying anything.

Three properties in Jersey City, one in Stamford. The seller is a bank under a consent order that needs the loans gone by December 31. We are offering forty-eight cents. I think we will get it. The landlord across the street will lose his shop; that is the mechanism. You do not clean house by leaving the dirty dishes in the sink. You throw them out, then you buy the house at the auction, and the house, at last, is yours.
image_alt: A top-hatted man toasts before a cracked skyscraper.

title: Fund Sits on Dry Powder, Discovers the Anxiety of Having It
dek: Eleven months dry, and the money still asks why.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Julian Toth, 54, sat on $340 million of dry powder for the eleventh month and felt the performance anxiety arrive like a thing he had to introduce at a party. He is a partner at a fund that raised the money to deploy it, and the money is ready, loaded, waiting — and every time he swings at a deal, the deal looks back at him the way a man looks at another man's enthusiasm in a dim room.

The partners called it dry powder. Around month nine, money that has not been used starts to question the man holding it. He can deploy at any moment. That is the problem. The ability to act has become the reason he does not. His own fund has begun to measure him by the untouchedness of the pile, as though the money being ready is itself the strategy, and the longer it stays ready the more ready it is.

Toth has started checking the balance at night, the way you check on an investment you are afraid has become a hostage. He has eleven months of dryness and no idea what the money is for, only that the money is still there, and that the staying there has become the whole performance.

“We are sitting on $340 million of powder-keg opportunity.”

— Julian Toth

title: Bid Arrives Unannounced, Board Arms the Shareholder-Defined Pill
dek: $23 became $91 behind a pill.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Gloria Vance, 62, watched the $23 hostile bid arrive the way you watch a stranger turn up at a door that was not locked: the envelope, the price, the name of a company she had not invited. She has held her shares for eight years and planned to hold them eight more, and the board has now made that plan more expensive to interrupt.

The poison pill puts the price at $91 for a share that was trading at $23, plus the cost of pretending the $23 was ever the real number. Gloria has spent the last month learning what a pill is. She knows it as the fake phone number you give someone who will not stop calling: it looks like a way in, and it is, right up until it is a recording playing your own voice back at you.

Rafael Nunez, the lead director who drafted the pill, says it protects the long-term shareholder, by which he means the shareholder who did not buy in the last month, by which he means the board, who own the pill and have never once called it by its effects. Gloria is a long-term shareholder. She would like the $23.

“The pill is the price of being wanted. She just doesn't see it yet.”

— Rafael Nunez, lead director

title: Fund Declares Complacency, Books Run Rate on Stamina
dek: The fund sells the calm as growth.
author: Dana Whitfield
body:
Trent Farber, 44, watched the VIX print 22.11 and felt the calm come off his retirement account like heat off a curb. He has $17,000 in a fund that bills its persistence as a skill. What the fund actually charges for is stamina. It books the calm at run rate: the staying still, capitalized, sold at the same price a volatility fund commands for the lurching.

He called the sales line to ask what he was paying for and was told, slowly, that he was paying for the not reacting. The firm calls it the patience product. It sells the ability to do nothing as the ability to grow, and it measures Trent by the sessions he lets pass without touching the account. This is month fourteen. He has touched the account twice, both times to add money.

On the tape above the story, the market is not moving, and the fund is charging him for the not moving as though the not moving were a yield. The roundest figures in finance are the ones that describe nothing happening. He pays $200 a year to watch the market do nothing and calls the flatness his allocation.

“We don't need the tape to move. We need the acolyte to believe it won't.”

— Paula Werner, the fund's portfolio director

title: Lease Slips in a Covenant, Tenant Reads It as a Premarital Agreement
dek: Yolanda read the lease and found the covenant.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Yolanda Reyes, 39, read the new lease on the shop she has rented for seven years and found the covenant: she cannot open within a mile of Gordon Licht's other property for eighteen months after she leaves. She signed the original lease when she could not afford a lawyer, and she signed the renewal the way you sign a marriage certificate on the way out of the courthouse, believing it is the last time you will sign anything that says you belong to someone.

Licht, who owns the block, describes the fine print as a promise that keeps the neighborhood from making him look bad. The covenant is a prenup written by the richer party, Yolanda read in a tenant-rights pamphlet that itself was published by a landlord. If she leaves, she cannot take her customers with her; the customers, Licht has decided, are the property they both pretend she brought to the marriage.

He calls it protecting the block. She calls it the eighteen months of her working life that now belongs to a man who has never once swept the sidewalk. The rent is up 9 percent this year and the covenant says nothing about the rent, only about her leaving.

“The lease protects me from competition. It doesn't protect her from me.”

— Gordon Licht

title: Bank Cuts the Dividend, Books It as Letting the Retiree Go
dek: Nineteen years of payouts ended with one call.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Dot Ellison, 71, called the dividend line on Thursday and was told the quarterly payout she had collected for nineteen years had been discontinued. She has been a shareholder since 2007, when she bought in at $9.80, and the dividend was the reason she stayed: a check that arrived every three months, small, regular, and hers.

The bank said the buyback, not the dividend, was where the money now went, because buying your own shares is a love you can keep, while paying a dividend is a love you have to keep giving. They called the cut a simplification, the way a marriage is simplified. Dot named it: nineteen years of alimony, paid as a check and now stopped, the closest she had to an income.

She is not selling. The shares are down $4.90 since the announcement, and she has the retired person's conviction that a loss only becomes real when you cash it out, so she is holding a check that no longer comes. The bank's investors cheered the buyback; the retail shareholders, the ones who opened the mail, were simply expected to understand that what was once mine is now theirs.

“In nineteen years the dividend never missed a quarter. Now I was the one who got cut.”

— Dot Ellison

title: CEO Priced to Leave, Companies the Buyout
dek: $12 million to jump. The board holds the chute.
author: Elena Marsh
body:
Rita Soriano, 58, read her own $12 million golden parachute as the board's way of pricing her to leave before it wanted her gone, and she has spent the year packing. The clause is the parachute: it makes the fall look chosen, the way a man strapping on gear calls the ledge a plan. She has the offer in progress, and the board knows it, and nobody in the room will say the word exit where the minutes can hear.

The board calls it retention, which is the polite name for the thing it has priced. Rita calls the parachute the most honest line in her contract — it is the one sentence that tells her exactly what her leaving is worth, and worth is the only number the company ever says without wincing. The buyout was half-assed, she told her brother, the way she says everything she is leaving behind: with both palms flat on the table, priced and ready.

“The $12 million is not severance; it is the board pricing me out before the market does.”

— Rita Soriano
first_sentence: Rita Soriano, 58, read her own $12 million golden parachute
closer: Pays: Rita. She was always priced to leave.
quotes: The $12 million is not severance; it is the board pricing me out before the market does.

title: Her Husband Refinances the Marriage
dek: He remortgages the marriage. She keeps the debt.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
body:
Maureen Tolliver, 58, signed away the $84,000 of equity she had paid into the house, watched her name slide off the note, and let her husband remortgage the marriage in the loan's vocabulary. He refinanced into an account that held only his signature, and the lower payment was the gift he dressed as arithmetic. She had carried the first eight years of that mortgage on a waitress's schedule.

She raised it at dinner. He said a refi is not a divorce, it is an extension, which is how courts mark the thing that looks like a marriage and no longer is one. The equity was now a number that moved in his name, and when she asked where she signed for the half she had paid, the only form left removed the other half without her pen. Fuck the paperwork, she told the mirror afterwards, low enough that no one heard, because she still loved him, and the fight costs more than the mortgage does.

“It is the lower payment that does it — $84,000 in equity, and the marriage remortgaged with one signature.”

— Vance Kettering, the closing agent
first_sentence: Maureen Tolliver, 58, signed away the $84,000 of equity
closer: Pays: Maureen. The signature was hers.
quotes: It is the lower payment that does it — $84,000 in equity, and the marriage remortgaged with one signature.

title: Goodwill Is What You Overpaid. The Impairment Is Morning After
dek: The company wrote off $2.1 billion and called it a refresh.
author: Emmett Voss
figcap: Paid to be a different company. Written off as a refresh.
body:
I am Emmett Voss, a clerk in the goodwill room, and I write the numbers down as they un-matter. On Monday the company decided the $2.1 billion it had paid to be a different company was an error that had finally been noticed, so we wrote it down to zero and called the write-off a refresh, like a coat of paint on a building being demolished. Nobody in the build room believes the number anymore. That is my job to believe it for them. I type it as an asset, then I type it as a loss, and I am the one who has to look at both numbers with the same hands. My supervisor calls it not a loss but an alignment, the word we use for a figure that has changed its mind. When goodwill goes, you are not losing value; you are admitting you were never paying for value — you were paying for the memory of having wanted it. The company is worth $18.3 billion without the goodwill it paid for, which is what it was before it got ambitious.

My prayer is a ledger. It writes: paid. It writes: gone. It never writes: why. Fuck.
first_sentence: I am Emmett Voss, a clerk in the goodwill room, and I write the numbers down as they un-matter.
closer: My prayer is a ledger. It writes: paid. It writes: gone. It never writes: why. Fuck.

title: Comp Package Is a Hand Job
dek: The board calls it retention. He calls it the hand job.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
body:
Walter Odin, 31, opened the compensation package the board had sent to him and read his own raise as the kind of thing you receive with one hand while the other is scribbling your signature. The $1.4 million package extends him two more years, and they wrote the hand job into the print so nobody has to say it out loud. He has fourteen months left on the leash and a mortgage that keeps time.

The board calls it retention. Walter calls the package a hand job on paper — the gesture that is pleasant to pretend is about loyalty, when it is really about the two years you will not be free. He told his wife the number. She asked how much of it he actually keeps, and he had read far enough to know the answer was the part that stops when he stops. Shit, he said, and neither of them could argue with the arithmetic.

“It's a million four to stay two more years. That's what a hand job is for — it makes the staying feel chosen.”

— Meredith Vale, the compensation committee chair
first_sentence: Walter Odin, 31, opened the compensation package the board had sent
quotes: It's a million four to stay two more years. That's what a hand job is for — it makes the staying feel chosen.

title: Portfolio Is Wet. The Rain Is the Print
dek: $240 billion in cash, and the blood is the liquidity.
author: Marcus Reid
body:
Simon Cribb, 52, ran his hand over the $240 billion in cash the fund was now calling liquid, the way a man feels a soaked sleeve and names the weather lucky. The market had swung, the fund had sold into it, and the proceeds sat in the account, wet with the thing they had not been at the top of the cycle: dry powder the size of a small country's deficit.

He is the portfolio manager, which means he is the one who has to say the word seriously every quarter without being a joke. The cash is liquid, they told the investor call, and Simon thought about how the wettest thing in finance is the thing that used to be yours before you needed it to stay. Cunt, he wrote in the margin beside the word liquidity, then erased it, because the minutes get read and the hand he was filling jobs no one applauds.

“We are $240 billion liquid, which means we are wet with the cash we no longer trust.”

— Simon Cribb
first_sentence: Simon Cribb, 52, ran his hand over the $240 billion in cash
closer: Pays: Simon. The cash is not his.
quotes: We are $240 billion liquid, which means we are wet with the cash we no longer trust.

title: Rights Issue Passes the Hat, Keeps Every Bit of the Change
dek: The firm needs cash. The shareholders hold the hat.
author: Omar Zayed
body:
Sofia Marchetti, 61, read the rights issue as a hat passed at her kitchen table, and she held it long enough to feel how light it was. The company needed $90 million, and the right to buy more of a thing she already owned thinly was being offered to her as a favor, the way a waiter offers you the check and calls it the experience. She had held the shares since 2004, through two boom-and-busts and one proud statement about discipline.

The notice called it an opportunity to participate. Sofia called it passing the hat, and the hat had already been around the room before it got to her: the board had subscribed first, at the bottom price, the way the house always takes its cut before the game. Asshole, she said to the letter, with real affection, because after twenty years she was too far in to leave and too honest to pretend the hat had not been passed at her before.

“The $90 million is for the company. The hat is how we let her pay for it.”

— Gerard Foley, the board chairman
first_sentence: Sofia Marchetti, 61, read the rights issue as a hat passed at her kitchen table
closer: Pays: Sofia. The hat gets heavier.
quotes: The $90 million is for the company. The hat is how we let her pay for it.

title: Bank Buries the Overdraft in the Fine Print
dek: The fee is one overdue transfer deep. She keeps the notice.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
first_sentence: Mabel Osei, 57, opened the envelope about the account change and read to the bottom of the second page before the overdraft fee surfaced.
closer: Pays: Mabel. The fine print wins.
quotes: They know which transfer is going to catch me. They just moved the $39 where I can't see it.
body:
Mabel Osei, 57, opened the envelope about the account change and read to the bottom of the second page before the overdraft fee surfaced. The fee is up to $39, buried in a paragraph about electronic transfers. She pays it once, short one transfer on a Tuesday, and the fee is now larger than the shortfall that caused it. She keeps the notice.

The bank calls the nine-dollar increase a maintenance adjustment. Mabel calls it the fine print doing its job. Her checking balance does not cover her gas and her groceries in the same week, and the bank knows the exact day of the month the hit lands, the shit-timing of it clockwork. The notice arrived on the first. The overdraft came on the ninth. "They know which transfer is going to catch me. They just moved the $39 where I can't see it."

Mabel reads the notice twice and files the paper with the year's others, the whole stack a shit ledger of what the bank took and what she let it.

title: Index Fund Shunts the Loss Onto the Fee
dek: The index fell. The fee rose, the bitch of it.
author: Tessa Nguyen
first_sentence: Darnell Okoye, 44, opened his statement on a red month and found the index down four percent and his fee up half a point.
closer: Pays: Darnell. The ratio moved with it.
quotes: You pay the ratio to own the market. Four grand is the toll, and the road still gets you there.
body:
Darnell Okoye, 44, opened his statement on a red month and found the index down four percent and his fee up half a point. The fund bills the loss back through the expense ratio, charging twice for the same trip when the road got worse. He pays for the tracking error twice, once when the market drops and once in the management line.

The prospectus calls it a cost of doing business. Darnell calls it the seams showing. He held the fund for nine years and never saw the ratio move on a good month, a shit trick the fund keeps for the ledger. The down months are where the arithmetic finds him. His $142,000 is $4,000 lighter than the market says it should be, and the gap is billed, not borrowed.

His neighbor Lester Poole, 61, who holds the same fund and reads the same statement, defends the fee on the landing.

“You pay the ratio to own the market. Four grand is the toll, and the road still gets you there.”

— Lester Poole, 61, his neighbor

The road did not move. The fund just charged the toll for it, then held the rate for the next quarter so the same four grand could be billed again. Darnell turns his own statement face down on the table. Fuck.

title: Firm Takes the Bonus Back From the Severance
dek: The check costs him $14,000 before he can read the total.
author: Omar Zayed
first_sentence: Terrance Boyd, 51, was laid off in June with eleven weeks' pay and a clause that let the company claw back his signing bonus if he left before the year was up.
closer: Pays: Terrance. The old signature did the work.
quotes: You sign for the bonus and you sign for the exit, and they bill you the $14,000 for the middle.
body:
Terrance Boyd, 51, was laid off in June with eleven weeks' pay and a clause that let the company claw back his signing bonus if he left before the year was up. They counted the layoff as the leaving. The severance check arrived with $14,000 already taken out of it, and the note called it a recovery of compensation. He did not sign anything new. The old signature did the work.

The company calls it protecting shareholder value. Terrance calls it the one time his badge was worth something, and it was worth exactly the $14,000 they kept. The job had been his for six years. The bonus was his for four of them. The clause outlived both, a shitty little signature he signed in his twenties.

“You sign for the bonus and you sign for the exit, and they bill you for the middle.”

— Terrance Boyd

Terrance files the notice, calls the clause shit, and lets the old signature stand.

title: Rate Keeps the House, the Bank Holds the Key
dek: The refi cost more than a year of the savings she was promised.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
first_sentence: Corinne Hale, 49, refinanced in May to take a full point off her mortgage, and by November the new rate is what the bank says it is and the math does not reach her.
closer: Pays: Corinne. The break-even moves with her.
quotes: The $2,100 in closing costs was a gift with a ticket. I bought the ticket and the gift stayed in the shop.
body:
Corinne Hale, 49, refinanced in May to take a full point off her mortgage, and by November the new rate is what the bank says it is and the math does not reach her. The closing costs, the appraisal, the new title insurance, the points, they add up to more than the first year of the savings. She keeps paying the old number anyway. The bank holds the key to the lower rate and charges admission.

The lender calls it the cost of a better position. Corinne calls it a revolving door she paid to walk through. Her payment is $118 lower than it was, but she paid $2,100 to get there, and the break-even lands past her plans. She did the arithmetic in the kitchen with a receipt from the closing and a shit calculator she has to press twice because her hands never stop.

“The rate was a gift with a ticket. I bought the ticket and the gift stayed in the shop.”

— Corinne Hale

Corinne presses the calculator twice, calls the break-even shit, and reruns it.

title: Rent Is Up and the Stairs Work
dek: A landlord keeps eleven percent and calls the cracked step an investment.
author: Ansel Whitby
role: Landlord, six units on North Margin
first_sentence: I raise the rent on North Margin every spring and I am not ashamed of it.
body:
I raise the rent on North Margin every spring and I am not ashamed of it. The stairs work. That is the part nobody books. I took eleven percent across the six units this year and I mapped it out for the tenants: three points to the boiler, two to the shared porch, the rest to the building doing what I said it would do. Meanwhile I live down the block and I look at the same cracked step I look at every morning, and I am shit at ever fixing it.

My tenants call it a family building. I call it six payments and one of them is going to be late, and that late one is the one I planned the year around. The boiler works because the rent pays for it, and the porch works because the rent pays for it, and the step I keep meaning to fix is the difference between what I keep and what I spend on keeping.

I am proud of the win. The rent went up and the stairs work, and those two facts sit on the same shelf. Shit, the step is still cracked.

title: The Bag Fee Is Now 40 Cents on the Curbside Can
dek: The cans cost $4.80 a week to throw away the same weight.
author: Elena Marsh
first_sentence: Rosa Nduta carries her cans to the curb and the bag fee climbs another dime.
body: Rosa Nduta carries her cans to the curb and the bag fee climbs another dime this quarter, to $0.40. The average bin is twelve bags, which makes the fee $4.80 a week, or $250 a year, for the privilege of throwing away the same weight, a shit bargain Rosa pays twice a week. The county calls it a recovery fee. The hauler calls it a line item. Nobody calls it a raise for Rosa. Forty cents a bag. Shit.
figcap: A fee, added at the curb, billed on the hauler's line.

title: The Hauler Bills the Curb and Keeps the Truck
dek: The monthly rate is up $38. Rosa carries the can either way.
author: Marcus Reid
first_sentence: Rosa Nduta, 62, lifts her can to the curb on Thursday the way she always has, and the hauler bills her $38 more this month than last.
closer: Pays: Rosa. The can is heavier.
quotes: If the truck comes either way, the billing is what you notice, $38 at a time. The route covers itself.
body:
Rosa Nduta, 62, lifts her can to the curb on Thursday the way she always has, and the hauler bills her $38 more this month than last. The truck still stops, the arm still lifts, and the can goes into the same hopper. The company says the rate now covers the route. Rosa asks which end of the route the money covers.

The tidy haul is the one thing she pays for outright, after the tax and the county fee and the bag surcharge. She keeps the receipt in the drawer with the ones from last year, and the numbers do not match. Rosa keeps a shit ledger of what the curb costs now. Last year the same can cost her $19 off the curb. This year the number is up again, and the service is not. Her neighbor pays the same rate and leaves the same three bags, and Rosa gives him her receipt to hold up next to his own.

“If the truck comes either way, the billing is what you notice, $38 at a time. The route covers itself.”

— Rosa Nduta, 62, who lives off the route

Rosa lifts the can with both hands and pays it anyway. The route covers someone, and it is not her route. Fuck.

title: Heir Forced to Pay $41 Million Because His Dad Owned a Utility
dek: Bartholomew Finch-Duarte paid $41 million and now wants the money back, understands what it was for.
author: Elena Marsh
first_sentence: Bartholomew Finch-Duarte, 61, paid the $41 million estate tax on his father's utility business and has since described the payment as a fee for everything his father owned, which he has confirmed includes him.
body:
Bartholomew Finch-Duarte, 61, paid the $41 million estate tax on his father's utility business and has since described the payment as a fee for everything his father owned, which he has confirmed includes him. The tax was due in full before the will could be read. Mr. Finch-Duarte paid it from an account set up for exactly that purpose by the man whose estate the account was now taxing, and the setup has struck him as needlessly personal.

The business was a utility his father assembled over sixty years and three mergers. The tax ate 23 percent of a figure the accountants had been careful to make large. Mr. Finch-Duarte has quoted the 23 percent at every dinner since, describing it as the amount the state charged for the privilege of his father having planned.

Mr. Finch-Duarte told his lawyer he had no idea what went into a bill that big; the lawyer walked him through it the previous week. When the lawyer explained that the bill was the market value of the assets, Mr. Finch-Duarte described it as the state valuing his father's life at the price of the father's house and his own inheritance at the price of the rest.

He has kept every page of the filing, including the page that itemizes the deduction for the exact amount the estate spent on the accountants who arranged for the deduction. When that was explained to him he said the state had found a way to tax his father twice for the same person and had credited the estate for half of it, the cunts. The estate has not moved on, and neither has Mr. Finch-Duarte, who is still in the house the tax almost took, using a stapler his father used on a document the stapler helped produce almost forty years ago.

title: Lost $19 Million and Wished It Had Been a Subscription
dek: Mona Voss thinks the money is down, says the arrangement is not losing, it is subscribing.
author: Priya Sharma
role: Washington Bureau, Fed & Rates, plus household costs (insurance, mortgages)
first_sentence: Mona Voss, 59, lost 12 percent of a nine-figure portfolio this year and has described the loss as a subscription, which she says she did not cancel because she forgot it was one.
body:
Mona Voss, 59, lost 12 percent of a nine-figure portfolio this year and has described the loss as a subscription, which she says she did not cancel because she forgot it was one. The amount was $19 million. She has confirmed that if it were a subscription she would have canceled it, but that the people who manage the money described it to her as a loss and she took their word for it.

The money is managed by a firm that sends a quarterly report. The report calls the 12 percent a drawdown and recommends against reacting, which Ms. Voss adopted in full and has since described as the most useful paragraph in her financial life. She keeps the report on the same nightstand as the subscription bills she does not read, and once confused the two.

Ms. Voss has asked whether it turns out she was subscribing to her own losses the whole time, and if so she would like the canceled checks back. Her advisor told the press the firm has no record of Ms. Voss purchasing a subscription, but that the firm does charge a fee every quarter regardless of whether the money makes money, which he said is a different arrangement.

Ms. Voss has asked whether the fee is what she is subscribing to. The advisor said no. Ms. Voss said she would like that in writing, and the advisor said the firm does not put that in writing, which Ms. Voss accepted, because a 12 percent loss, in her view, is the closest thing the market has to a refund that arrives every year and is always on time, and she is not pissed about it.

title: Founder Locked in Own Stock 4 Years, Says the Water's Cold
dek: Rafferty cannot sell his shares for five years, says his best years are in there.
author: Marcus Reid
first_sentence: Rafferty O'Dell, 44, called the five-year lockup on his own company's shares a pool when the deal was signed, and has spent three of those years in it, unable to sell, describing the water as cold.
body:
Rafferty O'Dell, 44, called the five-year lockup on his own company's shares a pool when the deal was signed, and has spent three of those years in it, unable to sell, describing the water as cold. The pool was his own idea. He proposed the lockup to the investors as a sign of confidence, and has since confirmed that the confidence was real at the time and that he would like out of the pool now.

The company's stock listed at $38 and trades at $14. Mr. O'Dell's shares are worth roughly $41 million on paper and cannot be sold until the fourth quarter of next year, which he has described as the quarter the pool empties. He has asked the board twice whether the pool could be drained early. The board said no.

Mr. O'Dell told a conference he had built a good pool. The conference was about AI, not liquidity, which he noted after he had finished speaking. He told reporters that the pool is cold because he built it in the winter of the deal, and that he has spent the time since trying to build a heater.

The heater is a second offering the company filed for, which would dilute his shares further but raise the cash he cannot access any other way. Mr. O'Dell has described the trade as heating the pool with the water in the pool, which is a bastard of a plan. When it was pointed out that this would make the pool colder, he said that was exactly the kind of cold the pool was already, and that he had gotten used to it, which he described as the entire problem.

title: Man Owns 3,000 Companies and Hates Every One of Them
dek: Salvador Kane owns the stock market and would prefer none, but the tax bill stops him.
author: Tessa Nguyen
first_sentence: Salvador Kane, 71, owns the stock market through 17 index funds and has told his advisor that he hates every company in them without exception, and that this is not going to change.
body:
Salvador Kane, 71, owns the stock market through 17 index funds and has told his advisor that he hates every company in them without exception, and that this is not going to change. His funds hold stakes in several thousand firms, for one of which Mr. Kane's son works. Mr. Kane has confirmed the fund holds the son's company and that he reinvests the dividends from it on principle.

The 17 funds cost $30 million a year in total. Mr. Kane does not know which fund owns what and has said he prefers it that way, because if he knew, he would have sold the ones holding companies he hates, which is all of them.

Mr. Kane told his advisor that he has looked at the statements and been told he owns it all, that he believes he owns it all, and that he would like it back in cash, who explained that selling everything would trigger a taxable event larger than Mr. Kane's annual income. Mr. Kane described this as the only reason he has not sold, and the advisor confirmed the reasoning was exactly that.

He asked whether the market had any companies he would like, since he owns all of them. The advisor said a handful. Mr. Kane said the handful were not worth seeing the statement. He has held the funds for 31 years and calls it diversification, which he has described as the asshole method by which he owns things he hates and is unable to sell them.

title: Margin Call Forces Rothko Sale, Owner Thanks Bank for the Exercise
dek: Phineas Grant sold a quarter of his art to cover margin, says market made him fitter.
author: Claire Reyes
role: Debt & Fixed Income, plus consumer credit
first_sentence: Phineas Grant, 58, was margin called on Wednesday and has described the call as a workout he did not sign up for, before selling a quarter of his art collection to complete it.
body:
Phineas Grant, 58, was margin called on Wednesday and has described the call as a workout he did not sign up for, before selling a quarter of his art collection to complete it. The call was for $12 million in collateral on a mortgage-style loan against his portfolio, which the bank said had fallen below the loan's coverage ratio for the second time this year.

Mr. Grant transferred the $12 million in cash by lunch. To do so he sold a Rothko he had owned since 1998, and has described the painting's departure as the market forcing him to make room. He has confirmed the room is a smaller office he was going to rent anyway.

'It is a good lesson, that the money has to move when the number moves,' Mr. Grant told the dinner party. The dinner party was in the smaller office. He described the reduced square footage as the market helping him decide what mattered, and the bank confirmed it did not intend to help him decide anything.

He has asked whether the margin call could happen again next month. The bank said it could. Mr. Grant said that was fine, that a workout a man can schedule is a workout a man can train for, and that he already had the trainers, which he said was the shit payment he was making for the privilege of being margin called on his own terms.

title: Woman Who Paid $55 Million in Fees Isn't Sure What For
dek: Aurelia Somerset paid fees for 24 years, would like the money to know it is safe.
author: Jake Sullivan
first_sentence: Aurelia Somerset, 63, has paid $2.3 million a year in management fees for 24 years without reading the agreements, and has described the payments as the light she leaves on so the money knows it is safe.
body:
Aurelia Somerset, 63, has paid $2.3 million a year in management fees for 24 years without reading the agreements, and has described the payments as the light she leaves on so the money knows it is safe. The money is in two buildings, a trust, and a desk she visits quarterly. She has confirmed the money has never once required a light to find any of them.

The fees total roughly $55 million over the course of her adult life, a figure the advisor's firm confirmed without embarrassment. Ms. Somerset has never asked what the fee is for, and confirmed she does not intend to start asking, because in her experience asking what a thing is for is the fastest way to find out the thing was for her.

Ms. Somerset said that as long as there is a building the money is in, she feels fine. The building is managed by the firm that charges the fee. She said that was the arrangement and that she had stopped interrogating the arrangement the year the money lost 18 percent and the bollocks fee still arrived, which she said was the money's way of staying in touch.

She keeps the quarterly statements stacked on the desk the money is in, unopened, which she said was the desk's entire purpose. When asked what she thinks the money is doing, Ms. Somerset said the money is where it is supposed to be, and she does not check on money that knows where it belongs, because a person who checks on money is a person who does not trust it, and a person who does not trust it is a person who did not leave the light on, which is bollocks.

title: Billionaire Calls His 20% Cut a Tip, Has Tipped Nobody Since 1987
dek: Cecil Hartigan takes $10 billion off the top and sees no reason the waiter costs him.
author: Omar Zayed
first_sentence: Cecil Hartigan, 68, of Greenwich, calls the 20 percent he takes from every fund a tip, and has spent four decades maintaining that the tip is money he does not actually have to tip anyone with.
body:
Cecil Hartigan, 68, of Greenwich, calls the 20 percent he takes from every fund a tip, and has spent four decades maintaining that the tip is money he does not actually have to tip anyone with. Over his career that 20 percent has come to roughly $10 billion. He has never once left one for a waiter, a driver, or the people who built the companies the tip is taken from, and he tells the people who ask that the tip does not work like that.

Mr. Hartigan earns the percentage whether the fund that pays it makes money or not. It is calculated on the capital a fund raises, not on what it returns, a detail he has described as the real generosity. When a portfolio company the fund owned went bankrupt last year, the 20 percent on the sum that entered the company was already collected.

'You leave the 20 on the table and the good money finds it,' Mr. Hartigan told the industry dinner. The 20 was not left on any table. It was wired to a management entity that does not appear in the fund's marketing materials, which he has called getting the tip while the room is still open.

He has two homes, a staff, and a standing reservation at a restaurant he has never once had to describe as expensive. When asked what the money actually buys, Mr. Hartigan said the money buys the position from which the tip is taken, and that the position is the whole point. The whole thing functions on the premise that a waiter who never receives a fucking tip will keep serving, because the waiter does not know what the percentage was.
